teile.einleitung: Cholera is a dangerous diarrhoeal disease caused by bacteria. In the 19th century it spread in several great waves from India as far as Europe. The fight against it led to clean drinking water and modern sewer systems.
wichtigste: From 1817 cholera spread out from Bengal in India.
In 1854 John Snow showed in London that cholera is passed on through water.
In 1883 Robert Koch identified the germ and made it well known.
In 1892 an epidemic hit Hamburg hard, because the drinking water was not filtered.
Max von Pettenkofer is regarded as the founder of scientific hygiene.
In 1867 over 500 people died of cholera in the canton of Zurich.

abschnitte.text: **Cholera** is caused by a **bacterium**. People catch it above all through dirty **drinking water**. The disease causes severe diarrhoea, and the body loses a great deal of water. The first great wave, a **pandemic**, began in 1817 in **Bengal** in the Ganges delta in India. From 1830 the disease reached Europe too.

The London doctor **John Snow** suspected that cholera is passed on through water. In 1854 he marked the deaths in the district of Soho on a **map**. They clustered around a **water pump** in Broad Street. After the handle of the pump was removed, the epidemic died down. Snow's map is regarded as an early example of research into epidemics.

The Italian Filippo Pacini had described the bacterium as early as 1854, but hardly anyone paid attention to him. The German doctor **Robert Koch** identified the germ in 1883 on an expedition to Egypt and India and made it well known. The Munich doctor **Max von Pettenkofer** received the first professorship of **hygiene** in 1865. He campaigned for sewers and clean water. He doubted Koch's germ theory, however.

In the hot summer of 1858 the polluted Thames in London stank unbearably. This was called the **Great Stink**. Afterwards the engineer Joseph Bazalgette built a modern **sewage system**, which also held cholera in check. In 1892 an epidemic hit **Hamburg** hard, because the city used unfiltered water from the Elbe. In the neighbouring town of Altona, which had a **sand filtration plant**, far fewer people fell ill. In Hamburg about 8,600 people died.

Switzerland was not spared either. In 1867 cholera was brought in via Italy. In the **canton of Zurich** over 500 people died, mostly from poorer parts of the population. The epidemic strengthened the calls for reforms in **public health** and for a better water supply.

gewusst: Today cholera can be treated well, above all by giving the body back plenty of water with salt and sugar.
In 1892 Max von Pettenkofer even drank a cholera culture to prove his view.

teile.einleitung: Fascism is a political movement and form of rule that came into being in the 20th century. It rejects democracy and freedom and relies on an all-powerful leader, a single party and exaggerated nationalism. The first fascists to come to power were those under Benito Mussolini in Italy.
wichtigste: The word comes from the Italian “fascio”, bundle, and recalls the Roman bundles of rods.
Benito Mussolini founded the fascist movement in 1919 in Milan.
Typical are the leader principle and a one-party dictatorship.
The uniformed fighting squads of the Italian fascists were called Blackshirts.
The authoritarian corporate state in Austria from 1933 to 1938 is often called Austrofascism.
In Switzerland there was the so-called Fronts' spring in 1933, but the Fronts remained a minority.
The historian Roger Griffin sees at the core a populist ultranationalism with the idea of a national rebirth.

abschnitte.text: The word fascism comes from the Italian **fascio**, which means bundle. It also means the bundles of rods with an axe that the attendants of high officials carried in ancient Rome. They were a sign of power and the right to punish. Mussolini made this bundle of rods the symbol of his movement.

Benito Mussolini founded a fighting league in 1919 in Milan. With the **March on Rome** in October 1922 he put pressure on the king, who named him head of government. By 1926 he built up a dictatorship, banned other parties and had himself called “Duce”, leader. His **Blackshirts** threatened and beat up political opponents.

Fascism includes the **leader principle**, a one-party dictatorship and the suppression of free newspapers. The state is to decide everything, and the individual counts for little. Violence against opponents is glorified, and so are war and conquest. The historian Roger Griffin describes the core as a populist ultranationalism that promises a national rebirth.

Similar movements came into being in many countries of Europe. In Austria an authoritarian corporate state ruled from 1933 to 1938, which scholars often call **Austrofascism**. It is disputed whether German National Socialism should also be called fascism. Many experts stress that racist antisemitism played a far more central role there and led to the genocide of the Jews.

After Hitler's appointment as Chancellor in 1933 far-right groups in Switzerland too experienced an upswing, the **Fronts' spring**. In 1933 the National Front won 10 seats on the city council in Zurich. In 1935 the Fronts supported an initiative for a total revision of the Federal Constitution, but the voters rejected it clearly. After that the Fronts quickly lost importance.

Fascism led Italy alongside Germany into the Second World War. In 1943 Mussolini was removed from power, and in April 1945 he was killed by resistance fighters. After the war the fascist party was banned in Italy. To this day people remember the victims so that something like this does not happen again, and groups with similar ideas are called **neo-fascists**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule in which one person or group has all the power and the people may not freely have a say.
The idea that a single leader decides and everyone must obey.
The attitude of putting your own people above all others.
Far-right groups in Switzerland in the 1930s.

gewusst: The bundle of rods of the ancient Romans can still be seen today in the coat of arms of the canton of St Gallen.
Before the First World War Mussolini was a member of the Socialist Party and a journalist on a socialist newspaper.
The term “fascism” is often used as an insult today, but experts use it only for very particular movements.

teile.einleitung: A factory is a large business in which many people make goods in great quantities with machines. The first factories came into being in the 18th century in England and changed people's lives so strongly that we speak of an industrial revolution.
wichtigste: The first factories came into being in the textile industry, where yarn was spun and cloth was woven.
Important inventions were the Spinning Jenny of 1764, the water frame of 1769 and the power loom of 1784.
Before factories many families worked at home for a merchant.
In the factory there is a division of labour: everyone does only one particular step.
Factory workers at first often worked 12 to 16 hours a day, children too.
Many people moved to the factory towns, which is called urbanisation.
Henry Ford introduced the assembly line in car production in 1913.

abschnitte.text: In the past yarn and cloth were mostly made at home. Whole families spun and wove as **outworkers** for a merchant, who brought them the raw materials and collected the finished goods. They worked with a spinning wheel and a hand loom. This was slow, and the amount was limited.

In the 18th century tinkerers in England invented machines that worked much faster. James Hargreaves built the **Spinning Jenny** in 1764, with which one person could spin many threads at the same time. Richard Arkwright invented the **water frame** in 1769, a spinning machine that ran on water power. Edmund Cartwright developed a power loom in 1784. Later steam engines, which James Watt had greatly improved, drove the machines.

Because the big machines did not fit into a living room, special buildings were built for them beside rivers. In 1771 Arkwright opened one of the first cotton mills driven by water power in Cromford. The English city of **Manchester** became the centre of the textile industry because of its many cotton factories. A **factory regulation** set the working hours, duties and punishments of the workers.

Factory workers often worked 12 to 16 hours a day, six days a week. Even small children had to work, because they were cheap and fitted between the machines. Pay was low, the air full of dust and accidents common. Many families lived in cramped, dirty flats, for through **urbanisation** the towns grew very fast.

Around 1811 and 1812 workers in England destroyed machines because they feared for their jobs. They are called **machine breakers** or Luddites. Gradually laws were passed that limited child labour and working hours. In Switzerland the federal Factory Act of 1877 banned factory work for children under 14 and introduced the eleven-hour day.

In 1913 Henry Ford introduced the **assembly line** in car production in the USA. The car moved from worker to worker, and each fitted only a few parts. In this way the Model T became much cheaper. Today robots and computers work in many factories, and people monitor and control the plants.

begriffe.erklaerung: Work is divided into small steps, and each person does only one of them.
The time when machines and factories more and more replaced handwork.
Work that you do at home for a client.
A moving belt on which the workpiece travels from one workplace to the next.

gewusst: The Spinning Jenny is said to be named after the daughter or wife of James Hargreaves, but this is not at all certain.
Thanks to the assembly line the time to build a Ford Model T fell from over twelve hours to about an hour and a half.
In the first factories there was often a big bell that announced the start of work, and anyone who came late had money taken from their pay.

teile.einleitung: A digital camera takes photos without film. It stores the pictures as data, and you can look at them straight away on a screen.
wichtigste: A digital camera stores photos on a memory card.
A digital picture is made of many tiny picture points, the pixels.
One megapixel is a million picture points.
Steven Sasson built the first digital camera in 1975 at the firm Kodak.
Its first picture was black and white.
A great advantage is that you see the photo at once.

abschnitte.text: Light falls through the **lens** into the camera. There it hits an **image sensor**, a small chip with millions of light-sensitive points. Each point measures how much light arrives. From this the camera works out a picture. This is stored as a **file** on a **memory card**. Older cameras needed **film** for this.

A digital picture is made of many tiny coloured points. These points are called **pixels**, a word that means picture element. If you look at a photo greatly enlarged, you can see the little squares. One **megapixel** is a million picture points, because “mega” means million. The more pixels a picture has, the more detail it can show.

The engineer **Steven Sasson** built the first digital camera in 1975 at the firm **Kodak**. It was about as big as a **toaster** and quite heavy. It only took small **black-and-white pictures**. To store a single picture it needed over 20 seconds. It was stored on a cassette of the kind used for music.

abschnitte.titel: From film to the mobile phone
abschnitte.text: With a film camera you first had to have the pictures **developed**. Only then did you see whether they had turned out well. With a digital camera you see the photo **at once** on the screen and can delete failed pictures. From about 2000 digital cameras became more and more popular. Today almost every **mobile phone** has a digital camera in it, and many people take photos with it every day.

gewusst: Kodak, of all firms, the maker of the first digital camera, earned its money for a long time mainly from film and later got into great difficulty.
The word pixel comes from the English words “picture” and “element”.

teile.einleitung: The potato is one of the most important foods in the world today. It originally comes from South America. It only reached Europe and Switzerland a few hundred years ago.
wichtigste: The potato comes from South America.
What people eat is the tuber, which grows under the ground.
In many Swiss dialects it is called Härdöpfel.
A well-known Swiss potato dish is rösti.
It became important because it is filling and grows well.
Green patches and the fruits of the plant are poisonous.

abschnitte.text: The potato comes from **South America**. In the Andes people grew it thousands of years ago. The **Incas** also knew many different varieties. In the 16th century the Spanish brought the potato to Europe. At first many people were suspicious and thought of it more as an ornamental plant.

From the potato plant people eat the **tuber**. It grows under the ground and stores nutrients, above all **starch**. The parts above ground, the small green fruits and patches of the tuber that have turned green contain the poison **solanine**. That is why potatoes are eaten cooked and green patches are cut away. The potato belongs to the **nightshade family**, like the tomato and the pepper.

The potato became very important in Europe because it is **filling** and also **grows well** on poor soil. On one field you harvest more food with potatoes than with many kinds of grain. In the 18th century it spread widely, in Switzerland too. In times of famine it saved the lives of many people. When the potato harvest failed, however, as in Ireland in the 1840s, severe famines followed.

In many Swiss dialects people say **Härdöpfel**, that is, “earth apple”. The best-known Swiss potato dish is **rösti**, made of grated potatoes fried until crisp in a pan. **Gschwellti**, potatoes boiled in their skins, are also popular, for example with cheese. Potatoes also go with raclette. Many potatoes are still grown in Switzerland today.

gewusst: “Röstigraben” is a joking name for the border between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.
There are several thousand varieties of potato worldwide, with yellow, white, red or even purple flesh.

teile.einleitung: Gerardus Mercator was one of the most famous cartographers in history. His world map of 1569 helped sailors to navigate, and the word “atlas” for a book of maps goes back to him.
wichtigste: Gerardus Mercator was a cartographer: he drew maps and built globes.
He lived from 1512 to 1594.
In 1569 he presented his famous world map.
On his map, sailors could draw their course as a straight line.
Countries near the poles, such as Greenland, look far too big.
Mercator lived in Duisburg for many years.
The word “atlas” for a book of maps goes back to him.

abschnitte.text: Gerardus Mercator was born in **1512** in Rupelmonde in Flanders, in present-day Belgium. He studied and learned to draw **maps** and build **globes**. He was a **cartographer**, that is, an expert in maps. In **1552** he moved to **Duisburg**. There he worked until his death in **1594**.

A **sphere** cannot be spread out flat without **distortion**. You notice this if you try to lay an orange peel flat on the table. So no flat map can show the Earth completely correctly. Either the **sizes** are wrong, or the **shapes** and **angles** are distorted. Mapmakers have to decide what matters most to them. This method of putting a sphere onto a flat surface is called **projection**.

In **1569** Mercator presented his large **world map**. He chose a projection in which the **angles** are correct. That is why the map was especially useful for **sailors**. They could draw their course as a **straight line** and always sail in the same direction with a compass. This kind of map is still called the **Mercator projection**. Many online map programs also use a similar display.

The Mercator map has a drawback: the nearer a country is to the **poles**, the bigger it looks. **Greenland** therefore looks huge, almost as big as Africa. In reality, Africa is many times bigger. Europe, too, looks bigger than it is compared with countries near the **equator**. Switzerland is closer to the equator than Greenland and is therefore enlarged less.

Mercator collected many maps in one book. He called this collection an **“atlas”**, after a figure from ancient legends. The complete work appeared shortly after his death. Since then, books of maps have been called an **atlas**. At school too you use an atlas to find the countries, rivers and mountains of the world.

gewusst: Mercator was actually called Gerard de Kremer. “Mercator” is the Latin form of his name and means merchant.
Africa is about fourteen times as big as Greenland, although the two look similar in size on the Mercator map.

teile.einleitung: The General Strike of 12 to 14 November 1918 was the biggest strike in the history of Switzerland. Around 250,000 workers downed tools to demand better living conditions and more say. The Federal Council had the army march in, and the country was deeply divided.
wichtigste: The General Strike took place from 12 to 14 November 1918, shortly after the end of the First World War.
It was led by the Olten Action Committee under the Social Democrat Robert Grimm.
Around 250,000 people took part in the strike.
The Federal Council and the army command called up around 95,000 soldiers as troops to keep order.
On 14 November 1918 soldiers in Grenchen shot three young watchmakers.
The Action Committee called off the strike after an ultimatum from the Federal Council.
Some demands were met later, such as proportional elections to the National Council in 1919 and the AVS in 1948.

abschnitte.titel: Hardship in the First World War
abschnitte.text: In the First World War from 1914 to 1918 Switzerland was not drawn into the fighting, yet many people suffered great hardship. Food became scarce and ever more expensive, but wages hardly rose. During the long **active service** soldiers received no compensation for lost wages, so their families often became poor. At the same time some firms and traders made a lot of money from the war. At the end of 1918 about one person in six in Switzerland depended on help to buy food.

abschnitte.titel: From the call-up of troops to the strike
abschnitte.text: At the beginning of November 1918 the Federal Council and General Ulrich Wille feared an overthrow like the one in Russia. They therefore had troops march into **Zurich**. The workers felt this as a provocation and answered with a protest strike. The **Olten Action Committee**, a leadership made up of trade unions and the Social Democratic Party, then called an open-ended General Strike for 12 November.

The strikers drew up nine demands. They included the immediate re-election of the National Council under the **proportional system**, **women’s suffrage** and the 48-hour week. They also demanded old-age and disability insurance, a better supply of food and a reform of the army. Many of these ideas were new and controversial at the time.

On 12 November factories, trains and trams stood still, above all in the cities and industrial towns. The Federal Council called up around 95,000 soldiers as **troops to keep order**, many of them farmers’ sons from the countryside. In Grenchen soldiers fired on demonstrators on 14 November and killed three young watchmakers. On 13 November the Federal Council issued an **ultimatum**, and the Action Committee then called off the strike. During the deployment, numerous soldiers also died of the Spanish flu.

After the strike Robert Grimm and other leaders were sentenced to prison by a military court. But as early as 1919 the National Council was elected early under proportional representation, which brought the Social Democrats many seats. The 48-hour week in factories also came in 1919. The **AVS** was introduced in 1948, and women’s suffrage at federal level only in 1971. The General Strike is now seen as an important turning point on the way to the Swiss welfare state.

begriffe.erklaerung: Workers down tools together to push through demands.
An electoral system in which the parties get as many seats as match their share of the vote.
A final demand with a deadline, after which force or punishment is threatened.
Old-age and survivors’ insurance, which pays pensions to older people in Switzerland.
Soldiers who are meant to ensure peace and order in their own country.

gewusst: The Landesstreik is often also called the “Generalstreik”, because almost all sectors were meant to strike at the same time.
More soldiers died of the Spanish flu during the deployment than people were killed by gunfire.
Robert Grimm, the strike leader, later even became President of the National Council.

teile.einleitung: John Calvin was a French theologian and one of the most important reformers. He lived from 1509 to 1564 and worked for most of his life in Geneva. His teaching shaped Reformed churches in Switzerland, France, the Netherlands, Scotland and North America.
wichtigste: Calvin was born in 1509 in Noyon in France.
In 1536 he published his main work, the “Institutes of the Christian Religion”, in Basel.
In 1536 Guillaume Farel persuaded him to stay in Geneva.
In 1538 Calvin was expelled from Geneva and went to Strasbourg.
His teaching on predestination is especially well known.
Under his influence, strict rules for conduct and church attendance applied in Geneva.
In 1559 he founded the Geneva Academy, the forerunner of the University of Geneva.
Calvin died in Geneva in 1564.

abschnitte.text: Calvin was born on 10 July 1509 in Noyon in Picardy, and his French name was Jean Cauvin. He studied first theology and then **law** in Orléans and Bourges. Around 1533 he turned to the ideas of the **Reformation**. Because Protestants were persecuted in France, he had to flee.

In Basel in 1536 Calvin published the “**Institutes of the Christian Religion**”. In it he explained the Protestant faith clearly and in order. He revised the book all his life and made it ever longer. It became one of the most influential books of Protestantism.

While passing through in 1536, the reformer Guillaume **Farel** kept him in Geneva. Because of a dispute with the town council, both were expelled in 1538. In Strasbourg Calvin led a French refugee congregation and married Idelette de Bure. In 1541 Geneva called him back, and he stayed until his death.

In 1541 Calvin created a new church order for Geneva. A body called the **Consistory** oversaw people's lives. Dancing, gambling and swearing were forbidden, and church attendance was compulsory. In 1553 the scholar Michael Servetus was burned in Geneva because of his teaching on the Trinity, which is still seen as a dark chapter.

In 1549 Calvin reached agreement with Heinrich Bullinger of Zurich on the Lord's Supper, which united the Reformed churches of Switzerland. The **Geneva Academy**, founded in 1559, trained pastors from all over Europe. In this way Calvinism spread to France among the Huguenots, to the Netherlands and to Scotland. Geneva earned the nickname “Protestant Rome”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement in the 16th century that wanted to renew the Church and led to the split into Catholic and Protestant.
The teaching that God has decided in advance which people will be saved.
A branch of the Reformed faith named after Calvin.
A council of pastors and elders that oversaw the lives of believers in Geneva.

gewusst: In the Parc des Bastions in Geneva stands the Reformation Wall, about 100 metres long, with large figures of Calvin, Farel, Beza and Knox.
Calvin did not want a grave monument, so nobody knows exactly where he is buried.

teile.einleitung: Huldrych Zwingli was the most important reformer in German-speaking Switzerland. From Zurich, from 1519, he changed the Church, the faith and the everyday life of many people. His Reformation still shapes the Reformed Church in Switzerland and across the world.
wichtigste: Huldrych Zwingli was born in 1484 in Wildhaus in the Toggenburg.
Before Zurich he was a priest in Glarus and Einsiedeln.
From 1519 he served as people's priest at the Grossmünster in Zurich.
The “sausage meal” of 1522 at the printer Christoph Froschauer's is seen as the starting signal of the Zurich Reformation.
At the First Zurich Disputation in 1523 Zwingli presented 67 theses.
From 1524 pictures and statues were removed from the Zurich churches.
Zwingli fought against Reislaufen, the mercenary service of young Swiss men.
In 1531 he fell in the Battle of Kappel.

abschnitte.text: Huldrych Zwingli was born on 1 January 1484 in **Wildhaus** in the Toggenburg, the son of a respected farming family. He studied in Vienna and Basel and was especially interested in ancient languages. He was strongly influenced by the scholar **Erasmus of Rotterdam**. In 1506 he became a priest in Glarus, and later he worked in Einsiedeln.

As a field chaplain, Zwingli accompanied mercenaries from Glarus to wars in Italy and in 1515 witnessed the defeat at Marignano. At that time many young Swiss men went off as mercenaries to foreign wars, which was called **Reislaufen**. Zwingli saw how many died in the process, while others grew rich from the mercenary trade. He therefore fought this practice all his life.

From 1519 Zwingli served as **people's priest** at the Grossmünster in Zurich. He preached directly from the Bible and explained it in language people could understand. In 1522, in the house of the printer Christoph Froschauer, people ate sausage on purpose during Lent, and Zwingli defended this **sausage meal**. His close colleague Leo Jud became pastor at the church of St Peter in 1523.

In January 1523 the **First Zurich Disputation** took place, a public debate about the faith. Zwingli presented 67 theses for it, and the council allowed him to go on preaching according to the Bible. From 1524 pictures and statues were removed from the churches, and in 1525 the Mass was replaced by a simple Lord's Supper. In 1524 Zwingli married Anna Reinhart publicly, which was unheard of for a priest at that time.

abschnitte.titel: Dispute with Luther and the Anabaptists
abschnitte.text: Zwingli agreed with Martin Luther on many things, but not on the **Lord's Supper**. For Zwingli, bread and wine were only signs; for Luther, Christ was really present in them. At the Marburg Colloquy in 1529 the two could not agree. Zwingli also acted harshly against the **Anabaptists**, who rejected infant baptism.

The Reformation split the Confederation into Reformed and Catholic places. In the Second **War of Kappel**, Zwingli fell on 11 October 1531 in the Battle of Kappel. His successor Heinrich Bullinger carried on his work in Zurich. The Zurich Bible, which came into being under Zwingli, is still used today in revised form.

begriffe.erklaerung: The renewal of the Church in the 16th century, from which the Protestant churches arose.
A priest responsible for the pastoral care and preaching of a congregation.
A public debate in which a question is discussed.
The service of young Swiss men as mercenaries in foreign armies.

gewusst: Zwingli took up his post at the Grossmünster exactly on his 35th birthday, on 1 January 1519.
During the First War of Kappel in 1529, soldiers from both sides are said to have eaten a milk soup together, the famous “Kappeler Milchsuppe”.
In 1519 Zwingli survived a serious illness with the plague and wrote a poem about it.

teile.einleitung: The British Empire was the largest empire in history. Around 1922 about a quarter of the land area of the Earth belonged to it, from Canada through Africa and India to Australia. It brought trade and wealth to Britain, but for many peoples in the colonies it also brought oppression and exploitation.
wichtigste: At its greatest extent around 1922 the British Empire covered about a quarter of the land area of the Earth.
It was called “the empire on which the sun never sets”.
The English East India Company was founded in 1600 and gradually conquered large parts of India.
After the Indian uprising of 1857 the British Crown took over direct rule of India in 1858.
In 1876 Queen Victoria took the title “Empress of India”.
Dominions such as Canada and Australia largely governed themselves.
After the Second World War most colonies became independent, and many belong to the Commonwealth today.

abschnitte.text: The **British Empire** grew over several centuries from colonies, trading posts and conquered territories. Around 1922 about a quarter of the world's population lived under British rule. Because the territories were spread across all time zones, the sun always seemed to be shining somewhere in the empire. That is where the saying about “the empire on which the sun never sets” comes from. The strong war fleet, the **Royal Navy**, ruled the seas for a long time and protected the trade routes.

abschnitte.titel: Trade and the East India Company
abschnitte.text: In 1600 the English **East India Company** was founded, a trading company for spices, tea, cotton and silk. It had its own soldiers and gradually conquered large parts of India. After the great Indian uprising of 1857 the British Crown took over direct rule in 1858. **Queen Victoria** was declared “Empress of India” in 1876. India was seen as the “jewel in the crown” of the Empire.

In 1776 13 North American colonies declared their independence, and the USA came out of them. After that the British looked more towards Asia, Africa and Australia. In 1869 the **Suez Canal** was opened, which greatly shortened the sea route to India. In 1875 Britain bought the Egyptian shares in the canal. The businessman and politician **Cecil Rhodes** dreamed of a railway line “from the Cape to Cairo” right across British-ruled Africa. In the Second Boer War from 1899 to 1902 the British fought in South Africa against the descendants of Dutch settlers.

Some settler colonies with many European immigrants gradually received self-government. They were called **dominions**, for example Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. Canada became a federation in 1867, and the Australian colonies joined together as one federation in 1901. With the **Statute of Westminster** the dominions became legally equal to Britain in 1931.

The Empire brought great suffering to many people. For a long time British merchants profited from the **slave trade** across the Atlantic, before it was banned in 1807 and slavery in the colonies was abolished in 1833. In many colonies local people were dispossessed, exploited and suppressed with violence. In India there were severe famines under British rule. Many borders that the British drew still lead to conflicts today.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Empire and the Commonwealth
abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Britain was weakened, and in the colonies the wish for freedom grew. India became independent in 1947 after the non-violent resistance under **Mahatma Gandhi**. In the following decades almost all colonies in Africa, Asia and the Caribbean became independent. In 1997 Britain gave Hong Kong back to China. Many former colonies work together voluntarily today in the **Commonwealth of Nations**, to which about 56 states belong (as of 2024).

begriffe.erklaerung: An area that is ruled and administered by a foreign country.
A largely self-governing settler colony such as Canada or Australia.
A voluntary association of Britain and many former colonies.
The effort of a state to extend its power over other countries and peoples.

gewusst: That people drive on the left in many countries such as India, Australia or South Africa is a legacy of the British Empire.
Because English was spoken everywhere in the Empire, it is one of the most important world languages today.
The British king Charles III is still head of state of Canada, Australia and New Zealand as well.

teile.einleitung: Child labour means that children have to work regularly instead of going to school and playing. It was especially bad during industrialisation in the 19th century, when even small children toiled in factories and mines. Even today many millions of children around the world still have to work.
wichtigste: During industrialisation children worked especially often in spinning mills and mines.
Factory owners liked to employ children because they were paid much less.
In 1833 Britain for the first time appointed state factory inspectors to protect children.
In 1815 the canton of Zurich issued one of the first Swiss ordinances against child labour in spinning mills.
Under the federal Factory Act of 1877, children could only work in factories from the age of 14.
The people accepted the Factory Act of 1877 by a narrow margin in a vote.
Contract children (Verdingkinder) in Switzerland had to work for strange families.

abschnitte.text: With **industrialisation**, big factories arose from about 1800, especially spinning mills for cotton. Children often worked there 12 to 14 hours a day. They were paid much less than adults, which is why factory owners liked to employ them. Many families were so poor that they depended on the children's money.

In **mines** children crawled through narrow tunnels because they were small. They opened ventilation doors, pushed coal wagons or sorted coal. The work was dark, dusty and very dangerous. Many children fell ill or were badly injured.

Because they had to work, many children could not go to **school** regularly. Some fell asleep in lessons, and others never learned to read and write properly. Doctors and teachers noticed that working children were smaller and weaker. Little by little this led to laws to protect children.

In 1815 the canton of Zurich issued one of the first Swiss ordinances against child labour in spinning mills. In 1864 Glarus introduced the 12-hour day for adults too. The federal **Factory Act** of 1877 banned factory work for children under 14 and limited the working day to 11 hours. **Factory inspectors** checked whether the rules were being followed.

Until well into the 20th century, poor or orphaned children in Switzerland were placed with strange families as **Verdingkinder** (contract children), often on farms. There they had to work hard and were often badly treated. This injustice was only addressed late. Since 2017 those affected have received a solidarity contribution of 25,000 francs from the federal government.

The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child of 1989 protects children from exploitative work. Even so, according to estimates by the International Labour Organization, around 138 million children worked worldwide in 2024. Many of them help in agriculture, and some work in mines or factories. 12 June is the **World Day Against Child Labour**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time when machines and factories replaced handwork, from about 1800.
An official who checks whether factories follow the protection laws.
A child placed by the authorities with a strange family, where they had to work.

begriffe.wort: Convention on the Rights of the Child
begriffe.erklaerung: A UN treaty of 1989 that sets out the rights of all children.

gewusst: In Switzerland young people aged 13 and over may do light work, for example delivering newspapers.
From Graubünden and Tyrol, so-called Swabian children used to walk to southern Germany every spring to work on farms there.

teile.einleitung: Maize is a cereal plant that originally comes from Mexico. Today it is grown all over the world, in Switzerland too. From maize people make, for example, polenta and popcorn.
wichtigste: Maize was first grown in Mexico.
The kernels sit on the cob of the maize plant.
In Ticino polenta is made from maize meal.
If you heat certain maize kernels, popcorn is produced.
Maize came to Europe after the voyages of Christopher Columbus.

abschnitte.text: Maize was first grown in **Mexico**, many thousands of years ago. People bred it from a wild grass that had only very small ears. For the peoples of Central and South America, such as the **Maya** and the **Aztecs**, maize was the most important food. After the voyages of **Christopher Columbus** maize came to Europe. From there it spread to many countries.

Maize belongs to the **grasses**, like wheat and rice. The plant often grows more than two metres high. The kernels sit close together on the **cob**. The cob is wrapped in green leaves, and fine threads peep out at the top. Maize needs a lot of warmth and sun. In Switzerland you see many tall maize fields in late summer, often it is fodder maize for animals.

In **Ticino** **polenta** is cooked from ground maize, the **maize meal**. In the past it was an important everyday food there, often cooked in a copper pot over the fire. A special kind of maize is suitable for **popcorn**. There is a little water inside the kernel. When it is heated it turns to steam, and the kernel bursts open.

gewusst: In the St Gallen Rhine Valley an old variety of maize is grown, the “Rheintaler Ribelmais”.
Maize cobs come not only in yellow, but also in white, red, blue and almost black.

teile.einleitung: The Counter-Reformation was the Catholic Church's answer to the Reformation of Luther, Zwingli and Calvin in the 16th and 17th centuries. The Church renewed itself from within and at the same time tried to win back lost territories. Many magnificent Baroque churches, in Switzerland too, still tell of this time.
wichtigste: Its centrepiece was the Council of Trent, which met from 1545 to 1563.
Pope Paul III called the council.
The council declared Scripture and tradition to be equal sources of faith and the Latin Vulgate to be binding.
Ignatius of Loyola founded the Jesuit order, which Paul III confirmed in 1540.
Every diocese was to set up a seminary for priests.
Many historians also speak of “Catholic Reform”, because it was about inner renewal.
The Church used the art of the Baroque to impress believers.

abschnitte.text: From 1517 the **Reformation** split the Church in western Europe. Many areas became Reformed, in Switzerland for example Zurich, Bern and Basel. The Catholic Church responded with the **Counter-Reformation**. Many historians also use the term **Catholic Reform**, because it stresses the inner renewal of the Church and not just the reaction to the Protestants.

Pope Paul III called a big meeting of bishops, the **Council of Trent**. With interruptions it met from 1545 to 1563 in the city of Trent in what is now northern Italy. The council decided that Scripture and tradition are equal sources of faith and that the Latin **Vulgate** is the binding Bible. As a result, the Roman Catechism appeared in 1566, meant to teach the faith in a uniform way.

The council also fought abuses within the Church itself. Bishops now had to live in their own diocese, which was called the **duty of residence**. Every diocese was to set up a **seminary for priests**, so that priests would be better trained. At the same time, control was tightened, for example with a list of forbidden books.

The Spanish nobleman **Ignatius of Loyola** founded the Jesuit order, which Pope Paul III officially confirmed in 1540. The Jesuits took a fourth vow, which demanded special obedience to the Pope when sent on missions. They founded many schools and colleges and travelled as missionaries as far as Asia and America. In this way they became the most important force of the Counter-Reformation.

In the Swiss Confederation, mainly Central Switzerland, Fribourg and the Valais stayed Catholic. The Archbishop of Milan, **Charles Borromeo**, strongly supported renewal in these places. The Jesuits founded colleges in Lucerne and Fribourg, where Peter Canisius worked, and Capuchins preached in many villages. In 1586 the Catholic cantons joined together in the Golden or Borromean League.

After the council, the Church relied heavily on the art of the **Baroque**. Magnificent churches with gold, stucco, ceiling paintings and music were meant to impress and inspire believers. One model was the Jesuit church Il Gesù in Rome. In Switzerland, the abbey church at Einsiedeln and the Jesuit Church in Lucerne are famous examples.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large assembly of bishops that decides on important questions of the Church.
The movement in the 16th century from which the Reformed and Protestant churches arose.
A community of men or women who live together following fixed religious rules.
The area for which a bishop is responsible, also called a bishopric.

gewusst: The Council of Trent lasted almost 20 years, with breaks.
The Pontifical Swiss Guard has protected the Pope since 1506, so even before the Council of Trent.
Pope Francis, who led the Church from 2013 to 2025, was the first Jesuit on the papal throne.

teile.einleitung: Under the gold standard, a currency is tied firmly to gold. Anyone who owns banknotes can exchange them for gold at the central bank at a fixed rate. In the 19th century this was usual in many countries.
wichtigste: Under the gold standard, money can be exchanged for gold at a fixed ratio.
Britain was the first country to introduce the gold standard, by law in 1816.
In the 1870s the German Empire switched to gold with money from French reparations.
The outbreak of the First World War in 1914 ended the classical gold standard.
Britain gave up the gold standard for good in 1931.
The Swiss franc was tied to gold by law until 2000.

abschnitte.text: Under a **gold standard**, the central bank promises to exchange every banknote for **gold** at a fixed rate. So it can only issue as much money as it owns gold or can safely obtain. This is meant to keep money stable. The drawback: in a crisis the central bank cannot simply provide more money.

The famous scientist **Isaac Newton** was also Master of the Mint in London. In 1717 he set a price for gold that in practice led Britain to the gold standard. By law it was introduced in **1816**. Because Britain was then the greatest trading power, many countries followed. The **German Empire** switched in the 1870s and paid for the gold with **reparations** from France after the war of 1870/71.

The Scottish philosopher **David Hume** described in 1752 how trade between countries is supposed to balance itself out. If gold flows out of a country, its money supply falls and prices drop. Then its goods become cheaper abroad, it sells more, and the gold comes back. This is called the **price-specie-flow mechanism**.

When the First World War broke out in **1914**, the warring states ended the duty to exchange money for gold. That let them pay for the war with new money. Britain returned to gold in 1925, but had to give it up again in the Great Depression in **1931**. After the Second World War the US dollar was tied to gold, until the USA ended this in 1971.

The franc stayed linked to gold for a particularly long time. Only the new **Federal Constitution** of 1999 cleared the way to end the link to gold. With the new currency law, which came into force on **1 May 2000**, it happened. But the **Swiss National Bank** still holds large gold reserves today.

gewusst: Today no major currency in the world can be exchanged for gold any more.
Because Newton valued gold quite highly compared with silver, fewer and fewer silver coins were used in England.

teile.einleitung: The First French Republic was the state that came into being in France after the abolition of the monarchy in September 1792. For the first time no king ruled there any more, but elected representatives of the people. It was a time full of hopes, but also full of wars and violence, and it ended in 1804 with Napoleon's empire.
wichtigste: On 21 September 1792 the National Convention abolished the monarchy.
The National Convention was elected by universal male suffrage.
The cannonade of Valmy on 20 September 1792 saved the young republic.
King Louis XVI was executed on 21 January 1793.
From 1795 a Directory of five directors led the government.
With the coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799 Napoleon Bonaparte took power.
The Republic ended in 1804 with the setting up of the Empire.

abschnitte.text: Since 1789 France had been in **revolution**. On 10 August 1792 insurgents stormed the Tuileries Palace in Paris, where the king lived. Hundreds of **Swiss Guards** who defended the king lost their lives, and the Lion Monument in Lucerne recalls them today. Afterwards the French elected a new **National Convention**, for the first time under universal male suffrage. On 21 September 1792 the Convention abolished the monarchy, and France was now a republic.

The kings of Europe feared that the Revolution might spread. Prussian and Austrian troops therefore marched against France. On 20 September 1792 the French stopped the Prussians in the **cannonade of Valmy** and so saved the young republic. In 1793 general conscription was introduced with the **levée en masse**, and huge armies came into being. The **Marseillaise**, today's national anthem of France, also dates from this time.

On 21 January 1793 the deposed king **Louis XVI** was executed with the guillotine. After that the radical Jacobins under **Maximilien de Robespierre** took power. In the **Reign of Terror** of 1793 to 1794 thousands of alleged enemies of the Revolution were killed. The Jacobin constitution of 1793 was accepted, but never came into force. In July 1794 Robespierre himself was overthrown and executed.

The Republic wanted to put everything in a new order, even time. The **Revolutionary calendar** began with the start of the Republic in September 1792 as Year I. Each of the twelve months had 30 days, and the names of the months came from nature and weather, for example **Brumaire** (month of mist) or Thermidor (month of heat). Instead of weeks there were ten-day periods, the decades. The **metric system** with the metre and the kilogram also dates from this time.

From 1795 a **Directory** of five directors led the government. It was weak, and many French people were unhappy with war and lack of money. At the same time the young general **Napoleon Bonaparte** became famous through victories in Italy. In 1798 French troops occupied Switzerland and founded the **Helvetic Republic** on the French model. On 9 November 1799, the 18th of Brumaire, Napoleon took power by a coup.

On 4 February 1794 the National Convention decided the **abolition of slavery** in the colonies, but Napoleon brought it back in 1802. In 1804 Napoleon crowned himself emperor, and with that the First Republic formally ended. Its ideas of **liberty, equality and fraternity** lived on, however. Today France is the Fifth Republic, and the motto still stands on many town halls. The thought that the people and not a king should rule also shaped the whole of Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state without a king, in which elected representatives govern.
The elected parliament of the First French Republic from 1792 to 1795.
A radical group of revolutionaries who set up a strict rule.
A small group seizes power in the state by force or cunning.
A government of five directors in France from 1795 to 1799.

gewusst: In the Revolutionary calendar every day had the name of a plant, an animal or a tool instead of a saint.
The Lion Monument in Lucerne recalls the Swiss Guards who died in 1792 in the storming of the Tuileries.
In the time of the Revolution the metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.

teile.einleitung: Separation of powers means that power in the state is shared between different bodies: parliament, government and the courts. That way nobody can seize all power alone. The idea comes from the Age of Enlightenment and is today a cornerstone of every democracy, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The three powers are the legislative, the executive and the judiciary.
The most important aim is to limit power and so protect the freedom of citizens.
The idea was made famous by the Frenchman Montesquieu in 1748.
In Switzerland, the Federal Council with seven members forms the executive of the Confederation.
The Federal Supreme Court has its main seat in Lausanne.
Vertical separation of powers means sharing tasks between the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.
In the USA there is a system of checks and balances, in which the powers keep one another in check.

abschnitte.text: The state has three main tasks: making laws, carrying out laws and administering justice. The **legislative** is the law-making power, that is, parliament. The **executive** is the power that carries out the laws, that is, the government and the administration. The **judiciary** is the power that administers justice, that is, the courts, which decide what is lawful.

In the past, in many countries all power lay with a king, who made the laws, governed and judged. The Englishman John Locke was already thinking about dividing power in the 17th century. The Frenchman **Montesquieu** described the separation of powers in 1748 in his book “The Spirit of the Laws”. He believed that anyone who has power tends to abuse it, and that is why power must set limits to power.

In Switzerland the **Federal Assembly**, with the National Council and the Council of States, is the legislative. The **Federal Council**, with seven members, forms the executive of the Confederation. The **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne is the highest judicial authority. One special feature: it cannot overturn federal laws for being unconstitutional, because in Switzerland parliament and the people have the last word.

Besides the division into three powers there is the **vertical separation of powers**. This means sharing responsibilities between the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. For example, the cantons look after schools, the Confederation looks after the army and the municipalities look after many things locally. Every municipality and every canton also has a parliament or an assembly, a government and courts.

In the USA the powers keep one another in check, which is called **checks and balances**. The President can, for example, veto laws passed by Congress, and the Supreme Court can declare laws unconstitutional. In parliamentary systems such as Germany one speaks rather of an **interlocking of powers**. There parliament elects the government, and many ministers are also members of parliament.

The free media are often called the “fourth power”, because they keep a close watch on politicians. In Switzerland the people also keep politics in check with initiatives and referendums. Where there is no separation of powers, for example in dictatorships, rulers can have opponents arrested at will. That is why the separation of powers is an important protection for the freedom of all people.

begriffe.erklaerung: The law-making power, that is, parliament.
The power that carries out the laws, that is, the government and administration.
The power that administers justice, that is, the courts.
The right to block a decision.

gewusst: Montesquieu was actually a judge in Bordeaux himself before he wrote his famous book.
In Switzerland the Federal Council is elected by parliament, but unlike in many other countries it cannot be removed by parliament.
Besides the Federal Supreme Court there are other federal courts in Switzerland, for example the Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona.

teile.einleitung: Jacques Piccard was a Swiss oceanographer, that is, a marine scientist. In 1960 he dived in the submersible “Trieste” to the deepest point of the world's oceans, the Mariana Trench.
wichtigste: Jacques Piccard was the son of the researcher Auguste Piccard.
Together with his father he built submersibles.
Their submersible was called “Trieste”, after the city of Trieste.
On 23 January 1960 he dived into the Mariana Trench with Don Walsh.
The Mariana Trench lies in the western Pacific.
They reached a depth of almost 11,000 metres.
His son Bertrand Piccard flew around the world in a balloon in 1999.

abschnitte.text: Jacques Piccard was born in 1922 in Brussels. His father **Auguste Piccard** was a famous Swiss physicist. In 1931 he rose in a balloon into the **stratosphere**, a very high layer of the atmosphere, as one of the first people to do so. After that he also wanted to explore the depths of the seas. Together, father and son built **submersibles**, so-called **bathyscaphes**.

The best-known submersible of the two was called the **“Trieste”**. It was named after the city of **Trieste** in Italy, where a large part of it was built. The Trieste had a large float and, beneath it, a small, very thick steel sphere for the crew. Later the US Navy bought the submersible. Jacques Piccard stayed on as an expert.

On **23 January 1960** Jacques Piccard and **Don Walsh**, an officer of the American navy, dived into the **Mariana Trench**. It lies in the western **Pacific**, east of the Philippines. It is the deepest point in the world's oceans. The Trieste reached **almost 11,000 metres** in depth. That is deeper than Mount Everest is high. The descent took several hours.

For the national exhibition **Expo 64** in Lausanne, Jacques Piccard built a submarine for passengers. With it, thousands of visitors could dive into the depths of **Lake Geneva**. Later he campaigned for the protection of lakes and seas. He died in 2008 on Lake Geneva. His son **Bertrand Piccard** circled the Earth without stopping in 1999 with Brian Jones in the balloon **“Breitling Orbiter 3”**.

gewusst: Three generations of Piccards set records: in the stratosphere, in the deep sea and in a balloon around the world.
After Jacques Piccard, people only reached the deepest point of the Mariana Trench again in 2012.

teile.einleitung: In 1923 Germany experienced hyperinflation: money lost its value so quickly that prices rose almost by the hour. Savings became worthless, and many people fell into hardship.
wichtigste: Inflation means that money loses value and prices rise.
In January 1923 France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr region.
The government paid the strikers with more and more freshly printed money.
Wages were paid out daily or even twice a day.
Savers lost especially much, because their savings became worthless.
Gustav Stresemann became Chancellor in August 1923 and ended the passive resistance.
The Rentenmark ended the hyperinflation in November 1923.

abschnitte.text: **Inflation** means that money loses value. Prices rise, and with the same money you can buy less. A small amount of inflation is almost always there. In a **hyperinflation**, however, prices rise extremely fast, often by many times in a single month. Money then loses people's trust and its job as a means of payment.

Germany had already printed a lot of money in the First World War. After the war it had to pay **reparations** to the victors. Because Germany had fallen behind, **France and Belgium** occupied the **Ruhr region**, an important industrial area, in January 1923. The government called for **passive resistance**: the workers were to strike. The state went on paying their wages, with money from the **printing press**.

Prices rose so quickly that money was worth much less by the evening than in the morning. So wages were paid **daily** or even twice a day. People ran to the shops straight after being paid. In November 1923 a US dollar cost about 4.2 trillion marks. **Savers** lost all their savings. Those who had debts, on the other hand, could pay them back easily.

In August 1923 **Gustav Stresemann** became Chancellor. He ended the costly passive resistance in the Ruhr. On **15 November 1923** the **Rentenmark** was introduced. One Rentenmark was worth one **trillion** of the old paper marks. The new currency quickly brought calm again. But many people had lost trust in the state, which weakened the young democracy.

gewusst: In 1923 the Reichsbank even printed banknotes for 100 trillion marks.
Children at that time played with bundles of worthless banknotes as if they were building blocks.

teile.einleitung: Frederick the Great, also called Frederick II, was King in Prussia from 1740 to 1786. Under him Prussia became a European great power. He fought wars, but he also loved music, books and philosophy.
wichtigste: Frederick II ruled Prussia from 1740 to 1786.
Among the people he was called “Old Fritz”.
His summer palace in Potsdam is called Sanssouci, which means “without worry”.
He conquered the rich province of Silesia from Austria.
The Seven Years' War lasted from 1756 to 1763.
He passionately loved playing the flute.
He encouraged the growing of potatoes.

abschnitte.text: Frederick was born in Berlin in 1712. His father **Frederick William I** was called the **“Soldier King”** because the army meant everything to him. He was very strict and did not like his son's love of music and books. In **1730** the young Frederick therefore wanted to **flee abroad**. The escape was discovered, and Frederick was put in custody. His friend **Hans Hermann von Katte** was executed, and Frederick had to watch.

In **1740** Frederick became king. Soon afterwards he marched into **Silesia**, a rich province of **Austria**. In the **Silesian Wars**, Prussia kept the province. From **1756** Prussia fought in the **Seven Years' War** against Austria, Russia and France. The war lasted until 1763. Prussia only just survived it, but kept Silesia and was seen as a **great power** afterwards.

In the 1740s Frederick had the palace of **Sanssouci** built in **Potsdam**. The name is French and means **“without worry”**. Frederick preferred to speak and write French rather than German. He played the **flute** very well, composed his own pieces and often gave concerts in the palace. He valued philosophers and invited the Frenchman **Voltaire** to his court.

Frederick wanted to prevent **famines**. So he had the growing of the **potato**, which was still little known at the time, encouraged. A well-known decree of 1756 is called the **Potato Order**. He largely abolished **torture** and promoted freedom of conscience in matters of faith. Frederick saw himself as the **“first servant of the state”**. Even so, he ruled as an **absolute monarch** and decided almost everything alone.

In his old age people called the king **“Old Fritz”**. The name “Soldier King”, on the other hand, belongs to his father. Frederick died in **1786** at Sanssouci. He had no children, so his nephew became king. To this day Frederick is judged in very different ways: as a clever reformer, but also as a ruler who fought many wars.

gewusst: Frederick wanted to be buried beside his dogs at Sanssouci. This wish was only granted in 1991.
Visitors still place potatoes on his grave at Sanssouci.

teile.einleitung: A cooperative is a union of people who help one another. The members belong to the business together and have a say. In Switzerland, for example, Migros, Coop and the Raiffeisen banks are cooperatives.
wichtigste: In a cooperative the members help one another through self-help.
The principle is: one member, one vote.
In 1844 the weavers of Rochdale in England founded a consumer cooperative.
Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen founded loan associations for farmers.
Hermann Schulze-Delitzsch is seen as the founder of the people's banks.
In 1900 the first Raiffeisen bank in Switzerland was created in Bichelsee in Thurgau.
In 1941 Gottlieb Duttweiler turned Migros into cooperatives.

abschnitte.text: In a **cooperative**, people join together to achieve something that would be hard alone. It might be cheap shopping, a loan or an affordable flat. The basic idea is **self-help**. In votes the rule is: **one member, one vote**. So unlike in a **public limited company**, it does not matter how much money someone has put in.

In the 19th century many workers lived in poverty. In **1844** **weavers** in the English town of **Rochdale** founded a **consumer cooperative**. They bought food together and sold it to their members at fair prices. Their group was called the “Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers”. Their **principles**, such as open membership and equal votes, still shape cooperatives today.

In Germany, **Friedrich Wilhelm Raiffeisen**, as mayor in the Westerwald, saw the hardship of farmers. Many had to borrow money from **loan sharks** who charged very high interest. Raiffeisen founded rural **loan associations** based on self-help and shared liability. **Hermann Schulze-Delitzsch** addressed craftsmen in the towns. His **credit cooperatives** gave rise to the **people's banks**.

In **1900** the pastor **Johann Traber** founded the first **Raiffeisen bank** in Switzerland in **Bichelsee** in Thurgau. From it came today's Raiffeisen Group. **Migros** was founded in 1925 as a public limited company. In **1941** **Gottlieb Duttweiler** gave it to his customers in the form of **cooperatives**. **Coop** is also a cooperative. In cities such as Zurich there are also many **housing cooperatives** that offer affordable flats.

gewusst: In 2016 UNESCO added the idea and practice of cooperatives to its list of intangible cultural heritage.
Anyone who is a cooperative member of Migros may vote on important questions.

teile.einleitung: The factory system is a way of making goods in which many workers work in one place with machines under strict supervision. From the 18th century it replaced outwork and shaped industrialisation. With it began a completely new world of work with clock, bell and factory regulation.
wichtigste: Before the factory system there was the putting-out system with outworkers.
Lombe's silk mill in Derby of about 1720 is regarded as one of the first fully mechanised factories.
Typical of the factory system are machines, division of labour and fixed working hours.
A working day in early factories often lasted 12 to 14 hours.
Under the truck system workers were paid in goods or vouchers instead of money.
Robert Owen showed in New Lanark that a factory could also be run more humanely.
The Luddites destroyed machines in England from 1811 in protest.

abschnitte.text: Before the factories the **putting-out system** prevailed. A merchant, the putter-out, supplied raw materials such as wool or cotton to families who spun and wove at home. Afterwards he collected the finished goods and sold them. The outworkers decided their working hours themselves, but depended on the merchant and his prices.

In the **factory system** the buildings, machines and raw materials belong to the owner. The workers come to the factory and receive wages. The making of the goods is broken down by **division of labour** into many simple steps. A source of power such as a waterwheel or later a steam engine drives many machines at the same time.

In early factories fixed working hours applied, which were shown by a bell or clock. A **factory regulation** laid down rules, such as a ban on talking during work. Anyone who came late or made a mistake had to pay a fine. A working day often lasted 12 to 14 hours, and children worked too.

Some factory owners paid under the **truck system**, that is, in goods or vouchers instead of money. The vouchers could only be redeemed in the factory owner's shop, where prices were often high. In this way many families fell into debt and dependence. In Britain the truck system was therefore restricted by law as early as 1831.

The businessman Robert Owen ran the cotton mill **New Lanark** in Scotland from 1800. He shortened working hours, built better homes and founded a school for workers' children. Owen wanted to show that contented workers also do good work. In Britain a Factory Act in 1833 restricted child labour in textile factories.

In Switzerland too, spinning mills came into being from about 1800, above all in the canton of Zurich and in eastern Switzerland. The canton of Glarus passed a factory law in 1864 that limited working hours to 12 hours even for adults. The federal **Factory Act** of 1877 introduced the eleven-hour day in the whole of Switzerland. With this Switzerland was among the pioneers of worker protection in Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A merchant gives outworkers raw materials and sells the finished goods.
Payment in goods or vouchers instead of money.
A list of rules and punishments for the workers in a factory.
English workers who destroyed machines in protest from 1811.

gewusst: The Luddites appealed to a supposed leader called Ned Ludd, who probably never existed.
The factory buildings of New Lanark are a UNESCO World Heritage Site today and can be visited.
In some early factories the clocks were supposedly altered so that the workers had to work longer.

teile.einleitung: An assembly line brings a workpiece from one workplace to the next. From 1913 Henry Ford had cars built this way and so changed work in factories all over the world.
wichtigste: On an assembly line the workpiece moves to the workers.
Each worker always does the same step.
Henry Ford built the Model T this way.
Ford's factory stood in Highland Park near Detroit.
Through the assembly line cars became cheaper.
From 1914 Ford paid many workers 5 dollars a day.
Most Model T cars were black.

abschnitte.text: On an **assembly line** the workers stay standing in their place. The **workpiece**, for example a car, moves on a belt from place to place. Each worker has a small task, such as screwing on a wheel. This **division of labour** makes the work very fast. For the workers, though, it was often **monotonous**, because they did the same thing all day.

abschnitte.titel: Henry Ford and the Model T
abschnitte.text: The American **Henry Ford** wanted to build a car that many families could afford. The **Model T** was built from 1908 to 1927. From **1913** Ford used a moving assembly line in his factory in **Highland Park** near **Detroit**. He got the idea partly from big **slaughterhouses**, where the animals were passed on hooks from worker to worker. Detroit became the **car city** of the USA.

With the assembly line cars were finished **much faster**. That is why Ford could sell them more **cheaply**. Because the work was monotonous, many workers quit. From **1914** Ford therefore paid many workers **5 dollars a day**. That was then about twice as much as in other factories. In this way Ford kept good workers, and they could more easily buy a car themselves.

For many years the Model T was available **only in black**. Black paint then dried particularly **quickly**, and that suited the fast pace on the line. Ford is said to have said that customers could have any colour as long as it was black. Today **robots** also work on many assembly lines, and the principle is not used only for cars.

gewusst: About 15 million Model T cars were built.
In the USA the Model T was given the nickname “Tin Lizzie”.

teile.einleitung: Colonialism means that a state conquers foreign territories, rules them and exploits them for itself. From the 15th to the 20th century, European powers above all subjugated large parts of America, Africa, Asia and Oceania. The consequences can still be felt today, and Switzerland, although it had no colonies of its own, was involved too.
wichtigste: Colonialism means direct rule over colonies, imperialism any form of extension of power.
In settler colonies many people from the mother country settled permanently.
A protectorate has its own government but is under the control of a foreign protecting power.
Britain often ruled indirectly through local rulers, while France relied on assimilation.
Switzerland had no colonies, but was involved through trade, missions and mercenaries.
Many colonial borders in Africa separated groups that belonged together and united enemies.
After the Second World War most colonies gained independence, which is called decolonisation.

abschnitte.text: With the voyages of discovery, such as the journey of Columbus in 1492, the age of European **colonies** began. Spain and Portugal conquered large parts of South and Central America. Later the Netherlands, Britain and France followed. Millions of people in America died from violence and from imported diseases.

In **settler colonies** such as North America or Australia, many Europeans settled permanently. In other colonies it was mainly about raw materials, plantations and trade. A **protectorate** kept its own government but was under foreign control. Britain often used indirect rule through local princes, while France, with its policy of assimilation, wanted to turn the local people into “Frenchmen”.

The colonial powers took gold, silver, sugar, cotton and spices from the colonies. For the plantations in America, about 12 million people from Africa were carried across the Atlantic as **slaves**. The local population had hardly any rights. Many Europeans justified this with the racist idea that they were superior to other peoples.

Switzerland never owned colonies, but was involved in other ways. Researchers therefore speak of “colonialism without colonies”. The **Basel Mission**, founded in 1815, worked among other places on the Gold Coast, today’s Ghana. The Winterthur trading house Volkart Brothers traded in cotton from India from 1851, and around 8,000 Swiss mercenaries served in the Dutch army in the Dutch East Indies between 1815 and the First World War.

Around 1900, so-called **human zoos** also took place in Swiss cities. People from Africa, Asia or other continents were put on show as if in a zoo. Many visitors found this exciting at the time. Today these exhibitions are regarded as inhuman and racist.

After the Second World War most colonies became independent, India in 1947 and in 1960 alone 17 states in Africa. This process is called **decolonisation**. The borders drawn by the colonial powers still lead to conflicts today. The poverty and economic dependence of many former colonies are also connected with this history.

begriffe.erklaerung: A territory that is ruled and administered by a foreign state.
A state’s striving to extend its power over other countries.
A territory with its own government under the control of a foreign protecting power.
The colonies’ path to independence, above all after 1945.
The state that rules a colony.

gewusst: Around 1920 the British Empire ruled about a quarter of the Earth’s land area.
1960 is called the “Year of Africa”, because 17 African states became independent then.

teile.einleitung: In a consumer society most people buy and use up many goods that they do not need in order to survive. After the Second World War in particular, prosperity grew in countries such as Switzerland. Supermarkets, cars and advertising changed everyday life greatly.
wichtigste: From 1913 assembly-line production made the Model T car affordable for many.
In 1948 Migros opened the first self-service shop in Switzerland, in Zurich.
In 1955 the first stretch of motorway in Switzerland was opened near Lucerne.
In 1970 the Shoppi Tivoli in Spreitenbach opened as Switzerland’s first big shopping centre.
Thorstein Veblen coined the term “conspicuous consumption” in 1899.
Vance Packard and John Kenneth Galbraith criticised advertising and affluence in the 1950s.

abschnitte.titel: Mass goods from the assembly line
abschnitte.text: In the past many goods were expensive because they were made individually by hand. From **1913** Henry Ford had his car, the **Model T**, built on an **assembly line**. Each worker made only a few movements, and the cars were produced much faster. As a result they became cheaper, and many families could afford one. This **mass production** was an important foundation of the consumer society.

In **1948** **Migros** opened the first **self-service shop** in Switzerland, in **Zurich**. Before that, a shop assistant served each customer individually at the counter. Now people took the goods from the shelf themselves and paid at the till. That saved time and money. In 1970 the **Shoppi Tivoli** opened in **Spreitenbach**, the first big shopping centre in Switzerland.

After the Second World War wages rose in Switzerland, and more and more people bought a **car**. That required new roads. In 1955 the first **stretch of motorway** in Switzerland was opened **near Lucerne**. Fridges, washing machines and televisions also came into many households. Holidays abroad became possible for many families.

As early as **1899** the economist **Thorstein Veblen** described **conspicuous consumption**: people buy things to show other people their wealth. In 1957 **Vance Packard** criticised in his book “The Hidden Persuaders” how advertising influences people. A year later **John Kenneth Galbraith** gave the affluent society its name with his book “The Affluent Society”. He thought that too much attention is paid to private goods and too little to public tasks.

There are different opinions about the consumer society. Supporters say it brought many people **prosperity** and a more comfortable life. Critics point to **waste**, damage to the environment and the high use of raw materials. Today people often talk about **sustainability**, for example about repairing, sharing and throwing away less.

gewusst: Migros began in Zurich in 1925 with five sales vans that brought goods directly to the neighbourhoods.
The Model T was built for almost 20 years, more than 15 million of them in all.

teile.einleitung: Mainframes are very powerful computers for big companies, banks and public authorities. The first electronic mainframes were so big that they filled whole rooms.
wichtigste: ENIAC was presented in the USA in 1946 and was one of the first electronic mainframe computers.
ENIAC weighed about 27 tonnes and had about 17,000 vacuum tubes.
The first mainframes filled a whole room.
In the past, programs and data were entered with punched cards.
The company IBM became world famous with mainframes.
In 1947 technicians found a moth in a computer: ever since, computer errors have been called “bugs”.

abschnitte.text: The first electronic computers were huge. The well-known **ENIAC** was presented in the USA in **1946**. It weighed about **27 tonnes** and filled a whole room. Inside were about 17,000 **vacuum tubes**, which looked rather like light bulbs. They got hot and often broke. Today a mobile phone is much more powerful than ENIAC.

In the past, programs and data were entered with **punched cards**. These were cards made of cardboard with holes in certain places. The computer read the holes as commands or numbers. As early as 1890, punched cards helped to analyse the census in the USA. For a bigger program you often needed whole stacks of them.

The company **IBM** built calculating machines early on and, from the 1950s, many mainframes. Companies, banks and insurers used them to manage wages, accounts and invoices. Mainframes can handle a very large number of tasks at the same time and very reliably. That is why big banks and public authorities still use them today.

The German inventor **Konrad Zuse** built one of the first working computers, the Z3, in 1941. His machine, the **Z4**, was used at **ETH Zurich** from 1950. That made ETH one of the first universities in Europe with its own computer. Soon afterwards ETH even built its own computer, the ERMETH.

gewusst: In 1947 technicians found a **moth** in a computer that had caused an error. They stuck it in their logbook. Computer errors are still called “bugs” today.
ENIAC was originally built for the army, to calculate the paths of shells.

teile.einleitung: Florence Nightingale was a British nurse. She is regarded as the founder of modern nursing and made nursing into a proper profession.
wichtigste: Florence Nightingale was born on 12 May 1820 in Florence and named after the city.
In the Crimean War from 1854 she nursed wounded British soldiers.
She ran a military hospital in Scutari near Constantinople.
She was called “the Lady with the Lamp”.
Cleanliness was especially important to her.
With diagrams she showed what the soldiers died of.
In 1860 she founded a nursing school in London.

abschnitte.text: Florence Nightingale was born on **12 May 1820** in **Florence** in Italy. Her British parents were travelling there. They named their daughter after the city, for in English Florence is **Florence**. The family was rich, and Florence received a good education. Against the wish of her family she wanted to become a **nurse**. At that time nursing was not seen as a respected job.

In the **Crimean War** Britain fought against Russia from 1854. Florence Nightingale travelled with other women to the military hospital at **Scutari**, today's Üsküdar in Istanbul. There they nursed **wounded soldiers**. Conditions were terrible: there was a lack of clean water, beds and bandages. Many soldiers died not of their wounds, but of **diseases**.

At night Florence Nightingale went through the wards with a **lamp** and looked in on the wounded. That is why she was called **“the Lady with the Lamp”**. For her **cleanliness** was especially important. She saw to clean beds, fresh air, washing water and good food. She was convinced that dirt makes many wounded men ill.

Florence Nightingale was also very good at **mathematics**. She counted the deaths exactly and drew coloured **diagrams**. From them you could see at a glance that most soldiers died of avoidable diseases. With these figures she convinced the government to improve the **hospitals**. She is therefore also regarded as a pioneer of **statistics**.

In **1860** Florence Nightingale founded a **school for nurses** in London. There women learned nursing as a proper profession. She also wrote books on nursing. Florence Nightingale died in 1910. Her birthday, **12 May**, is today **International Nurses Day**.

gewusst: The International Committee of the Red Cross in Geneva awards a Florence Nightingale Medal to especially deserving nursing professionals.
Florence Nightingale was the first woman to be admitted to the Royal Statistical Society in London.

teile.einleitung: The Crimean War lasted from 1853 to 1856. Russia fought against the Ottoman Empire, Britain, France and later Sardinia-Piedmont. The most important battles took place on the Crimean peninsula in the Black Sea.
wichtigste: The Crimean War lasted from 1853 to 1856.
Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire fought against Russia.
In 1855 Sardinia-Piedmont also entered the war.
The port city of Sevastopol was besieged for almost a year.
In 1854 the British Light Brigade made its costly charge at Balaclava.
The Peace of Paris ended the war in 1856.

abschnitte.text: The **Ottoman Empire** was weakened in the 19th century. **Russia** wanted to increase its influence on the Black Sea and in the Balkans. **Britain** and **France** wanted to prevent Russia from becoming too powerful. That is why they took the side of the Ottomans. In 1853 the war between Russia and the Ottoman Empire began, and in 1854 the Western powers intervened.

The allies landed on the **Crimean** peninsula in 1854. Their target was the Russian port city of **Sevastopol**, where the Russian Black Sea fleet lay. The city was **besieged for almost a year**. Soldiers on both sides suffered from cold, hunger and disease. In September 1855 the Russians had to give up Sevastopol.

In October **1854** the Battle of **Balaclava** took place. Because of a misunderstood order, the British **Light Brigade**, a cavalry unit, rode straight at Russian cannon. The charge was brave, but pointless and very **costly in lives**. The poet Alfred Tennyson wrote a famous poem about it. In 1855 **Sardinia-Piedmont** also entered the war on the side of France and Britain.

In the Crimean War more soldiers died of disease than in the fighting. The Briton **Florence Nightingale**, together with other nurses, looked after wounded soldiers.
