She made sure the hospitals were cleaner. Because she walked through the wards at night with a lamp, she was called “the Lady with the Lamp”. She is regarded as the founder of modern nursing.

The **Peace of Paris** ended the Crimean War in **1856**. Russia lost influence. The **Black Sea** was declared neutral: no more war fleets could be stationed there. The war also showed how much warfare was changing. For the first time newspaper reporters and photographers reported at length on a war.

gewusst: The Crimean War is among the first wars to be documented with photographs.
News of the war reached London much faster than before, thanks to the telegraph.

teile.einleitung: In the 19th century the middle class, the bourgeoisie, was the society layer that shaped the age, between the nobility and the working class. It included merchants, business owners, doctors, lawyers and professors. The middle class strongly shaped politics, culture and family life.
wichtigste: People distinguish the educated middle class from the business middle class.
The period from 1815 to 1848 is called Biedermeier.
In the Swiss federal state the Liberals held all seats in the Federal Council from 1848 to 1891.
The middle-class picture of roles was: the man at work, the woman at home.
The piano in the drawing room was a status symbol.
Clubs shaped social and political life.

abschnitte.text: The middle class was not a single group. The **educated middle class** got its standing from knowledge and culture. It included doctors, lawyers, pastors and professors, who had mostly studied at a university. The **business middle class** relied on property and companies, such as factory owners, bankers and merchants. What they had in common was that they wanted to rise not by birth, like the nobility, but by achievement.

The period between 1815 and 1848 is called the **Biedermeier**. Political freedoms were strongly limited at the time. Many citizens therefore withdrew into **family life**. Plain furniture, music at home and cosiness shaped this style. The word still stands for middle-class homeliness today.

The middle-class family had a clear **picture of roles**: the man worked in his job, the woman looked after the house and the children. Working-class families mostly could not afford this ideal, because everyone had to earn money. In the living room, the **drawing room**, there was often a **piano**. It showed wealth and education. Daughters were often given piano lessons.

In Switzerland the liberal middle class shaped the **federal state of 1848**. Liberals and Radicals had won the **Sonderbund War**. Their movement, the **Liberals**, held all seats in the Federal Council from 1848 to 1891. Only in 1891 was a Catholic Conservative, **Josef Zemp**, elected. Typical of the middle class was the **club**: gymnastics, singing and shooting clubs combined sociability with liberal ideas, and national festivals strengthened the feeling of belonging to one nation.

Many writers described middle-class life. Famous is the novel **Buddenbrooks** by **Thomas Mann** from 1901. Over four generations it tells of the decline of a merchant family from Lübeck. Thomas Mann received the **Nobel Prize in Literature** in 1929.

gewusst: The word Biedermeier goes back to an invented, narrow-minded figure from poems.
Thomas Mann spent his last years in Switzerland and died in Zurich in 1955.

teile.einleitung: Equal rights means that all people have the same rights, whether woman or man, and whatever their origin or religion. In Switzerland this goal was only reached step by step for women and men. Many important stages were only a few decades ago.
wichtigste: Since 14 June 1981, equality of women and men has been in the Swiss Federal Constitution.
Article 8, paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution demands equal pay for work of equal value.
Big women's strikes took place on 14 June 1991 and 14 June 2019.
The Gender Equality Act came into force on 1 July 1996.
Elisabeth Kopp was elected to the Federal Council in 1984 as the first woman.
Since the new marriage law of 1988, the husband is no longer the head of the family.
In September 2021 voters accepted “marriage for all” with about 64 per cent Yes.

abschnitte.text: **Equal rights** means that the law treats all people equally. Nobody may be disadvantaged because of their sex, origin, language, religion or a disability. This is set out in Article 8 of the Swiss Federal Constitution. But the difference from **actual equality** is important: equal rights in law do not automatically mean equal opportunities in everyday life.

For a long time women in Switzerland could neither vote nor take part in referendums. In 1959 Swiss men still rejected **votes for women** at federal level, with about 67 per cent voting No. Only on 7 February 1971 was it accepted. As the last canton, Appenzell Innerrhoden had to introduce votes for women in 1990 after a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court.

On 14 June 1981 the **equality article** was added to the Federal Constitution. Today Article 8, paragraph 3 demands, among other things, equal pay for women and men for work of equal value. The new marriage law was accepted in 1985 and came into force in 1988; since then the husband no longer counts as the “head of the family”. On 1 July 1996 the **Gender Equality Act** (GlG) came into force, which forbids discrimination at work.

The Gender Equality Act protects employees, for example in pay, hiring and promotion. Under this law, sexual harassment at work counts as discrimination. Thanks to the **easing of the burden of proof**, discrimination is presumed if it is made credible. Even so, women in Switzerland still earn less than men on average, and part of this difference cannot be explained.

Because the equality article was put into practice only slowly, the first nationwide **women's strike** took place on 14 June 1991. Hundreds of thousands of women stopped work or drew attention to themselves with actions. A second big strike followed on 14 June 2019; according to the organisers, over 500,000 people took part. Many wore the colour purple.

Equal rights are not only about women and men. Since 1 January 2007, same-sex couples in Switzerland can enter a **registered partnership**. On 26 September 2021 voters accepted **marriage for all** with about 64 per cent Yes. Since 1 July 2022, two women or two men can also marry.

begriffe.erklaerung: When someone is treated unfairly because of a characteristic such as sex or origin.
A Swiss law of 1996 that protects women and men at work.
Women and men receive the same pay for work of equal value.
The right of women to elect and to vote.

gewusst: Switzerland introduced votes for women at federal level only in 1971, much later than most countries in Europe.
14 June is a special date in Switzerland: on this day the equality article was accepted in 1981, and women's strikes were held in 1991 and 2019.
Since 2021, fathers in Switzerland have been entitled to two weeks of paid paternity leave.

teile.einleitung: The German Peasants' War was a great uprising of peasants, craftsmen and miners. It reached its high point in 1525 and was put down bloodily by the princes.
wichtigste: The Peasants' War reached its high point in 1525.
Uprisings took place above all in southern Germany, Thuringia and Austria.
The demands were set down in the Twelve Articles of Memmingen.
The peasants above all wanted to abolish serfdom.
At Frankenhausen the peasants under Thomas Müntzer were defeated.
The commander Georg Truchsess von Waldburg got the nickname Peasant Jörg.
It is estimated that about 70,000 rebels lost their lives.

abschnitte.text: The peasants had to pay their lords high **dues** and to work for them. Many were **serfs**: they belonged to their lord and, for example, were not allowed to move away freely or to marry without permission. In addition the lords restricted old rights, such as hunting and fishing. Through the **Reformation** the peasants read the Bible in a new way. They said that Christ had freed all people, so there should be no serfdom.

In March 1525 peasants in **Memmingen** wrote down their demands. These **Twelve Articles** demanded, for example, that every community be allowed to **choose its own pastor**. The peasants wanted lower dues and the end of serfdom. Thanks to the still young **printing press** the articles were printed quickly and spread widely. They are regarded as one of the first written demands for rights of freedom in Europe.

In spring 1525 peasants rose up in **southern Germany**, in **Thuringia** and in **Austria**. They joined together in large groups that were called **bands**. Even the knight **Götz von Berlichingen** for a time led a peasant band in the Odenwald. He had lost a hand in battle and wore an **iron hand**. The peasants, however, were poorly armed and hardly trained for war.

The princes sent well-equipped armies against the peasants. The army of the **Swabian League** was led by **Georg Truchsess von Waldburg**. Because he defeated the peasants again and again, he was called **Peasant Jörg**. In May 1525 the peasants under the preacher **Thomas Müntzer** were crushingly defeated in the **Battle of Frankenhausen** in Thuringia. In all about **70,000** rebels lost their lives, and many survivors were harshly punished.

gewusst: Martin Luther did not support the peasants. In 1525 he wrote a pamphlet in which he called on the princes to act harshly against the rebels.
There was a Peasants' War in Switzerland too: in 1653 peasants rose up in the Entlebuch and the Emmental, among other places.

teile.einleitung: Johannes Kepler was an astronomer and mathematician around 1600. He found out by what laws the planets move around the Sun. His laws of planetary motion still hold today.
wichtigste: Kepler was born in 1571 in Weil der Stadt in Württemberg, in present-day Germany.
In Prague he worked together with the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe.
He discovered that the planets move around the Sun in ellipses.
A planet moves fastest when it is close to the Sun.
Kepler improved the telescope with two curved lenses.
In his story “Somnium” he described a journey to the Moon.
From 2009 the Kepler space telescope searched for planets around other stars.

abschnitte.text: Johannes Kepler was born in **1571** in **Weil der Stadt**. He studied in Tübingen and was convinced early on that the Earth moves around the Sun, as **Copernicus** had taught. He first taught in Graz. In 1600 he went to **Prague** to the Danish astronomer **Tycho Brahe**. Brahe had observed the planets very precisely for years. After Brahe's death, Kepler became imperial mathematician.

Kepler calculated with Brahe's measurements for years. He found that the planets move around the Sun not in circles but in **ellipses**. An ellipse is a slightly stretched circle, and the Sun does not lie exactly in the middle. Also, a planet moves **faster when close to the Sun** and more slowly when further away. Later he found a third law about the times of the orbits.

Kepler also worked on light and on lenses. In **1611** he proposed a **telescope** with two lenses curved outwards. It shows the image upside down, but larger and with a wider field of view than the older telescope. It is called the **Keplerian telescope**. Many telescopes for the sky still work on this principle today.

Kepler also wrote the story **“Somnium”**, Latin for “dream”. In it he describes a journey to the **Moon** and how the Earth would look from there. It appeared only after his death and is one of the early stories about outer space. Kepler died in 1630 in Regensburg. The **Kepler space telescope**, launched in 2009, found thousands of planets around other stars.

gewusst: Kepler's mother was accused of being a witch. Kepler defended her himself in court, and she was released.
In 1604 Kepler observed a new bright star in the sky, a stellar explosion. It is now called Kepler's Supernova.

teile.einleitung: On the big sailing ships of the modern era, sailors were often away for months. Life on board was cramped, hard and sometimes dangerous. Food and drinking water had to be taken along for the whole journey.
wichtigste: On long voyages sailors ate hard bread, ship’s biscuit.
Many sailors slept in hammocks.
Drinking water was kept in wooden barrels.
Fresh fruit and vegetables were often missing, so many fell ill with scurvy.

abschnitte.text: On long voyages there was no fresh food. Sailors therefore ate **ship’s biscuit**, a very hard, dry bread. It hardly went off, but was so hard that it often had to be soaked. With it came salted meat and dried peas and beans. The **drinking water** was kept in **wooden barrels**. After a few weeks it often went bad and tasted foul.

Space was very tight on the ships. Many **sailors** therefore slept in **hammocks**, which were hung between beams. During the day they were rolled up so that there was room to work. The hammock swayed with the movements of the ship, so you did not fall out in rough seas. The idea comes from the people of the Caribbean.

Because fresh fruit and vegetables were missing, many sailors got **scurvy**. In this disease you become weak and your gums bleed. Today we know that the body gets too little **vitamin C** in this case. Later **lemons**, limes or sauerkraut were taken on board to prevent scurvy.

gewusst: The time on board was marked with a ship’s bell, which is called “striking the glasses”.

teile.einleitung: In October 1929 share prices collapsed on the stock exchange in New York. This stock market crash set off a worldwide economic crisis that lasted into the 1930s.
wichtigste: The crash began at the stock exchange on Wall Street in New York.
24 October 1929 is called “Black Thursday” in the USA.
Many Americans had bought shares with borrowed money.
The crash was followed by the Great Depression.
In Germany about 6 million people were registered as unemployed at the beginning of 1932.
From 1933 President Franklin D. Roosevelt fought the crisis with the New Deal.

abschnitte.text: In the 1920s share prices in the USA rose strongly. Many people wanted to get rich quickly. They bought **shares on credit**, that is, with **borrowed money**. They hoped to sell the shares later at a higher price. This only worked as long as prices kept rising.

On **24 October 1929** prices collapsed on the stock exchange on **Wall Street** in **New York**. Panic broke out, and everybody wanted to sell at the same time. In the USA this day is called **Black Thursday**. Because the news only reached Europe on Friday because of the time difference, people there often speak of “Black Friday”. Anyone who had bought on credit could no longer pay his debts.

The crash was followed by the **Great Depression**. Banks collapsed, firms went bankrupt, millions of people lost their jobs. President **Herbert Hoover** was accused of doing too little. Many countries introduced high **protective tariffs** to protect their economies. As a result world trade shrank even more. In **Germany** about **6 million** people were registered as unemployed at the beginning of 1932. The hardship strengthened radical parties.

In 1933 **Franklin D. Roosevelt** became president of the USA. With the **New Deal** the state created work through building projects such as roads and dams. It controlled the banks more strictly and introduced **social insurance**. Slowly the economy recovered.

Switzerland also suffered from the crisis. Especially the export industry, for example watches and textiles, sold much less abroad. **Unemployment** rose sharply in the 1930s. In 1936 Switzerland devalued the **franc** so that Swiss goods became cheaper abroad.

gewusst: The most important share index of the USA only reached its pre-crash level again in 1954.
Five days after Black Thursday came an even worse day with “Black Tuesday”.

teile.einleitung: The Eiffel Tower is the best known landmark of Paris. It was built for the World's Fair of 1889 and is one of the most visited structures in the world.
wichtigste: The Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889.
It is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose firm built it.
It is made of many thousands of parts of wrought iron.
The parts were joined with rivets.
At its opening it was about 300 metres high and for a long time the tallest structure in the world.
It was actually meant to be taken down again after about 20 years.

abschnitte.titel: A tower for the World's Fair
abschnitte.text: In 1889 a great **World's Fair** took place in Paris. It also recalled the French Revolution, which had begun 100 years earlier. As an entrance and eye-catcher a huge tower of iron was built. The firm of the engineer **Gustave Eiffel** built it. The building took about **two years**, and in spring **1889** the tower was finished.

The tower is made of many thousands of parts of **wrought iron**. They were prepared in a workshop and put together on the building site. Workers hammered glowing **rivets** into the holes of the parts. As they cooled, the rivets shrank and held the parts tight. So that the iron does not rust, the tower is **repainted** regularly.

At its opening the Eiffel Tower was **about 300 metres** high. This made it for a long time the **tallest structure in the world**. Only around 1930 was it overtaken by a skyscraper in New York. Today, with its antennas, it is a little taller than it was then. Visitors can climb by lift or by stairs to several **platforms** and look far out over Paris.

Many artists found the tower ugly at first and protested against it. It was also planned only for a certain time and was to be taken down after about **20 years**. But people discovered that it was very useful for **radio antennas**. That is why it stayed standing. Today it is the **landmark** of Paris and is visited by millions of people every year.

gewusst: Gustave Eiffel also built the iron framework inside the Statue of Liberty in New York.
In great heat the iron expands, so in summer the tower is a little taller than in winter.

teile.einleitung: The civil rights movement was a great movement in the USA that fought in the 1950s and 1960s for equal rights for African Americans. With court cases, boycotts, sit-ins and marches it resisted racial segregation. Its best known figures are Martin Luther King and Rosa Parks.
wichtigste: In many southern states of the USA a strict racial segregation applied for a long time, under the principle “separate but equal”.
In 1954 the Supreme Court, in Brown v. Board of Education, unanimously declared segregation in schools unconstitutional.
The arrest of Rosa Parks on 1 December 1955 set off the Montgomery bus boycott.
Martin Luther King relied on non-violent resistance.
Sit-ins and Freedom Rides made the injustice visible across the whole country.
On 2 July 1964 President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act.
In 1965 followed a law that protected the voting rights of Black people.

abschnitte.text: After the end of slavery in 1865 Black people in the USA did receive rights on paper, but in everyday life they were still treated unfairly. Especially in the southern states the so-called **Jim Crow laws** applied: Black and white people had to use separate schools, toilets, restaurants and seats on buses. The Supreme Court had confirmed the principle “separate but equal” in 1896 in the ruling Plessy v. Ferguson. In reality the facilities for Black people were almost always worse. Many Black people were also stopped from going to vote.

The organisation **NAACP**, founded in 1909, fought discrimination above all with court cases. Its lawyer **Thurgood Marshall** represented the plaintiffs in the case Brown v. Board of Education. In 1954 the nine judges decided unanimously, by 9 to 0, that separate schools break the Constitution. In 1967 Marshall himself became the first African American judge on the Supreme Court. Even so, many southern states resisted shared schools for years.

abschnitte.titel: Rosa Parks and the bus boycott
abschnitte.text: On 1 December 1955 the seamstress **Rosa Parks** in Montgomery (Alabama) refused to give up her seat on the bus to a white passenger. She was arrested. After that the Black residents of the city boycotted the buses for over a year and walked or shared cars. The boycott was led by the young minister **Martin Luther King**. In 1956 the Supreme Court decided that segregation on buses is forbidden.

On 1 February 1960 four Black students in Greensboro (North Carolina) sat down at a lunch counter that was meant only for white people, and simply stayed seated. Such **sit-ins** spread quickly to many cities. After a conference in April 1960 the student organisation **SNCC** came into being, which organised sit-ins and helped Black people to register as voters. From May 1961, in the **Freedom Rides**, Black and white activists travelled together on long-distance buses into the South and were sometimes brutally attacked there.

abschnitte.titel: March on Washington and new laws
abschnitte.text: On 28 August 1963 around 250,000 people demonstrated in Washington for jobs and freedom. There Martin Luther King gave his famous speech “I Have a Dream”. On 2 July 1964 President **Lyndon B. Johnson** signed the Civil Rights Act, which banned racial segregation in public places. Title VII of the law also forbids discrimination at work. Martin Luther King received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

abschnitte.titel: Selma and the right to vote
abschnitte.text: On 7 March 1965, **Bloody Sunday**, police in Selma (Alabama) attacked peaceful demonstrators on the Edmund Pettus Bridge with clubs and tear gas. The pictures on television shocked the whole nation. In the same year the **Voting Rights Act** was passed, which protected Black people from obstacles to voting. On 4 April 1968 Martin Luther King was murdered in Memphis. The fight against racism goes on to this day.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rights that all citizens of a state have equally, for example the right to vote.
People are separated because of their skin colour in schools, buses or restaurants.
Deliberately not using or buying something in order to put pressure on someone.
A protest in which people sit down peacefully and do not leave.

gewusst: The Montgomery bus boycott lasted 381 days.
Rosa Parks was not the first to refuse: months earlier 15-year-old Claudette Colvin had also refused to give up her seat.
In the USA the third Monday in January is a national holiday, Martin Luther King Day.

teile.einleitung: British India is the name for the time when Britain ruled large parts of South Asia. First a trading company governed, and from 1858 the British Crown ruled directly. In 1947 India became independent.
wichtigste: Until 1858 the British East India Company ruled large parts of India.
In 1857 Indian soldiers in British service, the sepoys, rose up.
From 1858 to 1947 the British Crown ruled directly, which is called the Raj.
The highest representative of the Crown in India was the Viceroy.
India was seen as the “jewel in the crown” of the British Empire.
Until 1911 Calcutta was the capital, afterwards Delhi.
On 15 August 1947 India became independent.

abschnitte.text: The **British East India Company** was a trading company from London. It traded in spices, cotton and tea. In the 18th century it gained more and more power in India. It had **its own armies** and soon ruled huge areas. Many soldiers in its armies were Indians.

The Indian soldiers of the British were called **sepoys**. In 1857 many of them mutinied. One reason was new cartridges that were said to be greased with beef and pork fat. This offended the religion of Hindus and Muslims. The uprising spread across northern India and was put down. Afterwards the East India Company lost its power.

From 1858 the British Crown ruled India directly. This rule is called the **Raj**, which means “rule” in Hindi. The **Viceroy** governed in the name of the British monarch. India was the most valuable colony and was seen as the “**jewel in the crown**”. It supplied raw materials, soldiers and a huge market for British goods.

From 1869 the **Suez Canal** greatly shortened the sea route from Britain to India. Ships no longer had to sail around the whole of Africa. In India the British built a large **railway network**. For a long time the capital was **Calcutta** in Bengal. In 1911 it was decided to move the capital to **Delhi**.

More and more Indians demanded **independence**. **Mahatma Gandhi**, who relied on non-violent resistance, became well known. On **15 August 1947** India became independent. At the same time the state of **Pakistan** came into being. During the partition a great many people had to leave their homes.

gewusst: In 1930 Gandhi led a famous march to the sea to protest against the British salt tax.
The East India Company was founded as early as 1600.

teile.einleitung: Colonialism in Asia means the rule of European powers, later also of the USA and Japan, over countries in South, South-East and East Asia. From the 16th to the 20th century they controlled trade, ports and whole countries such as India or Indonesia. Only after the Second World War did most Asian states become independent again.
wichtigste: The First Opium War began because China acted against British opium trading.
The Treaty of Nanking ended the war in 1842 and forced China to open five ports.
China had to conclude the “Unequal Treaties” under pressure.
In 1887 the French colony of Indochina was formed.
In the 19th century the Netherlands ruled what is now Indonesia.
Siam, today’s Thailand, was the only country in South-East Asia to remain free of colonial rule.
From 1868 Japan modernised quickly on the Western model.

abschnitte.text: In 1498 the Portuguese Vasco da Gama reached India by sea. Portugal founded bases such as Goa and Macau in order to trade in **spices**. In the 17th century the Dutch **East India Company** took over many trading posts and in 1619 founded Batavia, today’s Jakarta. In this way present-day Indonesia came under Dutch rule.

From the 18th century the British East India Company conquered large parts of India. After a great uprising in 1857 the British state took over direct rule in 1858. From 1877 Queen Victoria bore the title “Empress of India”. Only in 1947, after long non-violent resistance led by Mahatma **Gandhi**, did India become independent.

In the 19th century Britain sold large quantities of **opium** to China. When China acted against this, the First Opium War broke out, ended by the Treaty of Nanking in 1842. China had to open five ports and cede Hong Kong to Britain. Further **Unequal Treaties** followed, and in 1898 the German Empire leased Kiautschou for 99 years.

Around 1900 the so-called Boxers in China violently resisted foreigners and Christians. Eight powers joined forces and put down the **Boxer Rebellion**. At the farewell of his troops, the German Kaiser Wilhelm II gave the notorious **Hun speech**, in which he called for cruel harshness. China afterwards had to pay high compensation.

In 1887 France formed the colony of **French Indochina** from territories of today’s Vietnam, Cambodia and later Laos. After the Second World War Vietnamese fighters for independence fought against France. With the Battle of Dien Bien Phu, French rule ended in 1954, and the peace conference on it took place in Geneva. Siam, today’s Thailand, on the other hand, stayed independent thanks to skilful diplomacy.

From 1868 Japan responded to the threat from the West with the **Meiji Restoration**. The country built railways, factories and a modern army. Soon Japan itself became a colonial power and conquered Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910. After the Second World War Japan lost all its colonies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A drug made from poppies that is highly addictive.
Treaties that China had to conclude under pressure and that only benefited the foreign powers.
A powerful trading company that traded in Asia and even ruled territories.
You may use a territory for a set time without it belonging to you.

gewusst: Hong Kong was British until 1997 and Macau Portuguese until 1999.
The famous Tsingtao brewery in China was founded in 1903, in the time of German rule in Kiautschou.

teile.einleitung: The war in Afghanistan began in October 2001, when the USA and its allies overthrew the Taliban government after the terrorist attacks of 11 September. For almost 20 years international troops were in the country. In August 2021 the Taliban took power again as the last Western soldiers withdrew.
wichtigste: On 7 October 2001 Operation Enduring Freedom by the USA and its allies began.
The Northern Alliance took Kabul without a fight on 13 November 2001.
At the Petersberg near Bonn, Hamid Karzai became head of the interim government at the end of 2001.
UN Resolution 1386 created the international security force ISAF in December 2001.
In 2015 the NATO training mission Resolute Support followed.
On 29 February 2020 the USA and the Taliban concluded the Doha Agreement.
On 15 August 2021 the Taliban took Kabul, and President Ashraf Ghani fled.
On 30 August 2021 the last US soldiers left Afghanistan.

abschnitte.text: Afghanistan is a mountainous country in Central Asia. From 1979 to 1989 the Soviet Union fought there against resistance fighters, the **mujahideen**. A civil war followed, and from 1996 the radical Islamist **Taliban** ruled most of the country. They banned girls from going to school and gave shelter to the terrorist group al-Qaeda.

After the attacks of 11 September 2001 in the USA, the USA demanded the extradition of al-Qaeda leader **Osama bin Laden**. The Taliban refused. On 7 October 2001 Operation Enduring Freedom began with air strikes. Together with the Afghan **Northern Alliance**, the Taliban were quickly driven out, and Kabul fell on 13 November 2001.

At the Petersberg near Bonn, Hamid Karzai was chosen as head of the interim government at the end of 2001. The international security force **ISAF** was to provide security, later under the leadership of NATO. Schools were built, and girls were allowed to learn again. But the Taliban kept on fighting, and many soldiers and civilians died in attacks and battles.

In 2011 Osama bin Laden was killed in Pakistan by US special forces. In 2015 the training mission **Resolute Support** replaced ISAF. In the **Doha** Agreement of 29 February 2020 the USA agreed with the Taliban on the withdrawal of all troops. The Afghan government was not involved in this agreement.

In the summer of 2021 the Taliban conquered almost the whole country in a few weeks. On 15 August 2021 they entered Kabul, and President Ashraf Ghani fled abroad. At the airport thousands of people desperately tried to leave the country. On 30 August 2021 the last US soldiers flew out.

Since 2021 the Taliban have ruled Afghanistan again with strict rules. Girls are no longer allowed to go to school after sixth grade, and women are heavily restricted. Many people suffer from poverty and hunger and depend on **humanitarian aid**. Switzerland too supports the population with aid projects, and many refugees from Afghanistan live here today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A radical Islamist movement that ruled Afghanistan from 1996 to 2001 and again since 2021.
A terror network that carried out the attacks of 11 September 2001.
The International Security Assistance Force for Afghanistan from 2001 to 2014.
Help for people in need, for example with food, water and medicine.

gewusst: The Afghanistan war was the longest war in the history of the USA.
Afghanistan has no access to the sea and is largely covered by high mountains such as the Hindu Kush.

teile.einleitung: The Long March was a huge retreat of the Chinese communists in the years 1934 and 1935. They fled from the troops of the Nationalist government right across China. On this march Mao Zedong became the most important leader of the Party.
wichtigste: The Long March began in 1934.
The communists set out from the province of Jiangxi.
At the Zunyi Conference in January 1935 Mao Zedong gained decisive influence.
In 1935 the Red Army captured the Luding Bridge over the Dadu River.
The march ended in 1935 in the province of Shaanxi, and the centre later became Yan’an.

abschnitte.text: In the 1930s the **Nationalists** under Chiang Kai-shek fought in China against the **communists**. The communists had built up a territory of their own in the province of **Jiangxi**. In 1934 they were encircled there by the government’s troops. In October **1934** they broke out and began the **Long March**. Tens of thousands of soldiers and helpers set off.

On the way the **Red Army** suffered heavy losses. In January **1935** the Party leadership met in the city of Zunyi. At this **Zunyi Conference** the previous leadership was criticised. **Mao Zedong** gained decisive influence there. From then on he strongly helped to determine the direction of the march.

The march led over high mountains, through swamps and across raging rivers. A famous action in 1935 was the capture of the **Luding Bridge**, a **chain bridge** over the **Dadu** River. In communist historiography it is celebrated as a heroic deed. Historians do not agree, however, on exactly how it went. In October **1935** Mao’s troop reached the province of **Shaanxi**, and later the city of **Yan’an** became their centre.

gewusst: Only a small part of the people who set out in Jiangxi arrived at the end in Shaanxi.
In the People’s Republic of China the Long March is still revered today as an important founding myth.

teile.einleitung: Maria Theresa was one of the best-known rulers in Europe. From 1740 she reigned for forty years over the lands of the Habsburgs, which included Austria, Hungary and Bohemia. With many reforms she changed her realm greatly.
wichtigste: Maria Theresa lived from 1717 to 1780 and belonged to the Habsburg family.
Thanks to the Pragmatic Sanction she could inherit the Habsburg lands as a woman.
She became ruler in 1740 at the age of 23.
Right afterwards the War of the Austrian Succession broke out.
She had 16 children, among them Marie Antoinette, who became Queen of France.
In 1774 she introduced compulsory schooling.
She had Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna extended into her summer residence.

abschnitte.text: Maria Theresa was born in Vienna in 1717. She belonged to the **Habsburgs**, one of the most powerful ruling families in Europe. Until then only men were allowed to inherit the Habsburg lands. Her father, Emperor Charles VI, had no son. He therefore issued a law, the **Pragmatic Sanction**, so that a daughter could inherit too. In 1740 he died, and Maria Theresa became ruler at the age of 23.

Several princes did not want to recognise the young woman’s inheritance. So in 1740 the **War of the Austrian Succession** began, which lasted until 1748. In it the Prussian king Frederick II conquered the rich land of **Silesia**. Maria Theresa was able to keep her other lands, however. Her husband Francis Stephen was elected emperor in 1745. The Seven Years’ War followed later, in which Silesia nevertheless remained Prussian.

Maria Theresa wanted to make her realm stronger and better organised. She reorganised the **administration** and built up a standing army. In 1774 she introduced **compulsory schooling**: all children were to learn to read, write and do sums. For this, new schools arose in many villages. These reforms had effects long after her death.

Maria Theresa had **16 children**. Her son Joseph II followed her as ruler. Many daughters married into other royal houses so that Austria had good allies. The best known is **Marie Antoinette**, who became Queen of France. In Vienna Maria Theresa had **Schönbrunn Palace** extended into her splendid summer residence. She died in Vienna in 1780.

gewusst: The Maria Theresa thaler, a silver coin with her picture, is still minted today with the date 1780.
The name of the Habsburgs comes from the Habsburg, a castle in what is now the canton of Aargau.

teile.einleitung: John Locke was an English philosopher and doctor who lived from 1632 to 1704. He is seen as one of the fathers of the Enlightenment and of liberalism. His idea that every person has natural rights to life, liberty and property is still found today in many constitutions.
wichtigste: According to Locke, the state must above all protect people's life, liberty and property.
According to Locke, a government needs the consent of the governed.
If a government violates the rights of citizens, they may resist it and remove it.
With the image of the “tabula rasa” he said that the mind is empty at birth.
In 1683 Locke fled into exile in the Netherlands.
He distinguished the legislative, the executive and the federative as powers of the state.
His ideas influenced the American Declaration of Independence of 1776.

abschnitte.text: Locke was born on 29 August 1632 in Wrington in south-west England. He studied philosophy and medicine in Oxford. Later he worked as a doctor and adviser to the politician Lord Ashley, later the Earl of Shaftesbury. Because of political persecution he fled into **exile** in the Netherlands in 1683 and only returned in 1689, after the Glorious Revolution.

In his “Two Treatises of Government” Locke explains that people are by nature free and equal. They found a state so that it protects their **natural rights**. A government is only lawful if the governed consent. If it breaks this trust, the people have a **right of resistance**.

In his “Essay Concerning Human Understanding” of 1690, Locke describes the mind at birth as a **tabula rasa**, that is, a blank slate. According to him, all knowledge comes from experience, through the senses and thought. This view is called **empiricism**. With it he contradicted philosophers who believed that some ideas are inborn.

In his “Letter Concerning Toleration”, Locke demanded that the state should not persecute people because of their faith. Faith, he said, cannot be produced by force. However, he expressly excluded atheists from **toleration**. For its time the text was nevertheless an important step towards freedom of religion.

Locke's ideas shaped the American **Declaration of Independence** of 1776. Thomas Jefferson replaced Locke's term “property” there with “the pursuit of happiness”. The idea of the **separation of powers**, which Montesquieu developed further later, also goes back partly to Locke. Locke died on 28 October 1704 in Essex.

begriffe.erklaerung: A school of thought that puts the freedom of the individual at the centre.
Latin for “blank slate”, an image for a mind without inborn knowledge.
The teaching that all knowledge comes from experience and observation.
Dividing the power of the state between different bodies so that nobody has too much power.

gewusst: Locke first published his main political works without his name, because they were dangerous.
Locke also wrote a book about bringing up children, in which he recommended play and kindness instead of strictness.

teile.einleitung: The euro is the common currency of many countries of the European Union. Since 1 January 2002 people in the eurozone have paid with euro coins and euro banknotes.
wichtigste: The euro was first introduced in 1999 as book money.
Cash has existed since 1 January 2002.
When cash was introduced, twelve countries had the euro.
The European Central Bank has its seat in Frankfurt am Main.
In Germany the euro replaced the Deutsche Mark.
The banknotes show windows and gateways in different building styles.
Switzerland has the franc, not the euro.

abschnitte.text: In the past every country in Europe had its own money, such as the **Deutsche Mark**, the French franc or the Italian lira. In 1999 the **euro** was first introduced as **book money**, that is, only for transfers and accounts. On **1 January 2002** the coins and banknotes came. At that time **twelve countries** paid with the euro. Since then more have joined, and in 2023 there were 20.

The **European Central Bank**, the ECB for short, is responsible for the euro. Its seat is in **Frankfurt am Main**. It sets the **monetary policy** of the eurozone, for example the level of interest rates. Its most important aim is that prices stay stable. In Germany the mark was exchanged at a fixed rate: one euro was equal to **1.95583 marks**.

The **banknotes** are the same in all euro countries. On the front they show invented **windows and gateways** from different periods of European architecture, on the back **bridges**. In this way no single country is favoured. With the **coins** the value side is the same everywhere. Each country designs the **reverse** itself. Even so all coins are valid in the whole eurozone.

Switzerland is not a member of the EU and pays with the **Swiss franc**. Because it trades a great deal with its neighbours, the rate against the euro is still very important. From 2011 the **Swiss National Bank** prevented one euro from costing less than **1.20 francs**. This **minimum rate** was meant to protect the export industry. On **15 January 2015** the National Bank unexpectedly ended it, and the franc rose sharply.

gewusst: The bridges on the euro banknotes are invented. In the Dutch town of Spijkenisse they were later rebuilt as real bridges.
The sign € recalls the Greek letter epsilon and the E of Europe.

teile.einleitung: Concentration camps, KZ for short, were camps in which the National Socialists in Germany from 1933 imprisoned, tortured and murdered people without a court verdict. At first it affected political opponents, later above all Jews, Sinti and Roma and many other persecuted groups. The camps are a central part of the Holocaust, the genocide of the European Jews.
wichtigste: Dachau was built in March 1933 as one of the first permanent concentration camps.
Dachau later served as a model for other camps.
In the first camps mainly political opponents such as communists and social democrats were imprisoned.
“Extermination through labour” meant the deliberate death of prisoners through forced labour, hunger and disease.
In extermination camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau millions of people were murdered.
The Dachau camp was liberated by US troops on 29 April 1945.
Today memorial sites commemorate the victims.

abschnitte.text: Shortly after Adolf Hitler took power in January 1933 the first camps arose. In March 1933 **Dachau** near Munich was opened and later served as a model for further camps. At first political opponents such as communists and social democrats were imprisoned. The camps were run by the **SS**, an organisation of the National Socialists.

Soon more and more groups were taken to the camps: **Jews**, Sinti and Roma, Jehovah’s Witnesses, homosexual men and people who were regarded as “asocial”. In the Second World War prisoners from all over Europe were added, such as prisoners of war and resistance fighters. The prisoners had to wear striped clothing and coloured triangles showing their group. Their names were often replaced by numbers.

The prisoners had to do **forced labour** under terrible conditions, for example in quarries or for armaments firms. They got hardly any food, were poorly clothed and were beaten. The National Socialists called this “extermination through labour”, because many people were meant to die in the process. Diseases such as typhus spread quickly.

From 1941 the National Socialists built **extermination camps** in occupied Poland, such as Treblinka, Sobibor and Auschwitz-Birkenau. There people were deliberately murdered, most of them in gas chambers. In Auschwitz alone about 1.1 million people died. In all, the National Socialists murdered around six million Jews in the **Holocaust**.

In 1945 Allied troops liberated the camps. The Red Army reached Auschwitz on 27 January 1945, and US troops liberated Dachau on 29 April 1945. The soldiers found starved survivors and thousands of dead. 27 January is now the international **Holocaust Remembrance Day**.

At many former camp sites there are now **memorial sites** that school classes can visit. Survivors such as Anne Frank’s father Otto Frank or the writer Primo Levi told what had happened. Switzerland also deals with its role, for during the war it turned back many Jewish refugees at the border. The St Gallen police commander **Paul Grüninger**, on the other hand, saved hundreds of refugees and was punished for it; he was only rehabilitated in 1995.

begriffe.erklaerung: The genocide by the National Socialists of around six million Jews.
A feared organisation of the National Socialists that ran the camps.
Work that people are forced to do against their will.
A place where the victims are remembered and where you can learn about history.

gewusst: Above the gate of many camps stood the cynical slogan “Arbeit macht frei” (work sets you free).
Anne Frank, whose diary is world famous, died in early 1945 in the Bergen-Belsen camp.

teile.einleitung: Tall factory chimneys are a sign of industrialisation. They led the smoke of the furnaces and steam engines up into the air and shaped the look of many towns.
wichtigste: Factory chimneys led the smoke away from the furnaces.
A tall chimney draws better than a low one.
Many chimneys were built of bricks.
In the factories mainly coal was burned.
The smoke put soot on houses and washing.
In London smoke and fog often made smog.
The dirty air made many people ill.

abschnitte.text: In the factories of **industrialisation** big furnaces and **steam engines** ran. This produced a lot of smoke. A tall **chimney** was meant to lead the smoke high into the air so that it would not hang directly between the houses. A tall chimney also has a better **draught**. Warm air rises in the chimney and sucks fresh air into the fire. In this way it burns more strongly.

Many factory chimneys were built of **bricks**. Bricks can stand great **heat** and do not burn. At the bottom the chimneys were wide and became narrower towards the top. In this way they stood firmly. Many old chimneys of red brick still stand today, in Switzerland too, often as a **monument** to a past industrial age.

The most important fuel was **coal**. When burned, it gives off a lot of dark smoke. In the smoke there are many black particles, the **soot**. It settled on walls, roofs and freshly washed washing and made everything dark. In smoky parts of England even a moth, the **peppered moth**, became more often dark. On the sooty trees birds easily saw the pale moths, and the dark ones survived better.

In **London** the smoke often mixed with fog. This made **smog**, a word from “smoke” and “fog”. The dirty air irritated the lungs. Many people in industrial towns suffered from **coughs** and **lung diseases**. In December 1952 a particularly thick smog lay over London for days, and thousands of people died of the effects. Afterwards laws for **clean air** were passed.

Today factories and power stations have **filters** that hold back a large part of the pollutants. Many no longer heat with coal, but with gas or electricity. In Switzerland laws regulate how many pollutants may get into the air. The air in the towns is therefore much cleaner than in the time of the smoking chimneys.

gewusst: The peppered moth is a well-known example of how animals can adapt to a changed environment.
When the air later became cleaner, the pale peppered moths became more common again.

teile.einleitung: Fordism is the name for a way of making goods and organising the economy. The name goes back to the car maker Henry Ford, who combined assembly line work, high wages and mass production.
wichtigste: From 1908 Ford built the Model T in mass production.
In 1913 Ford introduced the moving assembly line at the Highland Park plant.
In 1914 Ford introduced a daily wage of 5 dollars.
Fordism was built on Taylorism.
Antonio Gramsci coined the term in his Prison Notebooks.
In 1936 Charlie Chaplin caricatured assembly line work in the film “Modern Times”.
The model shaped the industrial countries until the 1970s.

abschnitte.text: From **1908** Ford built the **Model T**, the “Tin Lizzie”. In **1913** he introduced the **moving assembly line** at the **Highland Park** plant. Now the vehicle moved to the worker and no longer the other way round. The assembly time of a chassis fell from over **12 hours** to about **1.5 hours**. By 1927 about **15 million** were built, and the car became affordable for broad sections of society.

Fordism was built on **Taylorism**. **Frederick Winslow Taylor** developed “scientific management”. He broke work down into the **smallest steps** and measured with a stopwatch how long each step takes. In this way every movement was to be as efficient as possible. Ford combined this idea with the assembly line. Planning and carrying out the work were thereby strictly separated.

The monotonous work led to a high **turnover**, and many workers quickly quit again. In **1914** Ford therefore introduced a **daily wage of 5 dollars**, which roughly doubled pay. The workers stayed longer and could more easily buy a car themselves. This is a core of Fordism: the **mass production** of standardised goods lowers the cost per item, and higher wages create **purchasing power** for **mass consumption**.

The term **Fordism** was coined by the Italian thinker **Antonio Gramsci**. In the prison of fascist Italy he wrote about “Americanism and Fordism” and saw in it a new form of work and society. Criticism also came from art: in the film **“Modern Times”** of 1936 **Charlie Chaplin** plays a worker who tightens screws on an assembly line and in the end gets caught in the machine.

The Fordist model shaped the **industrial countries** until the **1970s**, in Europe and Switzerland too. After that it fell into crisis. Customers wanted more **choice**, and new technology such as computers changed production. Experts therefore speak of **post-Fordism**. Since then firms often make smaller quantities in many variants and work more flexibly.

gewusst: For a time Ford had it checked how his workers lived at home before they received the full wage.
Ford saw the idea of passing work along in a row, among other places, in the big slaughterhouses of Chicago.

teile.einleitung: Giuseppe Garibaldi was a freedom fighter of the 19th century. He is seen as one of the most important heroes of Italian unification, that is, the creation of today's state of Italy.
wichtigste: Garibaldi was born in 1807 in Nice, which today belongs to France.
For many years he lived in exile and fought in Brazil and Uruguay.
That is why he is called the “Hero of Two Worlds”.
In 1860 he landed in Sicily with about a thousand volunteers: the “Expedition of the Thousand”.
His fighters wore red shirts and were therefore called Redshirts.
He conquered Sicily and southern Italy and handed them over to the King of Sardinia-Piedmont.
In 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was created.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the 19th century there was no united Italy yet. The peninsula was divided into several states, for example the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont, the Papal States of the Pope and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in the south. Large parts of the north belonged to Austria. Many people wanted a common state. This movement is called the **Risorgimento**, in English roughly “resurgence”.

Garibaldi was born in 1807 in **Nice** and went to sea as a young man. Because he had taken part in an uprising, he had to flee. For years he lived in **South America** and fought there in Brazil and Uruguay for the independence of regions and republics. In 1848 he returned to Italy. Because he fought on two continents, he is called the **“Hero of Two Worlds”**.

In May 1860 Garibaldi landed at **Marsala** in **Sicily** with about a thousand volunteers. This undertaking is called the **“Expedition of the Thousand”**. His fighters wore red shirts and were therefore called **Redshirts**. Within a few months they conquered Sicily and then southern Italy with Naples. Many people supported him along the way.

Garibaldi did not want to become king himself. He handed the conquered territories over to King **Victor Emmanuel II** of Sardinia-Piedmont. In 1861 the **Kingdom of Italy** was proclaimed. Rome and Venice only joined a few years later. Garibaldi withdrew to the little island of **Caprera** and died there in 1882.

gewusst: In many Italian towns, streets and squares are named after Garibaldi.
Nice, Garibaldi's home town, was handed over to France in 1860. Garibaldi was very unhappy about it.

teile.einleitung: The Founders' Crash (Gründerkrach) was a big stock market crash in 1873. It began in Vienna and ended a time in which very many new companies had been founded in central Europe.
wichtigste: On 9 May 1873 prices collapsed on the Vienna stock exchange.
Beforehand there had been a speculative bubble of overvalued joint-stock companies.
French war reparations of 5 billion francs fuelled the boom in the German Empire.
In the same year a World's Fair was held in Vienna.
In September 1873 the bank Jay Cooke & Company collapsed in the USA.
After that came a period, until about 1896, which is called the Long Depression.
Bismarck responded in 1879 with protective tariffs on grain and iron.

abschnitte.text: After the **Franco-Prussian War** of 1870/71, France had to pay **5 billion francs** to the new German Empire under the Treaty of Frankfurt. A lot of money flowed into the economy. At the same time the rules for **joint-stock companies** were relaxed. In a short time countless new companies were founded, for example for railways, banks and buildings. These years are called the **Gründerzeit**, the “founders' era”.

Many people bought shares because they wanted to get rich quickly. This is called **speculation**. But the new companies were often worth much less than their shares cost. A **speculative bubble** formed. When confidence suddenly disappears, everyone wants to sell at once, and prices crash.

On 1 May 1873 the **World's Fair** opened in Vienna. Only a few days later, on **9 May 1873**, prices collapsed on the **Vienna stock exchange**. The day went down in history as “Black Friday”. Many companies and banks went bankrupt, and the World's Fair had fewer visitors than hoped. In the autumn the crisis also reached Berlin.

In September 1873 the bank **Jay Cooke & Company** collapsed in the USA, having overreached itself with a railway. The New York stock exchange had to close for a time. A long period followed with falling prices and weak growth until about 1896. It is called the **Long Depression**. Industry did, however, partly keep growing.

Farmers and heavy industry in the German Empire suffered from cheap competition from abroad. Chancellor **Otto von Bismarck** therefore introduced **protective tariffs** on grain and iron in **1879**. A tariff is a charge on imported goods. This ended the era of **free trade** in the German Empire.

gewusst: The word “Gründerzeit” is also used for many magnificent residential buildings that were built in towns and cities in those years.
The crash of 1873 is seen as one of the first economic crises to affect several continents.

teile.einleitung: An electric car runs on an electric motor instead of a petrol or diesel engine. It stores the electricity for this in a large battery, which you charge at a socket or at a charging station.
wichtigste: An electric car is “filled up” with electricity.
The electricity is stored in a large battery, usually under the floor.
An electric car has no exhaust pipe and gives off no exhaust gases when driving.
Electric cars have existed for over 100 years.
On the road you charge at a charging station.
New electric cars make an artificial sound when driving slowly.
A hybrid car has an electric motor and a petrol engine.

abschnitte.text: An electric car runs on an **electric motor**. The electricity comes from a large **battery**, which usually lies under the floor of the car. When it is empty, you have to charge it again. This can be done at home at a **socket** or at a **wallbox**. On the road there are **charging stations** at car parks, service areas and filling stations. There you plug a cable into the car.

A petrol car burns fuel, and this produces **exhaust gases** that leave through the **exhaust pipe**. An electric car burns nothing and so needs no exhaust pipe. When driving it gives off no exhaust gases. How good for the environment it is overall, however, also depends on how the **electricity** is produced and how much energy is needed to build the battery. In Switzerland a large part of the electricity comes from **hydropower**.

Electric motors are very **quiet**. This is pleasant, but can be dangerous, because pedestrians and cyclists cannot hear the car. That is why new electric cars make an **artificial sound** when driving slowly. When braking the motor can also work as a **generator** and put electricity back into the battery. In this way energy is saved.

Electric cars are not new. As early as **around 1900** many electric cars drove on the roads. Later **petrol cars** became more popular, because they could go much further and petrol was cheap. Only in the last decades did batteries get better, and electric cars came back. An in-between solution is the **hybrid car**: “hybrid” means mixed, and it has an electric motor and a combustion engine.

gewusst: The first car to go faster than 100 kilometres per hour was an electric car: “La Jamais Contente” managed it in 1899.
An electric car needs no gearbox with many gears, because the electric motor has plenty of power even when starting off.

teile.einleitung: “Blitzkrieg” is the name for the fast campaigns of the German Wehrmacht at the start of the Second World War, above all in Poland in 1939 and in France in 1940. Tanks, aircraft and radio were used closely together in order to defeat the enemy in a few weeks. Historians stress today that the word was above all a propaganda term and not a finished military doctrine.
wichtigste: Blitzkrieg is the name for fast attacks with tanks and aircraft that are meant to take the enemy by surprise.
Well-known examples are the invasion of Poland in 1939 and the campaign in the West against France in 1940.
The dive bomber Junkers Ju 87, called the “Stuka”, became the symbol of Blitzkrieg.
Radio sets in the tanks allowed fast command of the units.
Heinz Guderian is regarded as an important pioneer of the German tank arm.
The historian Karl-Heinz Frieser describes Blitzkrieg as a propaganda slogan, not a finished doctrine.
In the Soviet Union the principle failed in 1941, because the war could not be decided quickly.

abschnitte.text: **Blitzkrieg** means a way of waging war in which an enemy is defeated in a short time by very fast, surprising attacks. Fast tank units pushed deep into enemy territory while aircraft attacked from above. The aim was often to **encircle** the enemy and cut him off from supplies. In this way Germany wanted to avoid a long war of position like the First World War, which it could hardly win.

An important pioneer was General **Heinz Guderian**, who as early as the 1930s argued for independent tank divisions. One advantage of the German tanks was that they were equipped with **radio sets** and so could quickly receive new orders. The Luftwaffe supported the tanks directly, especially with the dive bomber **Junkers Ju 87**, the “Stuka”. Its howling siren in the dive was meant to put additional fear into the enemy.

On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded **Poland**, and after a few weeks the country was defeated, also because the Soviet Union attacked from the east on 17 September. In May 1940 the Wehrmacht attacked France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. Tanks pushed forward by surprise through the wooded region of the **Ardennes**, which was thought to be hardly passable, and reached the English Channel. After only about six weeks France had to sign an armistice on 22 June 1940.

The historian **Karl-Heinz Frieser** showed in his book “The Blitzkrieg Legend” that there was no finished Blitzkrieg plan. Much was improvisation, luck and mistakes by the enemy. Besides, the Wehrmacht was by no means entirely modern: a large part of the troops marched on foot and transported guns and supplies by **horse**. The propaganda of Joseph Goebbels nevertheless presented the victories as proof of Germany's superiority.

On 22 June 1941 Germany attacked the **Soviet Union** and wanted to defeat it in a few months. Despite great early successes this did not work, because the country was huge and the Red Army could keep raising new troops. In December 1941 the attack got stuck in winter before Moscow. With that the plan of a short war had finally failed, and a long, costly war of attrition began.

The fast German victories of 1940 also frightened **Switzerland**, which was now almost completely surrounded by the Axis powers. General Henri Guisan decided to concentrate the army above all in the Alpine region, in the so-called **Reduit**. On 25 July 1940 he summoned the officers to the Rütli Report to strengthen the will to resist. An attack was to become so costly for any enemy that it would not be worthwhile.

begriffe.erklaerung: The armed forces of National Socialist Germany from 1935 to 1945.
Enemy troops are surrounded from all sides and cut off.
Deliberately influencing people, often with one-sided or false information.
The defensive position of the Swiss army in the Alps in the Second World War.

gewusst: The word Blitzkrieg was used rather rarely in Germany itself, but it became very well known abroad.
In English the German word “Blitz” is still used today for the German air raids on London in 1940 and 1941.
In 1940 many French tanks were more heavily armoured than the German ones, but often without a radio.

t1n5zzd7.t: End of the Second World War in Europe

teile.einleitung: In spring 1945 the Second World War in Europe came to an end after almost six years. On 8 May 1945 the unconditional surrender of the German Wehrmacht came into force. For millions of people this meant peace, but Europe lay in ruins and had to be rebuilt.
wichtigste: The unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht came into force on 8 May 1945 at 23.01.
In Russia the victory is celebrated on 9 May, because in Moscow, because of the time difference, it was already after midnight.
On 25 April 1945 American and Soviet soldiers met on the Elbe at Torgau.
Hitler took his own life in Berlin on 30 April 1945 and named Karl Dönitz as his successor.
With the Berlin Declaration of 5 June 1945 the four victorious powers took over government in Germany.
In the whole of the Second World War, according to estimates, over 60 million people died.
Switzerland was spared, but on 1 April 1944 American aircraft bombed Schaffhausen by mistake.

abschnitte.text: Since 1943 the German Wehrmacht had been in retreat everywhere. In June 1944 the western **Allies** landed in Normandy, and in the east the Soviet **Red Army** advanced further and further. At the start of 1945 the troops of both sides crossed the German borders. On 25 April 1945 American and Soviet soldiers met on the Elbe at **Torgau**. This “Elbe Day” showed that Germany was split into two parts.

In April 1945 the Red Army began the attack on **Berlin**. Hitler hid in a bunker under the Reich Chancellery and took his own life on 30 April 1945. In his political testament he named Grand Admiral **Karl Dönitz** as his successor at the head of the state. On 2 May the defenders of Berlin surrendered. The city was largely destroyed.

In the night before 7 May 1945 Colonel General **Alfred Jodl** signed the first instrument of surrender in the French city of **Reims**. At the wish of the Soviet Union the signing was repeated in Berlin-Karlshorst in the night from 8 to 9 May. The **unconditional surrender** came into force on 8 May 1945 at 23.01 Central European Time. In Moscow it was already 9 May, which is why Russia celebrates the victory one day later than Western Europe.

The Dönitz government in Flensburg was not recognised by the Allies and was arrested on 23 May 1945. With the **Berlin Declaration** of 5 June 1945 the USA, the Soviet Union, Britain and France took over supreme governmental authority in Germany. The country was divided into four **occupation zones**, and Berlin into four sectors. In summer 1945 the victorious powers discussed the future of Germany at the Potsdam Conference. In Asia the war went on until Japan surrendered on 2 September 1945.

In the Second World War, according to estimates, over 60 million people lost their lives, many of them civilians. The National Socialists had murdered about six million Jews, and this genocide is called the **Holocaust** or Shoah. When Allied soldiers freed the **concentration camps**, they saw unimaginable suffering. Millions of people had lost their homes and were on the move as refugees. Cities such as Berlin, Dresden or Warsaw lay in ruins.

abschnitte.titel: Switzerland at the end of the war
abschnitte.text: Switzerland was neutral throughout the war and was not attacked. Even so there were victims: on 1 April 1944 American aircraft bombed **Schaffhausen** by mistake, and about 40 people died. The army under General **Henri Guisan** had guarded the borders for years. When the news of the end of the war came on 8 May 1945, church bells rang all over Switzerland. Many people celebrated in the streets that the war in Europe was over.

begriffe.erklaerung: An army gives up the fight and yields.
Without conditions: the losers can no longer demand or negotiate anything.
Partners in an alliance. Mainly meant here are the USA, Britain, the Soviet Union and France.
A territory that was administered after the war by one of the victorious powers.

gewusst: In many countries 8 May is celebrated as Liberation Day or Victory in Europe Day.
The surrender was signed twice, first in Reims and then once more in Berlin-Karlshorst.
In the bombing of Schaffhausen in 1944 the Museum zu Allerheiligen was also badly damaged.

teile.einleitung: The running machine is the forerunner of the bicycle. Karl Drais invented it and rode it for the first time in 1817. You sat on it and pushed yourself along with your feet on the ground.
wichtigste: Karl Drais invented the running machine, the forerunner of the bicycle.
He rode it for the first time in 1817.
Karl Drais was born in Karlsruhe.
The running machine was mainly made of wood.
You moved it forward with your feet on the ground.
After its inventor it is also called a draisine.
It had no pedals yet; today the balance bike for children works in a similar way.

abschnitte.text: **Karl Drais** was born in **Karlsruhe** in 1785. He was a forestry official and an enthusiastic inventor. He thought up many machines. Best known became his **running machine**. In **1817** he rode it for the first time, setting off from Mannheim on a road. For the route he needed much less time than on foot.

The running machine was mainly made of **wood**. It had two wheels one behind the other and a seat in the middle. With a bar you could steer the front wheel. But there were **no pedals** yet. You sat on it and pushed yourself along alternately **with your feet on the ground**. When you had enough momentum, you could lift your feet and roll.

After its inventor the running machine is also called a **draisine**. Later the word was also used for small rail vehicles. Only decades after Drais did two-wheelers get **pedals**, at first on the front wheel. Later still came the chain and wheels of equal size, and so today’s **bicycle** came about. Small children today ride on the **balance bike**, which works exactly like the running machine.

Some researchers suspect a particular reason for the invention. After a huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia in 1815, there was a **“year without a summer”** in Europe in 1816. Harvests were poor, and fodder for horses became scarce. A vehicle without a horse was therefore especially useful. Whether that really spurred Drais on is not certain, however.

gewusst: The running machine was so fast that some towns soon banned riding it on pavements.
Karl Drais also invented an early typewriter with keys.

teile.einleitung: Votes for women means the right of women to vote in elections and to take part in referendums. For a long time only men were allowed to. In many countries, women had to fight for decades for it, and in Switzerland especially long.
wichtigste: With the right to vote and to elect, women can take part in referendums and elections.
The suffragettes fought for votes for women mainly in Britain.
Their best-known leader was Emmeline Pankhurst.
In Germany, votes for women were introduced in November 1918.
In Switzerland, women have been able to vote and elect at national level since 1971.
Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to introduce votes for women, in 1990.
On 14 June 1991 a big women's strike took place in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: With the **right to vote and to elect**, citizens can help decide in **referendums** and elect **politicians**. For a long time only men had this right. Many thought politics was not a matter for women. From the 19th century onwards, more and more women, and men too, demanded equal political rights. **New Zealand** was the first country to introduce votes for women at national level, in 1893.

The **suffragettes** in **Britain** became especially well known. They fought for votes for women with marches, posters and loud protests. Some went on **hunger strike** in prison. Their best-known leader was **Emmeline Pankhurst**. In 1903 she founded a women's group that drew attention to itself with striking actions. In 1918 some of the women in Britain gained the vote, and in 1928 all of them.

In **Germany**, votes for women were introduced in **November 1918**. In January 1919 women there were able to vote for the first time. In many other European countries, too, votes for women came after the First World War. During that time women had taken on many tasks that men had done before. This strengthened their demand for equal rights.

In Switzerland, it was the **men** at the ballot box who decided whether women could have a say. In 1959 they still said No. On **7 February 1971** they said Yes. Since then women have been able to vote and elect at **national** level. Compared with many European countries, that was late. In some cantons it took even longer. **Appenzell Innerrhoden** only had to introduce votes for women in **1990**, after a ruling by the **Federal Supreme Court**.

Even after 1971, women and men were not equal everywhere. On **14 June 1991**, hundreds of thousands of women in Switzerland stopped work. In the **women's strike** they demanded equal rights and **equal pay** for equal work. The date recalled the vote of 1981, which put equality of women and men into the Federal Constitution.

gewusst: The first woman on the Federal Council was Elisabeth Kopp. She was elected in 1984.
The word “suffragette” comes from the English word “suffrage”, which means the right to vote.

teile.einleitung: German reunification is the union of the GDR with the Federal Republic of Germany on 3 October 1990. After over 40 years of division Germany became a single state again, without war and without violence. This became possible through the peaceful revolution in the GDR and the agreement of the four victorious powers of the Second World War.
wichtigste: On 3 October 1990 the GDR joined the Federal Republic of Germany.
The accession took place under Article 23 of the Basic Law.
On 18 March 1990 the first free election to the People's Chamber of the GDR took place.
Lothar de Maizière was the first and only freely elected prime minister of the GDR.
On 1 July 1990 the GDR received the Deutsche Mark.
In the Two Plus Four Treaty the four victorious powers agreed to unity.
The 3rd of October is now a national holiday as the Day of German Unity.

abschnitte.text: In autumn 1989 more and more people in the GDR took to the streets, especially at the **Monday demonstrations** in Leipzig. They demanded freedom to travel, free elections and freedom of speech. At the same time thousands fled to the West through Hungary and embassies. On 9 November 1989 the **Berlin Wall** fell. The Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev kept the tanks in their barracks, so the revolution stayed peaceful.

On 28 November 1989 Chancellor **Helmut Kohl** presented a ten-point programme for German unity. On 18 March 1990 the first free **People's Chamber election** of the GDR took place. The clear winner was the Alliance for Germany, which wanted quick unity. **Lothar de Maizière** became the first and only freely elected prime minister of the GDR. His government negotiated with the Federal Republic over the Unification Treaty.

On 1 July 1990 the monetary, economic and **social union** came into force, and the GDR took over the Deutsche Mark. Wages and pensions were converted at a rate of 1 to 1, which pleased many people. For many GDR firms, however, this had terrible consequences: their products suddenly became too expensive, and they lost their customers in Eastern Europe. The **Treuhandanstalt** was meant to privatise the state-owned firms. Many companies were closed, and hundreds of thousands lost their jobs.

For unity the agreement of the four victorious powers of the Second World War was also needed. The Federal Republic and the GDR therefore negotiated with the USA, the Soviet Union, Britain and France, hence the name **Two Plus Four Treaty**. It was signed on 12 September 1990 in Moscow. Germany received full sovereignty, finally recognised the Oder-Neisse border with Poland and reduced its army. The Soviet troops withdrew by 1994.

In constitutional terms unity came about through the **accession** of the GDR under Article 23 of the Basic Law. The GDR joined with five new federal states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia. East and West Berlin were joined into one federal state. In the night leading to 3 October 1990 hundreds of thousands celebrated in front of the Reichstag in Berlin. In 1991 the Bundestag decided that Berlin would again be the capital and seat of government.

After unity roads, railway lines, houses and town centres in the east were renewed with a great deal of money. For this, among other things, the **solidarity surcharge** was introduced, an extra tax. Even so, differences still exist today, for example in wages and wealth between East and West. Many young people moved from the east to the west. The 3rd of October is now a national holiday in Germany as the **Day of German Unity**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two separated parts of a country become one state again.
The parliament of the GDR.
An agency that after 1990 was to sell or close the state-owned firms of the GDR.
A state decides freely and independently about its own affairs.

gewusst: The GDR existed for exactly 40 years and almost four days, from 7 October 1949 to 2 October 1990.
Helmut Kohl is often called the “Chancellor of Unity”.
The Ampelmännchen, the little traffic-light man from the GDR, was so popular that it also lights up in many West German cities today.

teile.einleitung: The Congo Free State was a huge territory in Central Africa that belonged personally to the Belgian King Leopold II from 1885 to 1908. There people were forced to work with great violence. The crimes triggered one of the first international human rights movements.
wichtigste: The Congo Free State was the private property of King Leopold II of Belgium.
From the 1890s people there were forced to collect rubber.
The troops of the Force Publique enforced forced labour and levies.
Severed hands became an international symbol of the crimes.
In 1904 Roger Casement presented a report that attracted wide attention.
Edmund Dene Morel founded the Congo Reform Association in 1904.
In 1908 Leopold II had to hand the territory over to the Belgian state.

abschnitte.text: After the **Congo Conference** in Berlin, the **Congo Free State** came into being in 1885. It did not belong to the state of Belgium, but to King **Leopold II** personally. The territory was much larger than Belgium. Leopold claimed that he wanted to bring progress to the people there. In truth he was mainly concerned with making money from the country’s riches.

From the **1890s** **rubber** was in great demand, for example for the tyres of bicycles and cars. Rubber is obtained from the sap of certain plants. The inhabitants of the villages had to collect large amounts of it and hand it over. The **Force Publique** troops enforced this **forced labour** with violence. Anyone who did not bring the required amount was harshly punished.

In the Congo Free State countless people were abused and killed. As proof of punishments, people even had their hands cut off. **Severed hands** therefore became an international **symbol** of the crimes in Leopold’s Congo. Many people also died of hunger, exhaustion and disease. How many victims there were in all is not known exactly; experts assume millions.

In **1904** the British consul **Roger Casement** presented a report on conditions in the Congo. It caused a great stir. In the same year the journalist **Edmund Dene Morel** founded the **Congo Reform Association**. It collected evidence, held meetings and showed photographs. The writer **Joseph Conrad** worked his experiences on the Congo into the story **“Heart of Darkness”** of 1899.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Free State
abschnitte.text: Because of international pressure, Leopold II had to hand the Congo Free State over to the **Belgian state** in **1908**. After that the territory was called the **Belgian Congo** and was a colony. Only in 1960 did the country become independent. Today most of it is the **Democratic Republic of the Congo**.

gewusst: The American writer Mark Twain also wrote a text against Leopold II’s rule in the Congo.
Leopold II himself never visited the Congo.

teile.einleitung: The outbreak of war in 1914 means the few weeks in the summer of 1914 in which an assassination in Sarajevo turned into the First World War. Within about a month the great powers of Europe declared war on one another. This diplomatic crisis is called the July Crisis.
wichtigste: On 28 June 1914 the Austrian heir to the throne, Franz Ferdinand, was murdered in Sarajevo.
In July 1914 Germany gave Austria-Hungary an unconditional promise of support, the “blank cheque”.
The ultimatum of 23 July 1914 gave Serbia only 48 hours.
On 28 July 1914 Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.
On 1 August 1914 Germany declared war on Russia.
The German invasion of neutral Belgium led to Britain entering the war on 4 August.
Alliances and mobilisation plans turned the regional conflict into a European war.

abschnitte.text: On 28 June 1914 the Austro-Hungarian heir to the throne, Archduke **Franz Ferdinand**, visited Sarajevo with his wife Sophie. The young Bosnian Serb nationalist Gavrilo Princip shot them both. He belonged to a group that was supported by a Serbian secret society. Austria-Hungary held Serbia responsible for the murder.

At the beginning of July Germany promised Austria-Hungary unconditional support, the so-called **blank cheque**. On 23 July Austria-Hungary presented Serbia with an **ultimatum** with very harsh demands and only 48 hours’ time. Serbia gave way on many points, but not on all. On 28 July 1914 Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.

Russia supported Serbia and mobilised its army on 30 July. Germany then declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August. According to the **Schlieffen Plan**, German troops marched through neutral Belgium in order to defeat France quickly. That is why Britain entered the war on 4 August 1914.
