On one side stood the **Central Powers**: Germany and Austria-Hungary, later the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria. On the other side stood the **Entente** of France, Russia and Britain. Italy remained neutral at first in 1914 and entered the war in 1915 on the side of the Entente. At the beginning many people believed the war would be over by Christmas.

At the beginning of August 1914 Switzerland declared its **neutrality** and mobilised its army. The Federal Assembly elected Ulrich Wille as General. A deep rift opened between German-speaking Switzerland, which leaned more towards Germany, and French-speaking Switzerland, which leaned more towards France. But Switzerland was spared throughout the whole war.

begriffe.erklaerung: A final demand with a deadline, after which force is threatened.
A state calls up its soldiers and makes its army ready for war.
An unconditional promise to support someone in any case.
An alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria.

gewusst: The car in which Franz Ferdinand was shot now stands in the Museum of Military History in Vienna.
The licence plate of this car happened to read “A III 118”, which some interpret as a reference to the armistice on 11.11.18.

teile.einleitung: The financial crisis from 2007 was the worst worldwide economic crisis since the 1930s. It began in the USA with bad house loans and shook big banks all over the world. In Switzerland too the state had to rescue a big bank.
wichtigste: The crisis began in the US market for second-rate mortgages, the subprime market.
On 15 September 2008 the US investment bank Lehman Brothers went bankrupt.
A US rescue law of October 2008 made 700 billion dollars available for the banks.
In Switzerland the Confederation and the National Bank propped up UBS in October 2008.
The National Bank's special-purpose company StabFund took over problematic securities from UBS.
From 2010 Greece became the first euro country to fall into a serious debt crisis.
“Too big to fail” means that a bank is so important that the state cannot let it fall.

abschnitte.text: In the USA banks for years gave out **mortgages**, that is, loans for houses, even to people with little income. These risky loans are called **subprime**, which means second-rate. The banks bundled the loans into securities and sold them all over the world. When house prices fell from 2006 and many people could no longer pay, these securities lost a great deal of value.

Because nobody knew any more which bank held how many bad securities, banks hardly lent each other money any more. On 15 September 2008 the big investment bank **Lehman Brothers** went bankrupt. After that panic broke out on stock exchanges worldwide. In October 2008 the US Congress passed a rescue law with 700 billion dollars to stabilise the banks.

The Swiss big bank **UBS** had also lost many billions on US mortgage securities. In October 2008 the Confederation, with 6 billion francs, and the National Bank propped up the bank. For this the National Bank founded the special-purpose company **StabFund**, which took over problematic securities from UBS. Later these securities were sold, and in the end the National Bank even made a profit.

In 2009 the banking crisis turned into a worldwide **recession**, that is, the economy shrank. Many firms went bust, and millions of people lost their jobs or their homes. States spent huge sums to support the economy. Central banks cut interest rates to almost zero.

Because states spent a lot of money, their debts grew strongly. From 2010 **Greece** became the first euro country to fall into a serious debt crisis and received emergency loans, and later Ireland and Portugal did too. In July 2012 the president of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, said that the ECB would do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. After that the markets gradually calmed down.

Many countries passed stricter rules for banks. Big banks today must have more **capital**, that is, their own money as a safety cushion. Switzerland created rules against the “too big to fail” problem, so that a bank in trouble can be wound up in an orderly way. Even so, in 2023 the big bank Credit Suisse had to be taken over by UBS in an emergency operation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A loan with which you buy a house or a flat.
Second-rate, meaning risky loans to people with little money.
A time when the economy shrinks instead of growing.
The bank of a country that issues the money and steers interest rates, in Switzerland the National Bank.

gewusst: Lehman Brothers was over 150 years old when the bank collapsed in 2008.
Photos of bank employees leaving the Lehman building with cardboard boxes full of their things went around the world.
In the end the National Bank made a profit of several billion francs with StabFund.

teile.einleitung: Carl Benz was a German engineer and is regarded as the inventor of the car. In 1886 he applied for a patent for his motor car with a petrol engine. His firm lives on today in the name Mercedes-Benz.
wichtigste: Carl Benz was born in 1844 in Mühlburg, which today belongs to Karlsruhe.
On New Year's Eve 1879 he got his first engine, a two-stroke engine, running.
His motor car ran on a petrol engine and had less than 1 horsepower.
The fuel was ligroin, a light petrol.
The original of the motor car stands in the Deutsches Museum in Munich.
In 1926 his firm merged with the Daimler-Motoren-Gesellschaft.

abschnitte.text: Carl Benz was born in 1844 in **Mühlburg**, which today belongs to **Karlsruhe**. His father was a locomotive driver and died young. His mother nevertheless made a good education possible for him. Carl studied **mechanical engineering** in Karlsruhe. Afterwards he worked in various firms and finally founded his own workshop in **Mannheim**.

abschnitte.titel: An engine on New Year's Eve
abschnitte.text: Benz wanted to build an engine that was small and light enough for a carriage. On **New Year's Eve 1879** his **two-stroke engine**, an upright gas engine, ran for the first time. By selling such engines he earned money for further development. His wife **Bertha Benz** supported him greatly in this.

In 1886 Benz applied for a **patent** for his **motor car**. It ran on a **single-cylinder four-stroke engine** that burned petrol. The engine produced only about three quarters of a horsepower, that is, **less than 1 horsepower**. The fuel was **ligroin**, a light petrol that people then bought as a cleaning agent. The **diesel engine** was only invented by Rudolf Diesel a few years later.

Almost at the same time **Gottlieb Daimler** built a motor vehicle in Stuttgart. The two car pioneers never worked together. In 1926, however, their firms merged into **Daimler-Benz AG**. From this came the well-known car brand **Mercedes-Benz**. Carl Benz died in 1929 in Ladenburg. The original of his first motor car stands today in the **Deutsches Museum** in Munich.

gewusst: A car today often has more than a hundred times as much power as the first Benz motor car.
Gottlieb Daimler and Carl Benz probably never met in person.

teile.einleitung: In the witch hunts, people were accused of causing harm through witchcraft. Many of them were put on trial, tortured and executed. The big persecutions did not take place in the Middle Ages, but in the Early Modern period.
wichtigste: The witch hunts in central Europe reached their peak from about 1560 to 1630.
Experts estimate that about 40,000 to 60,000 people were executed as “witches” in Europe.
Most of the accused were women, but men and children were also persecuted.
The book “Malleus Maleficarum” (“Hammer of Witches”) by Heinrich Kramer appeared in 1486.
Confessions were mostly forced by torture.
The Jesuit Friedrich Spee criticised the trials in 1631.
Anna Göldi was executed in Glarus in 1782 and rehabilitated in 2008.

abschnitte.text: In the past, people could not explain many misfortunes: **failed harvests**, storms, illnesses in people and animals. Some believed that witches, in league with the Devil, were behind them. So people looked for someone to blame. It often fell on people at the edge of society, for example poor or unmarried women. Quarrels between neighbours also led to accusations.

In **1486** the book **“Malleus Maleficarum”**, meaning “Hammer of Witches”, appeared. It was written by the Dominican **Heinrich Kramer**. It described alleged witchcraft and explained how to track down and convict witches. Thanks to the new **printing press** it spread widely. The biggest waves of persecution, however, came later, between about **1560 and 1630**.

In the **witch trials** the accused had hardly any chance. Judges forced confessions with **torture**. In pain, many also named other people, and so whole chains of trials arose. In the **water test** people were thrown into water bound, because it was believed a witch could not sink. An estimated **40,000 to 60,000** people were executed in Europe.

There were brave critics early on. The Jesuit **Friedrich Spee**, as a priest, had accompanied women who had been sentenced. In 1631 he wrote the book **“Cautio Criminalis”**. In it he explained that torture forces innocent people into false confessions. With the **Enlightenment** in the 18th century, thinking based on reason won through, and the trials gradually stopped.

In Switzerland, too, there were many witch trials, for example in Vaud and the Valais. The last person in Europe to be executed as a “witch” is thought to be **Anna Göldi**. She was a servant and was executed in **Glarus** in **1782**, officially for poisoning. In **2008**, more than 220 years later, the Glarus cantonal parliament officially cleared her. The verdict is now seen as a **judicial murder**.

gewusst: In Glarus there is now a museum that recalls Anna Göldi.
The big witch hunts took place at the same time as the discoveries of Johannes Kepler and Galileo Galilei.

teile.einleitung: Konrad Zuse was a German inventor and engineer. He built the first working programmable computer, the Z3. One of his machines even later stood at ETH Zurich.
wichtigste: Konrad Zuse built the first working programmable computer in Germany.
He had trained as a civil engineer.
He built his first machine, the Z1, in his parents’ flat.
His most famous machine is called the Z3 and was finished in 1941.
The Z3 calculated with the digits 0 and 1.
In 1950 the Z4 was rented to ETH Zurich.

abschnitte.text: Konrad Zuse was born in Berlin in 1910. He studied and became a **civil engineer**. In this job he had to do a great many long and boring calculations by hand. So he came up with the idea of building a **machine** that carries out such calculations itself. He gave up his job in order to work entirely on his calculating machines.

abschnitte.titel: The Z1 in the living room
abschnitte.text: Zuse built his very first calculating machine, the **Z1**, in his **parents’ flat** in Berlin. Friends helped him. The Z1 was finished in 1938 and worked entirely **mechanically** with many thin metal plates. But it did not yet work reliably. Zuse learned from this and improved his ideas.

In **1941** the **Z3** was finished. It is regarded as the world’s first working, freely **programmable computer**. Instead of metal plates it worked with electric switches, the **relays**. The Z3 calculated in the **binary system**, that is, only with the digits **0 and 1**. That is how computers still work today. The original Z3 was destroyed in an air raid in 1943 during the Second World War.

After the war Zuse finished building the **Z4**. In **1950** it was rented to **ETH Zurich**. That made ETH one of the first universities in Europe with a working computer. Researchers solved difficult mathematical problems with the Z4. Zuse later founded a company of his own, which made many more computers.

gewusst: Zuse also developed one of the first programming languages, the “Plankalkül”.
A replica of the Z3 stands today in the Deutsches Museum in Munich.

teile.einleitung: Alliance systems means the treaties by which the great European powers promised each other help before the First World War. In the end two blocs faced each other: the Triple Alliance around Germany and Austria-Hungary, and the Triple Entente of France, Russia and Britain. Because everyone was so closely tied together, a conflict in the Balkans quickly became a world war in 1914.
wichtigste: In 1879 the German Empire and Austria-Hungary concluded the Dual Alliance.
In 1882 Italy joined, and so the Triple Alliance came into being.
In 1890 Germany let the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia lapse.
In 1894 France and Russia concluded an alliance.
In 1904 Britain and France settled their colonial disputes in the Entente Cordiale.
In 1907 a treaty between Britain and Russia completed the Triple Entente.
In Germany the fear of being “encircled” grew before 1914.

abschnitte.text: An **alliance** is a treaty in which states promise to help one another in case of war. In the late 19th century the great powers of Europe concluded many such treaties, some public, some secret. They were meant to bring security and deter possible opponents. But the web of obligations also made the situation dangerous, because a small quarrel could drag in many states.

After the founding of the German Empire in 1871 Chancellor **Otto von Bismarck** above all wanted to isolate France, which could not accept the loss of Alsace-Lorraine. In 1879 he concluded the **Dual Alliance** with Austria-Hungary. In 1882 Italy was added, and so the **Triple Alliance** came into being. With Russia Bismarck concluded the secret Reinsurance Treaty in 1887, so that Germany would never have to fight on two sides at once. People often speak of Bismarck's complicated system of alliances.

In 1890 Bismarck was dismissed by the young Emperor **William II**. The new government did not renew the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia. As a result Russia moved closer to France, and in 1894 the Franco-Russian alliance, the **Dual Entente**, came into being. Germany now had to fear a war against France in the west and Russia in the east at the same time. At the same time Germany built a large war fleet, which worried Britain.

Britain and France had long been rivals in the colonies. In 1904 they agreed in the **Entente Cordiale**, which means “cordial understanding”, about their interests in Africa, for example in Egypt and Morocco. In 1907 Britain and Russia also reached a settlement in the Treaty of St Petersburg, above all about Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet. With that the **Triple Entente** was complete. In Germany people now spoke of “encirclement” by hostile powers.

On 28 June 1914 the Austrian heir to the throne, Franz Ferdinand, was murdered in **Sarajevo**. Germany promised Austria-Hungary unconditional support. When Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, Russia stood up for Serbia, and through the alliances Germany, France and Britain joined in within a few days. Italy stayed neutral at first and in 1915 changed to the side of the Entente after the secret **Treaty of London**, because territories were promised to it there.

**Switzerland** belonged to none of the alliances and stayed neutral in the First World War. Even so, it called up its army and guarded the borders, with Ulrich Wille as General. In the country a rift opened between German-speaking Switzerland, which rather sympathised with Germany, and French-speaking Switzerland, which sided with France. In 1914 Carl Spitteler warned of this split in his famous speech “Our Swiss Standpoint”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A treaty in which states promise one another help.
French for understanding, a loose alliance between states.
The fear of being surrounded on all sides by enemies.
A state takes part in no war and sides with no one.

gewusst: The German Emperor William II, the British King George V and the Russian Tsar Nicholas II were closely related to one another.
Italy was a member of the Triple Alliance, but fought against Germany and Austria-Hungary in the First World War.
In 1920 Carl Spitteler became the first Swiss person to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.

teile.einleitung: Ferdinand Magellan was a seafarer from Portugal. His fleet was the first to sail all the way around the Earth, even though he himself did not live to see the end of the voyage.
wichtigste: Magellan came from Portugal, but sailed in the service of Spain.
In 1519 he set out with five ships.
In 1520 he found a passage in the south of South America, today's Strait of Magellan.
Magellan died in 1521 in a fight in the Philippines.
Juan Sebastián Elcano led the last ship home.
Only the “Victoria” returned to Spain in 1522 with 18 men.
With that the first circumnavigation was achieved.

abschnitte.titel: A plan for the western route
abschnitte.text: Magellan was born around 1480 in **Portugal**. He wanted to reach the valuable **Spice Islands** in Asia by sailing **west**. The Portuguese king did not support him. So Magellan went to **Spain**. The Spanish king gave him ships and money for the great voyage.

In **1519** Magellan set out with **five ships** and about 240 men. The fleet crossed the Atlantic and sailed south along the coast of South America. The voyage was hard: there were storms, hunger and quarrels on board. One ship was wrecked, and another secretly returned to Spain.

In **1520** Magellan found a narrow passage between the seas in the south of South America. This waterway is called the **Strait of Magellan** today. After that the fleet reached a huge ocean. Because the sea was calm on arrival, Magellan called it the **Pacific**, which means “the peaceful one”. The crossing lasted many weeks, and many sailors fell ill.

In 1521 the fleet reached the **Philippines**. There Magellan got into a fight with local people and died. So he did not live to see the end of his voyage. The seafarer **Juan Sebastián Elcano** took over the command. He brought the last ship home across the Indian Ocean and around Africa.

Only the **“Victoria”** returned to Spain in **1522**. On board were still **18 men** of the fleet. They were the first to have sailed once around the whole Earth. This showed that the world can be sailed around and that the Earth is much bigger than many had thought. The Strait of Magellan and the **Magellanic penguin** are named after Magellan today.

gewusst: Two small neighbouring galaxies of our Milky Way also bear Magellan's name: the Magellanic Clouds.
On their return the sailors of the “Victoria” found that a day was missing for them. They had sailed round the Earth to the west and so “lost” a day.

teile.einleitung: The Thirty Years' War was a series of wars in central Europe that lasted from 1618 to 1648. It was about religion, that is, the quarrel between Catholics and Protestants, but also about power between the emperor, the princes and the great powers of Europe. Large parts of Germany were laid waste, and millions of people died from fighting, hunger and disease.
wichtigste: The war lasted from 1618 to 1648.
The trigger is regarded as the Second Defenestration of Prague on 23 May 1618.
In 1620 the Bohemian estates were defeated at the Battle of White Mountain.
In 1630 the Swedish King Gustavus Adolphus entered the war and fell in 1632 at Lützen.
In 1631 the city of Magdeburg was destroyed, and over 20,000 people died.
The Peace of Westphalia ended the war in 1648.
In the Peace of Westphalia the Swiss Confederation was recognised as independent of the Empire.

abschnitte.text: In the Kingdom of **Bohemia** Protestant nobles quarrelled with the Catholic Habsburg emperor over their freedom of religion. On 23 May 1618 they threw two imperial governors and a clerk out of a window of Prague Castle. All three survived the fall. This **Second Defenestration of Prague** is regarded as the beginning of the war. The Bohemians chose Frederick V of the Palatinate as their king, but in 1620 their army was defeated at the **Battle of White Mountain**. Because Frederick reigned for only about one winter, he was mockingly called the “Winter King”.

Historians usually divide the war into four phases: the Bohemian-Palatinate, the Danish-Lower Saxon, the Swedish and the **Swedish-French War**. On the Catholic side stood the emperor and the League, a group of Catholic princes. In 1629 Emperor Ferdinand II demanded in the **Edict of Restitution** that the Protestants give back church property that they had taken since the middle of the 16th century. This sharpened the conflict further.

In July 1630 the Swedish king **Gustavus Adolphus** landed with his army on the island of Usedom on the Baltic Sea and came to the help of the Protestants. In May 1631 troops of the League under the commander Tilly captured and destroyed the city of **Magdeburg**, and over 20,000 people died. Gustavus Adolphus won several battles, but fell in November 1632 at the Battle of Lützen. The imperial commander **Albrecht von Wallenstein** was murdered in Eger in 1634, because the emperor distrusted him.

In September 1634 the Swedes suffered a heavy defeat at **Nördlingen**. In the Peace of Prague of 1635 most of the Protestant states of the Empire made peace with the emperor. But now Catholic **France** openly entered the war against the Catholic Habsburgs. This showed that power politics had become more important than religion. The war went on for another 13 years.

The armies mostly consisted of **mercenaries**, who plundered villages, stole cattle and tormented people. On top of this came famines and diseases such as the plague. In some parts of Germany more than half of the population died, and altogether the German lands are estimated to have lost a third of their inhabitants. Many towns and villages lay in ruins. The writer Grimmelshausen later described the misery in his novel “Simplicissimus”.

abschnitte.titel: The Peace of Westphalia and Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In 1648 the Peace of Westphalia was made in **Münster and Osnabrück**. Catholics, Lutherans and Reformed became equal in the Empire, and France and Sweden gained territory. The Swiss Confederation stayed largely neutral in the war, and only Graubünden was fiercely fought over in the **Graubünden Troubles**. The mayor of Basel, **Johann Rudolf Wettstein**, achieved in Münster that the Confederation was recognised as independent of the Holy Roman Empire. This is regarded as an important step towards today's Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Throwing opponents out of a window as a sign of protest.
A soldier who fights for money, no matter for which side.
A particular branch of faith within a religion, for example Catholic or Reformed.
The peace treaties of Münster and Osnabrück that ended the war in 1648.

gewusst: The peace negotiations lasted about five years, because envoys from almost the whole of Europe took part.
The men in the Defenestration of Prague fell about 17 metres, but probably landed in a dung heap or a ditch.
The Peace of Westphalia is regarded as one of the first great peace congresses in European history.

teile.einleitung: At the Boston Tea Party in December 1773 settlers threw tea into the sea in the harbour of Boston. In this way they protested against British taxes. The event was an important step on the way to the independence of the USA.
wichtigste: The Boston Tea Party took place on 16 December 1773.
Boston was the most important city of the British colony of Massachusetts.
The trigger was the Tea Act of 1773.
The tea belonged to the British East India Company.
Many participants disguised themselves as Mohawk.
The Sons of Liberty and Samuel Adams played an important role.
In 1775 the War of Independence began at Lexington and Concord.

abschnitte.text: In North America in the 18th century there were 13 British **colonies**. Britain wanted more taxes from the settlers. In 1765 came the **Stamp Act**: for newspapers and documents a tax stamp had to be bought. After fierce protests the law was repealed in 1766. The settlers said that they had no representatives in the British Parliament and therefore should not be taxed either.

In 1773 the British Parliament passed the **Tea Act**. It allowed the **British East India Company** to sell tea cheaply in the colonies. The tax on tea remained, however. Many settlers saw in this an attack on their rights. Groups such as the **Sons of Liberty** organised resistance. One of the leaders was **Samuel Adams**.

In the harbour of **Boston** lay ships with tea of the East India Company. On the evening of **16 December 1773** many men went on board. They had disguised themselves as **Mohawk** so as not to be recognised. They opened hundreds of tea chests and tipped the tea into the water. Apart from the tea hardly anything was damaged.

The British government responded with strict punitive laws and closed the port of Boston. Tensions in the colony of **Massachusetts** grew ever greater. On 19 April 1775 the first fighting took place at **Lexington and Concord** between British soldiers and militias of the settlers. With that the **War of Independence** began. On 4 July 1776 the colonies declared their independence.

gewusst: At the Boston Tea Party over 340 chests of tea ended up in the harbour.
Samuel Adams was a distant cousin of the later president John Adams.

teile.einleitung: The Marshall Plan was a big aid programme of the USA with which the destroyed Europe was rebuilt after the Second World War. Officially it was called the European Recovery Program. It brought food, raw materials and machines to Europe and helped the economy in many countries to recover quickly.
wichtigste: The Marshall Plan is named after the US Secretary of State George C. Marshall.
Marshall presented his plan on 5 June 1947 in a speech at Harvard University.
President Harry S. Truman put the programme into effect in April 1948.
From 1948 to 1952 a total of around 13 billion US dollars flowed to Europe.
To distribute the aid, the recipient states founded the OEEC in Paris in 1948, from which the OECD later developed.
The Marshall Plan was part of the policy of containment, with which the USA wanted to hold back Soviet influence.
George C. Marshall received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953.

abschnitte.text: After the end of the Second World War in 1945, many cities of Europe lay in ruins. Factories, bridges and railway lines were destroyed, and there was a lack of food, coal and money. The very cold winter of 1946/47 made the hardship even greater. In many countries the fear grew that hunger and poverty could lead to political chaos.

On 5 June 1947 US Secretary of State **George C. Marshall** spoke at Harvard University near Boston. He said that American policy was directed against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos. The European countries were to plan together for themselves what they needed, and the USA would help. Already in March 1947 President Truman had declared, with the **Truman Doctrine**, that the USA wanted to support free peoples against threats.

The **European Recovery Program** ran from 1948 to 1952. The USA supplied mainly goods such as grain, fuel, cotton and machines, and part of it was given as a loan. The countries paid for the goods in their own currency into special funds, and with this money roads, power stations and factories were in turn financed. For coordination the recipients founded the **OEEC** in Paris on 16 April 1948.

In all, 16 Western European states and the Western occupation zones of Germany received aid. Most went to Britain, France, Italy and West Germany. The Soviet Union refused to take part and also forbade states such as Poland and Czechoslovakia to join in. In response it founded the **Council for Mutual Economic Assistance** with its allies in 1949.

Switzerland had not been destroyed in the war and needed no reconstruction aid. But it was a founding member of the OEEC and took part in the cooperation of the European economy. The reconstruction of the neighbouring countries was also important for Swiss firms, because their customers lived there. Today Switzerland is a member of the OECD, the successor organisation of the OEEC.

The Marshall Plan helped to start a strong economic upswing in Western Europe, called the “economic miracle” in West Germany. It linked Western Europe more closely with the USA and deepened the division of Europe in the **Cold War**. Cooperation in the OEEC is also seen as an early step towards European unification. Since 1961 the organisation has been called the OECD and today has members all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rebuilding of cities, roads and factories after destruction.
The policy of the USA against the spread of Soviet influence.
The Organisation for European Economic Co-operation, founded in 1948 to distribute Marshall Plan aid.
Tensions between the USA and the Soviet Union from 1947 to about 1990, without a direct war between them.

gewusst: The aid packages often bore a sign saying that they came from the USA for the reconstruction of Europe.
Before his time as Secretary of State, George C. Marshall was Chief of Staff of the US Army in the Second World War.
In Germany part of the Marshall Plan money is still used today as a fund for development loans.

teile.einleitung: Galileo Galilei was an Italian natural philosopher who lived from 1564 to 1642. He was one of the first people to point a telescope at the sky, and he made astonishing discoveries with it. Because he taught that the Earth orbits the Sun, he came into conflict with the Catholic Church.
wichtigste: Galileo came from Italy and was born in Pisa in 1564.
In 1609 he improved the telescope and pointed it at the sky.
In 1610 he discovered four moons of Jupiter.
He supported the view of the world in which the Earth orbits the Sun.
In 1633 he had to renounce his teaching before the court of the Inquisition, and then remained under house arrest until his death.
He found out that without air resistance all bodies fall at the same speed.
Only in 1992 did the Catholic Church officially rehabilitate him.

abschnitte.text: Galileo Galilei was born on 15 February 1564 in **Pisa** in Italy. At first he studied medicine, but soon became much more interested in mathematics and physics. He was a professor in Pisa and then for a long time in Padua. Later he worked as court mathematician for the rulers of Florence.

Galileo did many experiments with balls that he let roll down slopes. He found out that without **air resistance** all bodies fall at the same speed, whether heavy or light. He also studied the pendulum and noticed that the time of its swing does not depend on how far it swings out. He is therefore seen as one of the founders of modern **physics**, which is based on experiments and measurements.

In 1609 Galileo heard of a telescope from the Netherlands, built one himself and improved it greatly. He was one of the first to point it at the sky. On the Moon he saw **mountains and craters**, and he saw that the Milky Way was made up of countless stars. In 1610 he discovered four moons of **Jupiter**, which are now called the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

abschnitte.titel: A new view of the world
abschnitte.text: Galileo observed that Venus shows **phases** like the Moon. This could only be explained if Venus orbits the Sun. So he supported the **heliocentric view of the world** of Nicolaus Copernicus, in which the Earth orbits the Sun. At that time, however, the Church taught that the Earth stands at the centre of the world.

In 1632 Galileo published the book “Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems”. In it he defended the new view of the world, which led to a trial before the **Inquisition**. In 1633 he had to renounce his teaching and was kept under **house arrest** in his country house near Florence for the rest of his life. He is said to have said the famous words “And yet it moves!” afterwards, but that is probably a legend.

Galileo died on 8 January 1642, by then blind. His way of studying nature with experiments and mathematics still shapes science today. The Catholic Church officially rehabilitated him in 1992 under Pope John Paul II. The **Galileo spacecraft**, which explored Jupiter, and the European satellite navigation system Galileo are named after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device with lenses that makes faraway things look bigger.
The idea that the Sun is at the centre and the Earth orbits it.
A court of the Catholic Church that acted against teachings considered false.
To give someone back their rights and good name afterwards.

gewusst: Galileo's telescope magnified only about twenty times.
A middle finger of Galileo is now displayed in a museum in Florence.
Galileo was born in the same year as the poet William Shakespeare.

teile.einleitung: Digitalisation means that information such as texts, pictures, sounds or money is turned into numbers made of zeros and ones and processed by computers. Since the 20th century it has changed almost every area of our lives, from learning to shopping to free time. With the internet, the smartphone and artificial intelligence the development is going on at great speed.
wichtigste: Computers work with the binary system, that is, only with 0 and 1.
The ARPANET of 1969 is regarded as the forerunner of the internet.
From 1989 Tim Berners-Lee developed the World Wide Web at CERN in Geneva.
On 30 April 1993 CERN released the Web for free use.
In 2007 Apple presented the first iPhone, which began the triumph of smartphones.
Laws such as the EU's GDPR and the revised Swiss data protection act protect personal data.
On 28 September 2025 the Swiss voters narrowly accepted the law on a state e-ID.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “digitus”, finger, which we count with. In **digitalisation** information is translated into numbers, more exactly into the **binary system** of 0 and 1. The smallest unit is called a **bit**, and eight bits make a byte. A photo, for example, is made of millions of picture points whose colours are stored as numbers. In this way computers can store and copy texts, music, films and maps and send them around the world in seconds.

abschnitte.titel: From calculating machines to the PC
abschnitte.text: In 1941 the German Konrad Zuse presented the Z3 in Berlin, one of the first programmable computers. His machine **Z4** was used from 1950 at ETH Zurich and was then one of the few working computers in Europe. The first computers filled whole rooms, but thanks to transistors and **microchips** they became smaller and more powerful. From the 1980s personal computers came into offices and homes. The Zurich computer scientist Niklaus Wirth developed the programming language Pascal in 1970.

abschnitte.titel: The internet and the World Wide Web
abschnitte.text: The **ARPANET**, started in 1969 in the USA, first linked a few universities and is regarded as the forerunner of the internet. From 1989 the British physicist **Tim Berners-Lee** developed the World Wide Web at CERN in Geneva, so that researchers could link documents with links. On 30 April 1993 CERN released the Web for free use. After that the internet grew explosively: search engines, online shops, Wikipedia and social networks came into being.

In 2007 Apple presented the first **iPhone**, a phone with a touchscreen, internet and apps. Today most teenagers in Switzerland own a smartphone. With it you can take photos, write messages, pay, buy train tickets and navigate. In recent years **artificial intelligence** has made great progress: computer programs can understand language, write texts and recognise pictures. This brings new possibilities, but also questions about fairness, truth and jobs.

Anyone who uses digital services leaves behind a lot of **data**, for example about location, interests and contacts. To protect it, the **General Data Protection Regulation** (GDPR) has applied in the EU since 25 May 2018. In Switzerland the revised data protection act came into force on 1 September 2023. Secure passwords are also important, as is caution with unknown links and thinking before you share photos of yourself or others. What is once on the internet can only be deleted again with difficulty.

Authorities in Switzerland are also going digital: many forms and tax returns can be filled in online. On 28 September 2025 the voters narrowly accepted the law on a state **e-ID** with about 50.4 per cent in favour. With this electronic identity document people should in future be able to prove who they are safely on the internet too. In schools tablets, laptops and the subject Media and Computer Science are part of the curriculum today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number system that only knows the digits 0 and 1.
The smallest unit of information in a computer, which is either 0 or 1.
The network of web pages that are joined to one another by links.
Rules that protect personal information from misuse.
Computer programs that solve tasks for which human thinking is otherwise needed.

gewusst: The first website in the world ran on a computer of Tim Berners-Lee at CERN and can be seen online again today.
A smartphone today is far more powerful than the computers with which NASA steered the Moon landing in 1969.
On Tim Berners-Lee's computer a note was stuck saying that nobody was allowed to switch it off, because it was the web server.

teile.einleitung: On 14 May 1948 the independence of the State of Israel was declared in Tel Aviv. For many Jewish people, a long-held wish came true with it, and at the same time a war began that shapes the region to this day.
wichtigste: Israel's independence was declared on 14 May 1948.
David Ben-Gurion read out the declaration in the museum in Tel Aviv.
Until 1948 Britain administered Palestine as a mandate territory.
In November 1947 the UN General Assembly decided on a partition plan.
Immediately after the founding, Arab neighbouring states attacked the new state.
Chaim Weizmann became Israel's first president in 1949.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 19th century **Zionism** arose. This movement wanted a state of its own for the Jewish people in the historic land of Israel. In **1897** the first Zionist Congress took place in **Basel**, organised by **Theodor Herzl**. After the First World War the League of Nations gave **Britain** the administration of Palestine as a **mandate territory**. Arabs and a growing Jewish population lived there.

After the Second World War and the murder of millions of Jewish people in the **Holocaust**, the question became urgent. In November 1947 the **UN General Assembly** decided on a **partition plan**. It envisaged a Jewish and an Arab state, and **Jerusalem** was to be administered internationally. The Jewish leadership accepted the plan, the Arab side rejected it.

On **14 May 1948**, the day the British mandate ended, **David Ben-Gurion** read out the declaration of independence in the museum in **Tel Aviv**. Jerusalem was then contested. The declaration promises all citizens equal rights, regardless of religion and origin. Ben-Gurion became the first **prime minister**, and **Chaim Weizmann** the first **president** in 1949.

Immediately after the founding, **Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon** attacked the new state. In the **Palestine War**, hundreds of thousands of Palestinians fled or were driven out. In Israel, 14 May is celebrated as **Independence Day**. Many Palestinians remember this time as the **“Nakba”**, in English “catastrophe”. The conflict over the land has still not been resolved today.

gewusst: Chaim Weizmann, Israel's first president, was a chemist and had studied and worked in Switzerland, among other places.
Israel was admitted to the UN as a member in 1949.

teile.einleitung: James Cook was a British sailor and explorer in the 18th century. On three great voyages he explored the Pacific and drew very accurate maps.
wichtigste: James Cook came from England and sailed for the British navy.
On his first voyage, from 1768 to 1771, he sailed with the “Endeavour”.
In 1770 he explored the east coast of Australia.
He sailed around New Zealand and showed that it consists of two large islands.
On the second voyage he searched far to the south for a great southern continent.
Cook made three great voyages into the Pacific, the South Seas.
In 1779 he was killed in a dispute in Hawaii.

abschnitte.text: James Cook was born in **England** in 1728. He was the son of a farm labourer. As a young man he worked on coal ships and learned seafaring there. Later he joined the **British navy**. He became known because he could survey coasts very accurately and draw them on **maps**.

In 1768 Cook set off with the ship **“Endeavour”**. First he sailed to Tahiti to make observations of the stars there. After that he sailed around **New Zealand** and showed that it consists of **two large islands**. In **1770** he sailed along the **east coast of Australia** and drew it on a map. In 1771 he returned to England.

abschnitte.titel: The search for the southern continent
abschnitte.text: At that time many people believed there must be a **great southern continent** far to the south. On his second voyage, from 1772 to 1775, Cook sailed far south into the ice. He was one of the first to cross the **Antarctic Circle**. He did not find a habitable southern continent. He did not see Antarctica itself; it was only discovered later.

On the third voyage, from 1776, Cook looked for a sea route north around America. On the way he came to **Hawaii**. There in 1779 a dispute broke out with the inhabitants, and Cook was killed. His voyages brought Europeans a great deal of new knowledge. For many peoples in the Pacific, however, they also marked the start of a time of great change through foreign rulers and diseases.

gewusst: Cook had his crew given sauerkraut. As a result, far fewer sailors on his ships fell ill with scurvy, a dangerous deficiency disease.
The painter John Webber, whose father came from Bern, drew many landscapes and people on Cook's third voyage.

teile.einleitung: The Iraq War was a war that a coalition led by the USA began against Iraq in March 2003. It led to the overthrow of the dictator Saddam Hussein, but plunged the country into years of violence. The war is still very controversial, because its main justification turned out to be false.
wichtigste: The Iraq War began on 20 March 2003 with attacks by a coalition led by the USA.
The main reason given by the USA and Britain was the alleged possession of weapons of mass destruction.
Such weapons were not found after the war.
Germany and France openly rejected the war.
Saddam Hussein was arrested on 13 December 2003 and executed in 2006.
The last US troops left Iraq in 2011.
In the resulting chaos, the Islamic State proclaimed a “caliphate” in 2014.

abschnitte.text: **Iraq** lies in the Middle East on the rivers Euphrates and Tigris, and its capital is Baghdad. From 1979 **Saddam Hussein** ruled the country as a dictator. He fought wars against Iran and, in 1990, against Kuwait, and had opponents cruelly persecuted. After the Gulf War of 1991, Iraq had to let UN weapons inspectors into the country.

After the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001, the USA under President George W. Bush saw Iraq as a danger. It and Britain justified the attack mainly with the alleged possession of **weapons of mass destruction**. On 5 February 2003 US Secretary of State Colin Powell presented alleged evidence to the **UN Security Council**. But the Security Council did not give express permission for the war.

Germany and France openly rejected the Iraq War in 2003. In many cities around the world, millions of people demonstrated against the war, in Switzerland too. Other countries such as Britain, Australia and Poland took part in the **coalition**. Neutral Switzerland did not take part in the war.

On 20 March 2003 the attacks by the US-led coalition began. Already on 9 April 2003 the troops took **Baghdad**, and pictures of a toppled statue of Saddam went around the world. Saddam Hussein fled and was arrested by US troops in a hiding place on 13 December 2003. An Iraqi court sentenced him to death, and in 2006 he was executed.

After the victory, order could not be established in the country. There were attacks on the occupying troops and bloody fighting between **Sunnis** and **Shias**. Hundreds of thousands of people died, and millions fled from their homes. No weapons of mass destruction were found, which in hindsight made the war even more controversial.

In 2011 the last US troops left Iraq. In the resulting chaos the terror militia **Islamic State** grew strong and, after conquests in Iraq and Syria, proclaimed a “caliphate” in 2014. Only after years of fighting was it driven out of its strongholds in Iraq by 2017. Today the Iraq War is seen as an example of how hard it is to bring peace and democracy by means of a war.

begriffe.erklaerung: Nuclear, biological or chemical weapons that can kill very many people.
An alliance of several states that act together.
A ruler who governs alone, without control by the people.
The body of the United Nations that is meant to deal with questions of war and peace in the world.

gewusst: On 15 February 2003, millions of people demonstrated around the world against the threatened war; it was one of the biggest protests in history.
Saddam Hussein was found in a small hole in the ground near his home town of Tikrit.
The International Committee of the Red Cross from Geneva provided help in Iraq throughout the war.

teile.einleitung: Martin Luther was a German monk and professor who set off the Reformation with his criticism of the Church. From it the Protestant churches arose. With his translation of the Bible he also shaped the German language to this day.
wichtigste: Martin Luther was born in Eisleben in 1483 and died there too in 1546.
After a severe thunderstorm he became a monk in the Augustinian order in Erfurt in 1505.
In 1517 he published his 95 Theses against the sale of indulgences.
In 1521 he had to answer to Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms.
The imperial ban was imposed on him, which made him an outlaw.
At the Wartburg he translated the New Testament into German.
In 1525 he married the former nun Katharina von Bora.

abschnitte.text: Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 in **Eisleben**. His father worked in mining and became well off through it. He wished his son to study **law** and become a lawyer. Luther therefore studied at the University of Erfurt.

In the summer of 1505 Luther was caught in a severe **thunderstorm** near Erfurt. In fear of the lightning he vowed to become a monk. Shortly afterwards, against his father’s will, he entered the monastery of the **Augustinians** in Erfurt. Later he became a Doctor of Theology and professor at the University of Wittenberg.

At that time the Church sold **indulgences**, which were meant to remit punishments for sins in return for money. Luther thought this wrong, for he was convinced that God forgives people by grace alone. On 31 October 1517 he published **95 theses** on the subject. Thanks to printing, his ideas spread across the whole of Germany within a few weeks.

The Pope excluded Luther from the Church at the beginning of 1521. After that he had to answer to Emperor Charles V at the **Diet of Worms**. Luther refused to retract his writings. As a result the **imperial ban** was imposed on him, and he was an outlaw whom anyone could seize.

Elector **Frederick the Wise** of Saxony protected Luther and had him kidnapped for show. Luther then lived in hiding as “Junker Jörg” at the **Wartburg** near Eisenach. There, in only about eleven weeks, he translated the New Testament from Greek into German. In this way ordinary people could at last read the Bible in their own language; the whole Bible appeared in 1534.

In 1525 Luther married **Katharina von Bora**, and the couple had six children. From his movement the Lutheran churches arose, and Europe split into Catholic and Protestant territories. In Switzerland Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich and later John Calvin in Geneva carried out reformations of their own. In late writings Luther expressed himself sharply against the Jews, which is clearly criticised today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement of renewal in the 16th century from which the Protestant churches arose.
A remission of punishments for sins, which the Church at that time also offered for money.
A claim that one wants to have discussed.
A punishment by which someone was left without legal protection and became an outlaw.
A Catholic order, that is, a community of monks.

gewusst: Many words and expressions, such as “stopgap” or “casting pearls before swine”, go back to Luther’s translation of the Bible.
31 October is celebrated as Reformation Day and is a public holiday in several German states.
Luther also wrote many hymns that are still sung in church services today.

teile.einleitung: Fidel Castro was a Cuban revolutionary and politician. In 1959 he led a revolution and afterwards ruled Cuba for almost 50 years. Even today people judge him very differently.
wichtigste: Fidel Castro was born in 1926 and died in 2016.
On 26 July 1953 he unsuccessfully attacked the Moncada barracks.
He called his group the “26th of July Movement”.
At the start of 1959 the revolutionaries took power in Cuba.
In 2008 he handed the office of head of state to his brother Raúl.

abschnitte.text: Fidel Castro was born in Cuba in 1926 and studied law. Cuba was then ruled by the dictator **Fulgencio Batista**. On **26 July 1953** Castro and his followers attacked the **Moncada barracks** in Santiago de Cuba. The attack failed, and Castro went to prison. Later he named his **“26th of July Movement”** after the date. After his release he went to Mexico and returned in 1956 with a small group that also included **Che Guevara**.

At the start of **1959** Batista fled, and the revolutionaries took power. Castro made Cuba a **socialist state** with only one party. Companies and land were nationalised. Cuba worked closely with the **Soviet Union**, and the quarrel with the USA grew great. Supporters praise the free **education** and **health care**. Critics complain that there were no free elections and no free press and that opponents were persecuted.

In 2006 Fidel Castro temporarily handed over his duties because of an illness. In **2008** his brother **Raúl Castro** officially became head of state. Fidel Castro afterwards still spoke out now and then in newspaper articles. He died in **2016** at the age of 90.

gewusst: From 1961 to 2015 Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba, because the two countries had no official relations.

teile.einleitung: The Gotthard Railway is one of the most famous railway lines in the world and leads from Central Switzerland through the Alps into Ticino. It was opened in 1882 and linked northern Europe with Italy. Building it was a technical masterpiece, but also cost many lives.
wichtigste: The Gotthard Railway was fully opened in 1882.
Its centrepiece is the Gotthard Tunnel, about 15 kilometres long, between Göschenen and Airolo.
Alfred Escher was president of the Gotthard Railway company, and Louis Favre led the building of the tunnel.
Italy and Germany helped pay for the construction.
About 200 workers died building the tunnel, most of them from Italy.
At Wassen you see the church three times from the train, from different heights.
Since 1922 the Gotthard Railway has run entirely on electricity.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel, opened in 2016, is about 57 kilometres long.

abschnitte.text: The **Gotthard Railway** leads from Lake Lucerne up the Reuss valley in Uri to Göschenen. There it disappears into the Gotthard Tunnel and comes out again at Airolo in Ticino. After that it runs down through the Leventina to Bellinzona and on to Chiasso on the Italian border. It is part of an important link between Germany and Italy.

The Zurich politician and businessman **Alfred Escher** strongly supported the railway and was president of the Gotthard Railway company. Because building it was very expensive, Italy and Germany also helped finance it. They had a great interest in a fast link across the Alps. When costs rose sharply, Escher had to resign as president in 1878.

The building of the roughly 15 kilometre long **Gotthard Tunnel** was led by the Geneva contractor Louis Favre. On 29 February 1880 the tunnel builders from the north and the south met at the **breakthrough**. Favre did not live to see this moment; he had died in the tunnel in 1879. Most of the workers came from Italy, and about 200 of them lost their lives.

The workers toiled in great heat, bad air and noise. Many were injured or killed by accidents, blasting or illness. In 1875 the tunnel workers in Göschenen went on strike for better conditions. Armed men fired into the crowd, and four workers died.

abschnitte.titel: Spiral tunnels and the church of Wassen
abschnitte.text: To overcome the steep steps in the valley, **spiral tunnels** were built, in which the train turns in a circle inside the mountain and gains height as it does so. The village of **Wassen** in the canton of Uri is particularly famous. Its church can be seen from the train three times from different heights, once from below, once at the same height and once from above. There are such spiral tunnels in the Leventina too.

abschnitte.titel: From steam locomotive to base tunnel
abschnitte.text: At first steam locomotives ran on the Gotthard Railway, and from 1922 the line could be used entirely by electric trains. In 1909 the Gotthard Railway was taken over by the Swiss Federal Railways **SBB**. Since 2016 most trains have run through the roughly 57 kilometre long **Gotthard Base Tunnel**, which lies much lower. The old mountain line is still used by regional trains and tourists, though.

begriffe.erklaerung: The moment when the workers from both sides meet in the tunnel.
A tunnel in the shape of a loop, in which the train gains height inside the mountain.
The old, higher railway line over the Gotthard with the summit tunnel.
New Rail Link through the Alps, the project with the new base tunnels.

gewusst: The church of Wassen is so well known that many travellers wait specially to see it three times.
At Airolo station, a monument by the sculptor Vincenzo Vela recalls the victims of the tunnel construction.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.

t2bug3i.t: The fall of the Berlin Wall

teile.einleitung: The fall of the Wall means the opening of the Berlin Wall in the night of 9 to 10 November 1989. The Wall had divided Berlin into East and West for 28 years. Its fall became a symbol of the end of the GDR, of the Cold War and of the division of Europe.
wichtigste: The Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989.
Günter Schabowski announced the new travel rules at a press conference and said they applied “immediately, without delay”.
The first border crossing to open in the evening was Bornholmer Strasse.
As early as the summer of 1989 many GDR citizens fled to the West via Hungary.
The Monday demonstration in Leipzig on 9 October 1989 with around 70,000 people stayed peaceful and is seen as a turning point.
Less than a year later, on 3 October 1990, Germany was reunified.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Germany was divided into the Federal Republic in the west and the **GDR** in the east. Because more and more people were fleeing from the GDR to the West, the GDR leadership had a wall built around West Berlin on 13 August 1961. It was about 155 kilometres long and strictly guarded. At least 140 people lost their lives at the Berlin Wall.

abschnitte.titel: The hole in the Iron Curtain
abschnitte.text: In 1989 the Eastern Bloc began to crumble, partly because of the reforms of Mikhail Gorbachev. On 27 June the foreign ministers Gyula Horn and Alois Mock symbolically cut through the border fence between Hungary and Austria. At the **Pan-European Picnic** on 19 August 1989 near Sopron, organised by the Paneuropean Union and the Hungarian Democratic Forum, hundreds of GDR citizens fled to Austria. On 11 September Hungary opened the border for good.

In the embassy of the Federal Republic in Prague, thousands of GDR refugees crowded together. On 30 September 1989 Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher announced from the balcony that they were allowed to leave. In Leipzig people took to the streets every Monday and shouted “We are the people”. On 9 October around 70,000 people demonstrated without the state using violence, and in October the head of state Erich Honecker had to resign.

On 9 November 1989 the SED Politburo member **Günter Schabowski** presented a new travel regulation at a press conference. The journalist Riccardo Ehrman of the Italian news agency ANSA asked when it would apply. Schabowski answered “Immediately, without delay”, although that was not what had been planned. Thousands of East Berliners streamed to the border crossings, and late in the evening the crossing at **Bornholmer Strasse** opened first.

In the night people from East and West fell into each other’s arms, and many climbed onto the Wall at the Brandenburg Gate. Two days later the cellist **Mstislav Rostropovich** played at Checkpoint Charlie in front of the Wall. Soon afterwards people began to tear down the Wall, and many knocked off pieces as souvenirs. On 22 December 1989 the Brandenburg Gate was also opened again.

After the fall of the Wall, free elections were held in the GDR for the first time in March 1990. On 3 October 1990 the GDR joined the Federal Republic, which was the **reunification**. In other countries of Eastern Europe too, communist rule came to an end. Today the memorial at Bernauer Strasse and the painted East Side Gallery recall the Wall.

begriffe.erklaerung: The German Democratic Republic, the communist German state from 1949 to 1990.
The ruling party of the GDR, which governed the country alone.
An image for the strictly guarded border between Eastern and Western Europe in the Cold War.
The growing together of the GDR and the Federal Republic into one state in 1990.

gewusst: The opening of the Wall was actually a slip, because the new rule was meant to apply only the next day.
Pieces of the Berlin Wall stand today all over the world, in Switzerland too.
9 November 1989 is linked with the cry “Madness!”, which many people shouted for joy at the time.

teile.einleitung: The Treaty of Versailles ended the First World War in 1919 between Germany and the victorious powers. It placed harsh conditions on Germany and was very controversial there.
wichtigste: The treaty was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
Germany was not allowed to take part in the negotiations, so many called it a “dictated peace”.
Alsace-Lorraine went back to France.
Because of the Polish Corridor, East Prussia was cut off from the rest of Germany.
Danzig became a Free City, and the Saar region came under the League of Nations for 15 years.
The Rhineland was not allowed to have German troops.
Germany lost all its colonies.

abschnitte.text: The **First World War** ended in November 1918 with an armistice. After that, the victorious powers negotiated the terms of peace in Paris. Germany was **not allowed to negotiate** and had to accept the terms. On **28 June 1919** the treaty was signed in the **Hall of Mirrors** of the palace of **Versailles**. The German Empire had also been proclaimed there in 1871.

The most important statesmen were **Woodrow Wilson** from the USA, **David Lloyd George** from Britain and **Georges Clemenceau** from France. Clemenceau, known as **“the Tiger”**, wanted to protect France from Germany for good. He pushed for especially **harsh terms**, such as high payments and strict disarmament. Wilson, on the other hand, wanted a fair peace and an organisation for world peace.

Germany had to give **Alsace-Lorraine** back to France; it had been German since 1871. Poland received access to the Baltic Sea, the **Polish Corridor**. As a result, **East Prussia** lay cut off from the rest of the Reich. **Danzig** became a **Free City** under the protection of the League of Nations. The **Saar region** came under the League of Nations for 15 years, and France received the coal mines. In addition, Germany lost **all its colonies**, such as German South West Africa and Cameroon.

The German army was limited to **100,000 soldiers**. The **Rhineland** had to remain free of German troops and was partly occupied by Allied troops. Germany also had to pay **reparations**, that is, money for the damage caused by the war. One article made Germany responsible for the war. Many Germans felt the treaty was unfair and called it a **“dictated peace”**. Later, nationalists exploited this mood.

abschnitte.titel: The League of Nations in Geneva
abschnitte.text: The treaty also created the **League of Nations**. It was meant to settle disputes between states peacefully and prevent new wars. Its seat was in **Geneva**. Switzerland joined the League of Nations in 1920 after a popular vote. However, the League of Nations could not prevent the Second World War. After that war, the United Nations was created.

gewusst: In the Saar region, the population voted in 1935 by a large majority to return to Germany.
The USA signed the treaty, but its parliament never approved it. The USA never joined the League of Nations either.

teile.einleitung: The internet is a worldwide network of computers that exchange data with one another. Over the internet we write messages, watch videos, look for information and learn.
wichtigste: The internet links millions of computers all over the world.
It grew out of ARPANET, which linked computers in the USA from 1969.
The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 at CERN in Geneva.
With Wi-Fi, devices at home get onto the internet without cables.
You find websites with a search engine.
Passwords must be kept secret.
The ending “.ch” stands for Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **internet** is a huge network in which computers all over the world are connected. The data travels over cables, including under the sea, and over radio. It is broken into small **data packets** and put back together at its destination. So that all devices understand one another, there are shared rules, which are called **protocols**.

From **1969** in the USA, **ARPANET** linked computers at universities. From it, today's internet developed. In 1989 **Tim Berners-Lee** invented the **World Wide Web** at the research centre **CERN** in **Geneva**. With it you could link pages with text and pictures and view them in a browser. In 1991 the first website went online.

At home, a phone and laptop often connect to the internet by **Wi-Fi**. That is a wireless local network. A **router** sends the signal. To find information you use a **search engine**. It searches the internet for the words you type in and shows matching pages. But not everything on the internet is true.

A **password** protects your accounts from strangers. Keep it secret and choose one that cannot easily be guessed. Do not give your address or phone number to people you do not know. If something on the internet seems odd to you or frightens you, talk to your parents or a teacher.

Every country has its own ending for internet addresses. Switzerland has **“.ch”**. It comes from the Latin name of Switzerland: **Confoederatio Helvetica**. These two letters are also on car number plates abroad. Germany has “.de”, Austria “.at” and Liechtenstein “.li”.

gewusst: The very first website in the world was created in Switzerland, at CERN.
A lot of data between continents travels through cables lying on the sea floor.

teile.einleitung: In the Cuban Revolution, rebels around Fidel Castro overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista. On New Year’s Eve of 1958 into 1959 Batista fled the country. After that Cuba became a socialist state, and relations with the USA broke down.
wichtigste: Fulgencio Batista ruled Cuba as a dictator.
In December 1956 Fidel Castro and a good 80 fighters landed in Cuba with the yacht Granma.
The rebels waged their guerrilla war in the Sierra Maestra mountains.
The revolutionary Ernesto “Che” Guevara came from Argentina.
On New Year’s Eve 1958/59 Batista fled Cuba.
From 1961 Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba as protecting power.

abschnitte.text: **Fulgencio Batista** took power in Cuba through a coup in 1952 and ruled as a **dictator**. Many Cubans were poor, while a few were very rich. American companies owned a large part of the sugar plantations and other businesses. Opponents of the government were persecuted. The young lawyer **Fidel Castro** wanted to overthrow Batista.

After a failed attack Castro had to go into exile in **Mexico**. There he prepared a return with like-minded people. In **December 1956** he and a good 80 fighters landed in Cuba with the yacht **Granma**. Among them was the doctor **Ernesto “Che” Guevara** from **Argentina**. Most of the fighters were captured or killed shortly after the landing, and only a few escaped.

The survivors withdrew into the **Sierra Maestra** mountains in the east of Cuba. There they waged a **guerrilla war**: small, mobile groups attacked the army from ambush. More and more people supported the rebels. Batista’s army lost many battles. On **New Year’s Eve 1958/59** Batista fled the country, and the rebels took power.

Castro nationalised companies and land, including those of Americans. Cuba moved closer to the **Soviet Union**. In 1961 the USA broke off diplomatic relations. From then on **Switzerland** represented the interests of the USA in Cuba as **protecting power**. It took on this task until 2015, when the two countries opened embassies again.

The revolution is still disputed today. Supporters stress that Cuba expanded schools and health care for everyone. Critics point out that Cuba became a **one-party state** in which opponents are persecuted and freedom of speech is lacking. Many people have left Cuba since, most of them for the USA.

gewusst: The yacht Granma is now on display in a glass building in Havana.
The picture of Che Guevara in a beret is one of the best-known photographs in the world.

teile.einleitung: The brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière from France are among the inventors of the cinema. In 1895 they showed films to a paying audience in Paris for the first time.
wichtigste: The brothers were called Auguste and Louis Lumière.
They lived and worked in Lyon in France.
Their device was called the Cinématographe and could both film and show films.
In December 1895 they showed films to a paying audience in Paris.
This show is regarded as the birth of the cinema.
Their first films lasted less than a minute and had no sound.

abschnitte.text: **Auguste** and **Louis Lumière** grew up in **Lyon** in **France**. Their father had a factory there for **photographic plates**. The brothers worked in the firm from an early age. They were interested in how to make pictures move.

The brothers developed the **Cinématographe**. This device could record films and also project them onto a wall. It was light and handy. Our word **cinema** comes from the word Cinématographe. A film is made of many single pictures. If you show them quickly one after the other, it looks as if something is moving.

In **December 1895** the Lumières showed their films in a room under a café in **Paris**. The spectators paid an **entrance fee**. This show is regarded as the **birth of the cinema**. Soon the brothers showed their films in many countries. They also sent camera operators all over the world to film there.

The first films lasted **less than a minute**. No more film fitted into the camera. They showed scenes from everyday life, for example workers leaving a factory. A famous film shows a **train** arriving at a station. It is said that some spectators were frightened. The films were **silent films** without sound, and sometimes someone in the hall played the piano to go with them.

gewusst: The name Lumière means “light” in French.
The Lumière brothers later also developed a process for colour photographs.

teile.einleitung: The demographic transition is a model. It describes how births and deaths in a country change as it develops from a farming society into an industrial society.
wichtigste: The model divides the development of a population into several phases.
At the start the birth rate and the death rate are both high.
In the second phase the death rate falls, while the birth rate stays high.
The gap between the two rates is called the population scissors.
At the end both rates are low, and the society ages.
Warren Thompson was the first to describe the basic pattern in 1929.
For a population to stay the same size without immigration, about 2.1 children per woman are needed.

abschnitte.text: The **birth rate** tells how many children are born in a year per 1,000 inhabitants. The **death rate** shows how many people die per 1,000 inhabitants. If the birth rate is higher, the population grows. The difference between the two rates gives the **natural population growth**. Immigration and emigration are not counted here.

At the start both rates are **high**, and the population hardly grows. In the **early transition phase** the death rate falls, because food and hygiene get better. The birth rate, however, stays high at first. In this way the **population scissors** open, and the population grows strongly. After that the birth rate falls too. In the **late phase** both rates are low, and growth is small or even negative.

In the 19th century the death rate in Europe fell clearly. What mattered was **better food** thanks to higher harvests, **clean drinking water** and the building of **sewers**. As a result there were fewer epidemics. Medicines such as antibiotics only came into wide use in the 20th century. Today people in industrial countries live to a much greater age on average than in the past.

For a stable population without immigration, industrial countries need about **2.1 children per woman**. This **replacement level** is a little above 2, because not all children grow up. Switzerland has been clearly below it for decades. Because at the same time people live longer, there are more older people. This is a great challenge for the **AHV**, for example, because fewer working people pay for the pensions of more retired people.

As early as 1798 the Englishman **Thomas Robert Malthus** warned that the population grows faster than the food supply. He therefore expected famines again and again. In Europe it turned out differently, because farming produced far more. The American demographer **Warren Thompson** was the first to describe the basic pattern of the demographic transition in 1929. **Frank Notestein** later developed the model further.

gewusst: The model is based mainly on the history of Europe. Whether all countries follow exactly the same course is disputed among experts.
A demographer is an expert who studies the population and how it develops.

teile.einleitung: The steam locomotive was the first locomotive to pull railway trains over long distances. It is driven by hot steam. In the 19th century it changed travel and the transport of goods all over the world, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: George Stephenson from England was one of the most important locomotive builders.
In the steam locomotive coal burns and heats water into steam.
The fireman shovelled the coal into the fire, and the driver steered.
In the tender behind the locomotive lay coal and water.
In 1847 the first railway entirely on Swiss soil ran from Zurich to Baden.
In the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne stands a replica of the locomotive “Limmat”.

abschnitte.text: In a steam locomotive a **fire** of coal burns. It heats water in a large **boiler** until it turns into **steam**. The steam pushes pistons back and forth, and these move the wheels. Smoke and steam rise from the **chimney**. The **fireman** shovelled the coal into the fire, and the **driver** steered the locomotive.

Directly behind the steam locomotive hung a special wagon, the **tender**. In it lay the supplies of **coal** and **water** for the journey. Without fresh supplies the locomotive would soon have come to a halt. That is why stations had water towers and coal stores.

The first railways ran in **England**. **George Stephenson** was born in 1781 near Newcastle, where there were many coal mines. He built locomotives and railway lines. His locomotive **Rocket** won a famous competition in 1829. Soon railways were built in many countries of Europe.

In 1847 the first railway line was opened that lay entirely in **Switzerland**. It ran from **Zurich** to **Baden** in Aargau and was about 23 kilometres long. It is called the **Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn**, the Spanish Bun Railway, after a fine pastry from Baden. One of the first locomotives was called **Limmat**, after the river in Zurich.

Today almost all trains in Switzerland run on **electricity**. Steam locomotives can still be seen on nostalgic journeys, for example on the **Brienz Rothorn Railway**. In the **Swiss Museum of Transport** in Lucerne stands a replica of the locomotive “Limmat”. The museum shows vehicles on land, on water and in the air and is one of the most visited museums in Switzerland.

gewusst: The Spanish Bun Railway got its name from a pastry that Zurich gentry liked to have fetched from Baden.
Because coal became scarce in the First World War, Switzerland began to convert its railways to electricity.

teile.einleitung: The Boxer Rebellion was a movement in northern China around 1900 that was directed against foreigners and their influence. The high point was the siege of the legations in Beijing. An alliance of eight states put down the uprising.
wichtigste: The movement spread in northern China from 1899.
The Boxers called themselves Yihetuan, Righteous and Harmonious Fists.
In the summer of 1900 they besieged the legation quarter in Beijing for about 55 days.
The German envoy Clemens von Ketteler was killed in June 1900.
The Eight-Nation Alliance occupied Beijing in August 1900.
In the Boxer Protocol of 1901 China had to pay 450 million taels of silver.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century European powers, Japan and the USA gained more and more influence in **China**. They forced trading rights and occupied territories. Christian **missionaries** also came into the country. Many Chinese felt threatened. In addition there were droughts and famines in northern China.

From 1899 a movement spread in northern China. Its members called themselves **Yihetuan**, which means Righteous and Harmonious Fists. The foreigners called them “**Boxers**” because they practised martial arts exercises. The movement was directed against foreigners, missionaries and Chinese Christians. In the end the imperial court of the **Qing dynasty** supported the Boxers.

In June 1900 the German envoy **Clemens von Ketteler** was shot on his way to the Chinese foreign office. Afterwards Boxers and government troops besieged the **legation quarter** in Beijing. There diplomats, soldiers and many Chinese Christians had taken refuge. The siege lasted about **55 days** and ended on 14 August 1900.

Eight states sent troops to China: Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, the USA, Italy and Austria-Hungary. This alliance is called the **Eight-Nation Alliance**. It occupied Beijing in August 1900. The supreme command went to the German Field Marshal **Alfred von Waldersee**, who only arrived after the relief of Beijing. Afterwards many punitive expeditions followed.

In 1901 China had to sign the **Boxer Protocol**. It had to pay **450 million taels** of silver in compensation, spread over decades and with interest. This put a heavy burden on the state finances. The weakness of the Qing dynasty became visible to all. A few years later, in 1912, the imperial era in China ended.

gewusst: The compensation amounted roughly to one tael of silver for every inhabitant of China.
The USA later used part of its share to pay for Chinese students to study in America.

teile.einleitung: Laika was a dog from Moscow who flew into space in 1957. She was the first animal to orbit the Earth. Her flight helped to prepare space flight for humans, but Laika did not return.
wichtigste: Laika was a dog, more precisely a female dog.
Before she was chosen, she lived on the streets of Moscow.
She flew into space in 1957 on the spacecraft Sputnik 2.
She was the first animal to orbit the Earth.
People wanted to test whether living creatures could survive such a flight.
Laika died in space and did not come back alive.

abschnitte.text: **Laika** was a small mongrel female. She first lived on the **streets of Moscow**. Researchers in the **Soviet Union** liked to choose stray dogs, because they were used to cold and hunger. Laika was calm and friendly. Before the flight she was trained, for example in very cramped cabins and with loud noise.

In November **1957** Laika launched into space on board **Sputnik 2**. Only a month earlier the Soviet Union had put the first artificial satellite into space with Sputnik 1. Laika was the **first animal to orbit the Earth**. Her cabin was very small. Instruments measured her heartbeat and her breathing and radioed the data to Earth.

At that time nobody knew exactly whether a living creature could survive the **launch**, **weightlessness** and the conditions in space. That is why animals were sent first. With Laika people wanted to **test whether living creatures survive the flight**. Her data showed that a living creature can endure the launch and weightlessness for a time. That was important for the first flight of a human into space in 1961.

A return to Earth was not possible for Sputnik 2. Laika **died in space**, only a few hours after the launch, because it became too hot in the cabin. The Soviet Union only made this known many years later. Her fate made many people sad, and there was argument about whether animals should be used in this way. In Moscow a **monument** to Laika stands today.

gewusst: The name Laika means roughly “barker” in Russian and is also the name of a dog breed.
In 1960 the dogs Belka and Strelka flew into space and returned alive.

teile.einleitung: Louis Pasteur was a French scientist of the 19th century. He showed that tiny germs can spoil food and cause diseases. Pasteurising is named after him, and he developed a vaccine against rabies.
wichtigste: Louis Pasteur came from France.
He showed that tiny germs spoil food.
In pasteurising, milk is heated; the process is named after him.
With glass flasks with a long, curved neck he disproved spontaneous generation.
He developed a vaccine against rabies for humans.
Even before him, Edward Jenner made the first smallpox vaccination.
In Paris the Institut Pasteur is named after him.

abschnitte.text: **Louis Pasteur** was born in **France** in 1822 and died in 1895. He was a trained chemist. With the **microscope** he investigated why wine, beer and milk turn sour or spoil. He found out that **tiny germs**, which cannot be seen with the naked eye, are responsible. This discovery changed medicine and the way food is handled.

In the past many people believed that life could simply arise by itself from dead matter. This idea is called **spontaneous generation**. Pasteur filled nutrient broth into **glass flasks with a long, curved neck** and boiled it. Air could get in, but dust and germs stuck in the curved neck. The broth stayed fresh. Only when germs got in did it spoil. In this way he **disproved** spontaneous generation.
