Pasteur developed a process to make drinks last longer. They are **heated** for a short time, but not to boiling. Most harmful germs die in the process, but the taste is largely kept. This process is called **pasteurising**, after him. Today almost all the milk you buy in the shop is treated in this way.

A **vaccination** protects against diseases because the body learns to fight off a pathogen. The first vaccination, against **smallpox**, had already been made by **Edward Jenner** in 1796. Pasteur developed a vaccine against the dangerous **rabies**. In 1885 the boy **Joseph Meister** was bitten by a rabid **dog**. Pasteur vaccinated him, and the boy survived.

After the success many people donated money. With it the **Institut Pasteur** was founded in **Paris**. There scientists still research diseases and vaccines today. Together with the German Robert Koch, Pasteur is regarded as the founder of **microbiology**, the science of tiny living things.

gewusst: Joseph Meister later worked as an adult at the Institut Pasteur in Paris.
Pasteur also helped the French silk industry, because he researched a disease of silkworms.

teile.einleitung: Elizabeth I was Queen of England from 1558 to 1603. During her long reign England became an important sea power, and art and theatre flourished.
wichtigste: Elizabeth I was a daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn.
Her mother was executed in 1536, when Elizabeth was not yet three years old.
She reigned for 45 years, from 1558 to 1603.
Because she never married, she was called “the Virgin Queen”.
In 1587 she had the Scottish queen Mary Stuart executed.
In her time William Shakespeare wrote his first plays.
With her death the House of Tudor ended.

abschnitte.text: Elizabeth was born in 1533. Her father was King **Henry VIII**, who was married six times. Her mother **Anne Boleyn** he had beheaded in 1536. Elizabeth was then not yet three years old. As a child she received a very good **education** and learned several languages. Under her half-sister, Queen Mary I, she was even held prisoner for a time.

In **1558** Elizabeth became queen. She reigned for **45 years**, until 1603. In matters of faith she strengthened the **Anglican Church**, which was independent of the Pope. Elizabeth never married, although many princes courted her. That is why she was given the nickname **“the Virgin Queen”**. Her time is called the **Elizabethan age**.

Under Elizabeth England became an important **sea power**. Seafarers such as **Francis Drake** sailed around the world. In 1588 Spain sent a great fleet, the **Armada**, against England. It was defeated by the English and by heavy storms. This success made Elizabeth very popular with her people.

**Mary Stuart** was Queen of Scotland and a Catholic. She fled to England and was held prisoner there for almost twenty years. Many Catholics saw in her the rightful queen of England. Mary became involved in **plots** against Elizabeth. That is why Elizabeth had her executed in **1587**.

In Elizabeth's time **theatre** flourished in London. **William Shakespeare** wrote his first plays then, for example “Romeo and Juliet”. Elizabeth died in **1603** without children. With her the royal house of the **Tudors** ended. Her successor was the Scottish king **James** of the House of **Stuart**, the son of Mary Stuart.

gewusst: Besides English, Elizabeth I also spoke French, Italian and Latin.
The American state of Virginia was named after the nickname of Elizabeth I.

teile.einleitung: The Bretton Woods system was an order for money that applied after the Second World War. Currencies had fixed exchange rates against the US dollar, and the dollar was tied to gold. The system lasted from 1944 until the early 1970s.
wichtigste: The conference took place in July 1944 in Bretton Woods in the USA.
Delegates from 44 countries took part.
One troy ounce of gold cost a fixed 35 dollars.
At Bretton Woods the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were agreed.
In 1971 President Richard Nixon ended the exchange of dollars for gold.
Switzerland joined the International Monetary Fund in 1992.

abschnitte.text: While the **Second World War** was still going on, delegates from **44 countries** met in July 1944. They gathered in a hotel in **Bretton Woods** in the state of New Hampshire in the **USA**. They wanted to create a stable order for money and trade. After the experiences of the Great Depression, currencies were no longer to swing wildly.

The **US dollar** was tied to **gold**: one **troy ounce** cost a fixed **35 dollars**. The USA promised to exchange dollars for gold at this price for foreign central banks. The other currencies had **fixed exchange rates** against the dollar. The Swiss National Bank also kept the franc at a fixed rate against the dollar for a long time.

abschnitte.titel: The IMF and the World Bank
abschnitte.text: Two organisations were agreed at Bretton Woods. The **International Monetary Fund** (IMF) was to help countries that temporarily had too little foreign currency. The **World Bank** was to pay for rebuilding after the war. Both have their seat in Washington. The British economist **John Maynard Keynes** had proposed a world currency called **Bancor**. In the end, though, the plan of the American Harry Dexter White, with the dollar at its centre, largely won through.

The world needed more and more dollars for trade. For that the USA had to run deficits. The more dollars were in circulation, the less the gold reserves covered them. The economist **Robert Triffin** described this problem in 1960. It is called the **Triffin dilemma**.

On 15 August 1971 US President **Richard Nixon** closed the “gold window”. The USA no longer exchanged dollars for gold. This is called the **Nixon shock**. Soon afterwards many countries moved to **floating exchange rates**, which are set by the market. Switzerland only joined the IMF and the World Bank in 1992, after a **referendum**.

gewusst: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank still exist today.
Since the end of Bretton Woods no important currency in the world has been tied to gold.

teile.einleitung: Yuri Gagarin was the first human in space. On 12 April 1961 the Soviet cosmonaut orbited the Earth once in the spacecraft Vostok 1 and became world famous.
wichtigste: Yuri Gagarin from the Soviet Union flew into space in 1961 as the first human.
His spacecraft was called Vostok 1; “Vostok” means East.
He orbited the Earth exactly once.
The flight lasted about 108 minutes, so just under two hours.
At the launch he called out “Poyekhali!”, which means roughly “Let's go!”.
Shortly before landing he ejected and floated down to Earth on a parachute.
Gagarin died in 1968 in the crash of a training aircraft.

abschnitte.text: Yuri Gagarin was born on **9 March 1934** in a village in Russia. He first worked in a factory and learned to fly on the side. Then he became a **fighter pilot** in the air force. In 1960 he was chosen from among many pilots for space flight. Space travellers from the Soviet Union and from Russia are called **cosmonauts**; in the USA they are called astronauts.

On **12 April 1961** Gagarin launched in the spacecraft **Vostok 1** from the Baikonur Cosmodrome. At the launch he called out **“Poyekhali!”**, roughly “Let's go!”. He orbited the Earth **exactly once**. The whole flight lasted about **108 minutes**. Gagarin was **27 years** old at the time. He reported by radio how beautiful the Earth looks from above.

The capsule could not land softly. So shortly before landing, at a height of several kilometres, Gagarin ejected with his **ejector seat**. He floated down to Earth on a **parachute**. He landed in a field, where farmers received him in surprise. After the flight Gagarin was celebrated as a hero all over the world.

Gagarin's flight took place in the middle of the **space race** between the Soviet Union and the USA. After it, Gagarin did not fly into space again; he trained other cosmonauts. On **27 March 1968** he died on a training flight in a fighter jet. He was only **34 years** old. Many streets, schools and even a crater on the Moon bear his name.

gewusst: Since 2011, 12 April has been the UN's International Day of Human Space Flight.
Gagarin was only about 1.57 metres tall. That was an advantage in the cramped space capsule.

teile.einleitung: Ludwig van Beethoven was one of the most famous composers in the world. He lived in Vienna for most of his life. Although he became deaf in later life, he kept on writing magnificent music.
wichtigste: Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770.
He spent most of his life in Vienna.
He was a great master of the piano.
He wrote 9 symphonies.
A famous piano piece by him is called “Für Elise”.
As he got older he became deaf, but he heard the music in his head.

abschnitte.text: **Ludwig van Beethoven** was born in **Bonn** in **1770**. His father was a singer and taught him even as a small child. Beethoven became a great master of the **piano**. As a young man he moved to **Vienna**, which was then a capital of music. He lived there for most of his life, until he died in 1827.

Beethoven wrote a great many works: piano sonatas, concertos, string quartets and an opera called “Fidelio”. Especially famous are his **9 symphonies**, great works for orchestra. His music is often powerful and full of feeling. One well-known piano piece bears a girl’s name: **“Für Elise”**. Who this Elise was has still not been settled with certainty.

Already at about the age of 30 Beethoven noticed that his hearing was getting worse. As he got older he finally became **deaf**. That was very bad for a musician. Even so he kept on composing, because he **heard the music in his head**. He knew the sounds of the instruments so well that he could imagine them exactly. To talk with others he had people write questions in notebooks.

In his last symphony, the **9th**, a large choir sings at the end. The text is the poem **“Ode to Joy”** by Friedrich Schiller. People all over the world know the melody today. It is the **anthem of the European Union**. At the first performance Beethoven is said not to have heard the audience’s cheering.

gewusst: Beethoven moved very often in Vienna; it is said he lived in dozens of flats.
Many people know the beginning of his 5th symphony with the four notes “da da da daaa”.

teile.einleitung: Gregor Mendel was a monk and natural scientist in the 19th century. With experiments on peas he discovered rules by which characteristics are passed from parents to offspring.
wichtigste: Gregor Mendel was a monk in the monastery in Brno and later became its abbot.
Brno lies in what is now the Czech Republic.
From 1856 to 1863 he grew many thousands of pea plants in the monastery garden.
He wanted to know how characteristics are inherited.
For example, he crossed peas with yellow seeds and peas with green seeds.
His discoveries are now called Mendel's laws.
Mendel is seen as the father of the study of heredity.

abschnitte.text: Gregor Mendel was born in 1822 in a village in Silesia that now belongs to the Czech Republic. He entered the **Augustinian** monastery in **Brno** and became a monk. The monastery sent him to the university in Vienna, where he studied natural sciences. After that he taught at a school. In 1868 he became **abbot**, that is, head of his monastery.

In the **monastery garden**, from 1856 to 1863, Mendel planted many thousands of **peas**. Peas are well suited because they have clear characteristics: the seeds are, for example, **yellow or green**, round or wrinkled. Mendel **crossed** plants with different characteristics. Then he counted very precisely how often each characteristic appeared in the offspring.

Mendel found that characteristics are inherited by fixed rules. When he crossed yellow peas with green ones, all the seeds in the next generation were yellow. So yellow was **dominant**, that is, stronger. In the generation after that, green appeared again, in about one seed in four. Green is called **recessive**. These rules are now called **Mendel's laws**.

Mendel published his results in 1866. Hardly anyone at the time understood how important they were. He died in 1884 in Brno. Only around **1900** did three researchers rediscover his work. Today Mendel is seen as the **father of the study of heredity**, which is also called **genetics**.

gewusst: Mendel used mathematics in his research and counted tens of thousands of peas. That was very unusual in biology at the time.
In Brno there is now a museum about Mendel in the monastery where he lived.

teile.einleitung: The Council of Trent was a great assembly of the Catholic Church from 1545 to 1563. It was the Church’s answer to the Reformation of Martin Luther and others. Its decisions shaped the Catholic Church for centuries, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The city of Trent lies in present-day Italy.
The council met, with interruptions, from 1545 to 1563.
It confirmed the seven sacraments of the Catholic Church.
It taught that faith and good works belong together.
The Mass continued to be celebrated everywhere in Latin.
The office of indulgence preacher was abolished.
In 1564 a list of forbidden books appeared.

abschnitte.text: A **council** is a great assembly of bishops and other representatives of the Church. The **Council of Trent** took place in the city of **Trent**, which today lies in **Italy**. It met, with long interruptions, from **1545 to 1563**. With it the Catholic Church wanted to answer the **Reformation**, which was spreading across Europe. At the same time it wanted to remedy abuses within its own ranks.

Martin Luther taught that a person is made righteous before God by faith alone. The council, by contrast, taught that **faith and good works belong together**. It confirmed the **seven sacraments**, for example baptism, confirmation and the Eucharist. The Reformers recognised only a few of them. The council also stressed that, besides the Bible, the tradition of the Church is important too.

The council also wanted to renew the Church. The **sale of indulgences** had fallen into great disrepute, so the office of **indulgence preacher** was abolished. Bishops were to live in their diocese and look after the faithful. **Seminaries** were to be set up for the training of priests. The **Mass** continued to be celebrated everywhere in **Latin**, so that it was the same in all countries.

In **1564** the Church had a **list of forbidden books** published. It is called the **Index**. The faithful were not to read books that in the Church’s opinion endangered the faith. This list was extended again and again. Only in the 20th century was it abolished.

The Archbishop of Milan, **Charles Borromeo**, enforced the decisions of Trent with particular zeal, in **Catholic Switzerland** too. He visited central Switzerland and Ticino and promoted new monasteries and schools. In Milan he founded a school for priests from Switzerland, the **Collegium Helveticum**. In the Reformed places of the Confederation, on the other hand, the decisions of Trent did not apply.

gewusst: The form of the Mass that was laid down after the council is still called the “Tridentine Mass” today, after the Latin name of Trent.
Charles Borromeo was later canonised; a huge statue of him stands in Arona on Lake Maggiore.

teile.einleitung: Karl Marx was a German philosopher, economist and journalist of the 19th century. He studied how the economy shapes society, and he criticised capitalism. His ideas have strongly influenced politics worldwide and are still controversial today.
wichtigste: Karl Marx was born in Trier in 1818.
In 1842 and 1843 he edited the Rheinische Zeitung until it was banned.
In 1848 and 1849 he published the Neue Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne.
From 1849 until his death in 1883 he lived in London.
His main work is called “Capital”; the first volume appeared in 1867.
Important concepts of his teaching are surplus value, class struggle and historical materialism.

abschnitte.text: Karl Marx was born in **Trier** in 1818. He studied first law and then mainly philosophy in Bonn and Berlin. In Berlin he was shaped by the thinking of **Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel**. Hegel explained history as a development through opposites, which is called **dialectics**. Marx took over this idea but reinterpreted it **materialistically**: for him it is economic conditions that drive history, not ideas.

In 1842 and 1843 Marx edited the **Rheinische Zeitung** in Cologne until censorship banned it. After that he lived in Paris and Brussels. There he met **Friedrich Engels**, with whom he wrote the **Communist Manifesto** in 1848. In the revolutionary years of 1848 and 1849 he published the **Neue Rheinische Zeitung** in Cologne. After the failure of the revolution he had to leave Germany.

From 1849 Marx lived with his family in **London**. The family was often poor, and Engels supported them with money. Marx worked for many years in the library of the British Museum. In 1867 the first volume of his main work **“Capital”** appeared. Marx died in London in 1883 and is buried there.

Marx saw society as divided into two classes: the **bourgeoisie**, who own factories and machines, and the **proletariat**, the workers. He called **surplus value** the value that workers create beyond their wages and that the capitalist keeps. His view of history is called **historical materialism**. After a revolution, a **dictatorship of the proletariat** was to rule first, and later a society without classes would arise.

The ideas of Marx influenced workers' movements, trade unions and socialist parties, in Switzerland too. In the 20th century, communist states such as the Soviet Union appealed to him. These states were dictatorships in which many people were persecuted. That is why Marx is still **controversial** today: some value his criticism of poverty and inequality, while others think his teaching is wrong or dangerous.

gewusst: Volumes 2 and 3 of “Capital” appeared only after Marx's death, edited by Friedrich Engels.
In Trier you can visit the birthplace of Karl Marx as a museum.

teile.einleitung: In 1917 the United States entered the First World War. For a long time they had stayed out of it. With their fresh troops and plenty of equipment they helped the Entente to win the war.
wichtigste: The USA entered the First World War in April 1917.
The president at the time was Woodrow Wilson.
Germany’s unrestricted submarine warfare contributed strongly to the entry into the war.
The American infantrymen were called “Doughboys”.
John J. Pershing commanded the American troops in Europe.
In January 1918 Wilson presented his Fourteen Points.
Despite Wilson’s efforts the USA never joined the League of Nations.

abschnitte.text: When the **First World War** began in 1914, the USA at first stayed **neutral**. President **Woodrow Wilson** wanted to keep the country out of the war in Europe. But the USA traded a great deal with Britain and France. In 1915 a German submarine sank the passenger ship **Lusitania**, and many Americans died too. The mood in the USA then turned more strongly against Germany.

abschnitte.titel: The reason for entering the war
abschnitte.text: At the beginning of 1917 Germany began **unrestricted submarine warfare**. German submarines now also attacked ships of neutral countries without warning. In addition it became known that Germany had offered Mexico an alliance against the USA. This letter is called the **Zimmermann Telegram**. In **April 1917** the USA declared war on Germany.

The USA first had to build up a large army. The American infantrymen got the nickname **“Doughboys”**. Their commander in chief in Europe was General **John J. Pershing**. By the end of the war about two million American soldiers had come to France. The **Entente** thereby received **fresh troops and equipment**, while Germany was exhausted. In November 1918 the war ended with an armistice.

In January **1918** Wilson presented his **Fourteen Points**. In them he called, for example, for free seas, fewer weapons and the right of peoples to decide for themselves. An important point was a league of states that was to prevent future wars. From this came the **League of Nations** with its seat in **Geneva**. The US Senate, however, rejected membership, so the USA **never joined**.

gewusst: Woodrow Wilson received the Nobel Peace Prize for the year 1919 for his work for peace.
The Palais des Nations in Geneva was built for the League of Nations; today the UN uses it.

teile.einleitung: Marie Curie was one of the most important women scientists in history. She researched radioactive rays and discovered two new chemical elements. She was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize, and later even a second one.
wichtigste: Marie Curie was born in 1867 in Warsaw in Poland.
She did her research in Paris for most of her life.
With her husband Pierre Curie she investigated radioactive rays.
She discovered the elements polonium and radium.
She was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize.
She received two Nobel Prizes, in physics and in chemistry.
In the First World War she helped the wounded with X-ray vans.

abschnitte.text: Marie Curie was originally called **Maria Skłodowska** and was born in **Warsaw** in 1867. Poland was then under Russian rule, and women were not allowed to go to university there. So she moved to **Paris** and studied physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne. There she met the scientist **Pierre Curie**. The two married in 1895 and from then on researched together.

Marie Curie investigated substances that give off invisible rays by themselves. For this property she coined the word **radioactive**. In 1898 she discovered two new elements with Pierre. One she called **polonium**, after her homeland Poland. The other was called **radium**, because it radiates strongly. To obtain just tiny amounts of radium, the two had to process tonnes of rock.

In 1903 Marie Curie received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** together with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. She was thereby the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize. In 1906 Pierre died in an accident in Paris. Marie carried on researching alone and became the first woman professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911 she received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry**. She is still the only person with Nobel Prizes in two different natural sciences.

In the **First World War** Marie Curie wanted to help the wounded soldiers. She had cars fitted with **X-ray equipment**. With these X-ray vans, doctors close to the front could see broken bones and splinters in the body. Marie Curie went along herself and trained helpers. In France the vans were called “Petites Curies”, that is, “little Curies”.

At that time people did not yet know how dangerous **radioactive radiation** is for the body. Marie Curie worked without protection and even carried samples in her pocket. She often fell ill and died in 1934 of a blood disease that probably came from the rays. Today researchers protect themselves with thick walls of lead and with measuring instruments.

gewusst: Marie Curie’s notebooks still give off radiation today and are kept in lead boxes.
Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie also later received a Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The chemical element curium was named in honour of Marie and Pierre Curie.

teile.einleitung: George Washington was the commander in chief in the American War of Independence and the first President of the United States of America. He lived from 1732 to 1799 and is called the “Father of his Country” in the USA. His face can be seen today on the one-dollar bill.
wichtigste: Washington was born in 1732 in the British colony of Virginia.
He gained his first military experience in the French and Indian War.
In June 1775 he became commander in chief of the Continental Army.
The surprise attack on Trenton at the end of 1776 and the hard winter camp at Valley Forge in 1777/78 are among the best-known moments of the war.
In 1787 he chaired the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia.
In 1789 he took office as the first President of the USA.
By giving up a third term he set an important tradition.

abschnitte.text: George Washington was born in February 1732 in the British colony of **Virginia**. His family owned land and plantations on which enslaved people were forced to work. As a young man he worked as a land surveyor. In the **French and Indian War** from 1754 he fought as an officer on the British side and gained his first military experience.

The 13 colonies resisted taxes and laws from London. In June 1775 the Continental Congress named Washington commander in chief of the **Continental Army**. At the end of 1776 he crossed the Delaware River on an icy night and won a surprise victory at **Trenton**, which raised the army's morale. In the winter of 1777/78 his soldiers suffered from cold, hunger and disease in the camp at **Valley Forge**.

With the help of France, the decisive victory over the British army was won at Yorktown in 1781. In 1783 Britain recognised the independence of the USA. After that Washington gave up his command and returned to his country estate. Many people admired him for this, because he gave up power voluntarily.

In 1787 Washington took the chair of the **Constitutional Convention** in Philadelphia, which drew up the Constitution of the USA. In 1789 he was elected the first **President** unanimously and took office in New York. He built up the new government and kept the USA out of wars in Europe. In 1796 he gave up a third term, and the limit of two terms became a tradition.

In his **Farewell Address** of 1796, Washington warned against party quarrels and lasting alliances with foreign powers. He died in December 1799 at his estate **Mount Vernon** in Virginia. In his will he ordered the freeing of the enslaved people who belonged to him directly. The fact that he himself held slaves is viewed critically today.

The capital of the USA, Washington, D.C., and a whole state in the north-west bear his name. His head is carved in stone at **Mount Rushmore**, together with three other presidents. He is shown on the one-dollar bill and the quarter-dollar coin. Only in 1951 was the limit of two terms also written into law, with the 22nd Amendment.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area ruled by a faraway country.
The assembly of representatives of the 13 colonies during the revolution.
The most important law of a state, which sets out the rules for government and rights.
The time for which someone is elected to an office.

gewusst: Washington is the only US president who never lived in the White House, because it was only finished after his time in office.
He had bad teeth and wore dentures, but they were not made of wood, as is often said.
Washington was elected unanimously by all the electors in both presidential elections.

tana2do.t: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

teile.einleitung: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen is one of the most important documents of the French Revolution. It was adopted in Paris on 26 August 1789 and states that all people are born free and equal in rights. Many of its ideas stand today in the constitutions of almost all democratic states, Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The Declaration was adopted on 26 August 1789 by the French National Assembly.
It consists of 17 articles.
Article 1 says that people are born free and equal in rights.
The ideas come mainly from the philosophers of the Enlightenment.
The Marquis de La Fayette presented an important draft.
Women were excluded from many rights, especially the right to vote.
Olympe de Gouges therefore demanded equal rights for women in 1791.

abschnitte.text: Human rights are rights that every person has from birth, no matter where they come from. The **Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen** of 1789 wrote this idea down solemnly for the first time in Europe. It has 17 short articles. The famous **Article 1** says that people are born free and equal in rights and remain so. With this it set itself against the old order, in which nobility and clergy had many privileges.

In summer 1789 the **French Revolution** began in France. On 14 July 1789 citizens of Paris stormed the Bastille, a prison that was seen as a sign of the king's power. A few weeks later, on **26 August 1789**, the **National Assembly** adopted the Declaration. An important draft had been presented by the **Marquis de La Fayette**. He had earlier fought in the American War of Independence and knew the American declarations of rights of 1776.

The Declaration is based on the thoughts of the **Enlightenment**. Philosophers such as John Locke, Montesquieu and Jean-Jacques Rousseau had demanded that people use their reason and not simply obey the king. Locke named life, liberty and property as natural rights. Montesquieu demanded the **separation of powers**. That is why Article 16 says that a state without secured rights and without separation of powers has no real constitution.

The Declaration protects, among other things, liberty, **freedom of speech** and freedom of religion. It also contains the **presumption of innocence**: everyone is considered innocent until a court has convicted them. All citizens are to be equal before the law and to have access to all offices. It calls **property** “inviolable and sacred”. Laws are to be the expression of the general will of the people.

Although the Declaration spoke of all people, many rights did not apply to everyone. **Women** were not allowed to vote and had fewer rights than men. That is why **Olympe de Gouges** wrote a “Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen” in 1791. She was executed in 1793 during the Reign of Terror. Slavery in the French colonies was not abolished in 1789 either, and only in 1794 did the National Convention decide to end it.

The Declaration of 1789 is still part of the French constitution today. It became a model for many other countries. In 1948 the United Nations adopted the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights**, which is meant to apply to all people in the world. In Switzerland the Helvetic Republic first brought equality of citizens in 1798. Today the **Federal Constitution** guarantees fundamental rights, and Switzerland has been a member of the European Convention on Human Rights since 1974.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rights that every person has from birth.
Everyone is considered innocent until a court has convicted them.
Power in the state is divided between lawmaking, government and courts.
The assembly of the representatives of the people in France at the start of the Revolution.

gewusst: The Declaration of 1789 has only 17 articles and fits on a single big tablet.
Olympe de Gouges wrote that if a woman has the right to climb the scaffold, she must also have the right to climb the speaker's platform.
The Marquis de La Fayette later sent the key of the Bastille as a gift to George Washington.

teile.einleitung: Isaac Newton was an English physicist, mathematician and astronomer and is seen as one of the greatest scientists of all time. He explained why an apple falls to the ground and why the planets orbit the Sun. His laws of motion are still learned in every school today.
wichtigste: Isaac Newton came from England and lived from 1643 to 1727.
With his law of gravitation he described the force that keeps the planets on their paths.
His main work of 1687 is called “Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy”.
His three laws of motion form the basis of classical physics.
With a glass prism he showed that white light is made up of many colours.
He was the first to build a usable reflecting telescope.
From 1703 he was President of the Royal Society and headed the Royal Mint.
The unit of force is called the newton in his honour.

abschnitte.text: By today's calendar, Isaac Newton was born on 4 January 1643 in **Woolsthorpe** in England; by the calendar valid in England at the time, it was Christmas Day 1642. He studied at Trinity College in **Cambridge** and became professor of mathematics there as early as 1669. When the university was closed because of the plague in 1665 and 1666, he had many of his most important ideas at home. Newton died in 1727 in London and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

The story goes that Newton saw an **apple** fall from a tree and asked himself why it falls downwards. From this he developed the **law of gravitation**: all bodies attract one another. The same force that makes the apple fall also keeps the Moon on its path around the Earth and the planets around the Sun. In this way he explained heaven and Earth with the same laws.

In 1687 his main work appeared, the “Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy”, often called the “Principia” for short. It contains the three **Newtonian laws**. The first, the **law of inertia**, says that a body stays at rest or in motion if no force acts. The second links force, mass and acceleration, and the third says that for every force there is an equal and opposite force.

Newton let sunlight pass through a **glass prism** and saw a rainbow of colours. In this way he showed that white light is made up of many colours. He published his research on light in 1704 in the book “Opticks”. He was also the first to build a usable **reflecting telescope**, which works with a curved mirror instead of lenses.

Newton developed **calculus**, with which changes such as speeds can be calculated precisely. Almost at the same time, and independently of him, the German scholar Gottfried Wilhelm **Leibniz** also developed it. A fierce quarrel flared up between the two about who had invented it. Today both are seen as inventors, and we mostly use Leibniz's notation.

In London Newton took on a public office as head of the Royal **Mint** and fought counterfeiters there. From 1703 he was President of the **Royal Society**, the famous scientific society, and in 1705 he was knighted. The unit of force is called the newton in his honour. His physics still holds today for almost all processes in everyday life; only Albert Einstein extended it to very high speeds and masses.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of attraction between all bodies, also called gravity.
The property of a body of keeping its state of motion.
A body of glass that splits light into its colours.
A part of mathematics with which changes and areas are calculated precisely.

gewusst: Whether Newton really saw an apple fall is not certain, but he told the story himself in his old age.
In Woolsthorpe there is still an apple tree today said to be descended from Newton's famous tree.
Newton also spent a long time on alchemy and on interpreting the Bible.

teile.einleitung: The Korean War was a war between North Korea and South Korea from 1950 to 1953, in which the USA, the UN and China also intervened. It was one of the first big wars of the Cold War. To this day there is only an armistice and no peace treaty, and Korea is still divided.
wichtigste: After the Second World War the 38th parallel divided Korea into a Soviet and an American zone.
On 25 June 1950 North Korea attacked South Korea.
The UN Security Council was able to intervene because the Soviet Union was boycotting its sessions.
In September 1950 General Douglas MacArthur turned the course of the war with the landing at Incheon.
At the end of October 1950 the People’s Republic of China intervened on the North Korean side.
On 27 July 1953 an armistice was signed at Panmunjom.
Since 1953 Switzerland has helped to monitor the armistice in the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission.

abschnitte.text: From 1910 to 1945 Korea was a Japanese colony. After the Second World War the Soviet Union occupied the north and the USA the south, with the **38th parallel** forming the border. In 1948 two states arose: communist North Korea under Kim Il-sung and South Korea under Syngman Rhee. Both wanted to rule the whole country.

On 25 June 1950 North Korean troops invaded the south and quickly captured the capital, Seoul. The **UN Security Council** decided on military intervention, because the Soviet Union was boycotting the sessions and did not use its veto. In September 1950 General Douglas **MacArthur** landed by surprise at Incheon. The UN troops pushed the North Koreans back almost to the border with China.

At the end of October 1950 the People’s Republic of China sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers, who were described as “**volunteer units**”. They pushed the UN troops back south again. MacArthur wanted to extend the war to China and defied the government. President Harry Truman therefore dismissed him in April 1951.

From mid-1951 the front froze roughly at the 38th parallel, and negotiations went on for two years. On 27 July 1953 the armistice was signed at **Panmunjom**. Between the two states a **demilitarised zone** about 4 kilometres wide came into being. Several million people died in the war, among them a great many civilians.

Since 1953 Switzerland has been a member of the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission, **NNSC** for short. Together with Sweden it monitors compliance with the armistice at Panmunjom. At the beginning Poland and Czechoslovakia belonged to it too. To this day some Swiss Army members are on duty there; it is the oldest overseas deployment of the Swiss Army.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line around the Earth that runs parallel to the equator.
An agreement to stop the fighting without peace having been made yet.
The right to block a decision on one’s own.
A strip of land in which no armies may be stationed.

gewusst: The capital, Seoul, changed hands four times in the Korean War.
Because a peace treaty was never concluded, North and South Korea are legally still at war to this day.

teile.einleitung: The International Space Station, the ISS, is a huge laboratory that orbits the Earth. Since the year 2000, astronauts from many countries have been living and doing research there all the time.
wichtigste: The ISS circles the Earth in about 90 minutes.
That is why the crew sees about 16 sunrises in one day.
Since November 2000 the ISS has been permanently inhabited.
In the ISS people float: this is called weightlessness.
The astronauts sleep in sleeping bags that are fastened down.
From Earth you can see the ISS as a bright, fast-moving dot.
ESA, of which Switzerland is a member, also takes part in the ISS.

abschnitte.text: The **ISS** was put together piece by piece in space from 1998. Rockets and Space Shuttles carried up the individual parts, the **modules**. The station is about as big as a football pitch. It flies at a height of about 400 kilometres. In **November 2000** the first crew moved in. Since then the ISS has always been inhabited.

The ISS is very fast: it races around the Earth at about 28,000 kilometres an hour. It needs only about **90 minutes** for one orbit. That is why the crew experiences about **16 sunrises** in one day. From Earth you can see the ISS in the evening or in the morning as a **bright dot** moving quickly across the sky.

In the ISS you feel no weight and you float. This is called **weightlessness**. Everything has to be fastened down, or it floats away. The astronauts sleep in **sleeping bags** that are attached to the wall. So that their muscles and bones do not get weak, they exercise for about two hours every day.

The ISS is a joint project of several space agencies: from the USA, Russia, Japan, Canada and Europe. For Europe, **ESA**, the **European Space Agency**, takes part. Switzerland is a member of ESA. Since 2008 ESA has had its own laboratory on the station, the **Columbus module**. There researchers carry out experiments that are not possible on Earth.

gewusst: On the ISS, even water from the humidity in the air and from urine is treated again to make drinking water.
The ISS is the largest structure that people have ever put into space.

teile.einleitung: In 1848 gold was found in California. As a result, hundreds of thousands of people from all over the world set off to get rich. This rush is called the California Gold Rush.
wichtigste: In January 1848 James W. Marshall found gold while building a sawmill.
The sawmill belonged to the Swiss emigrant Johann August Sutter.
Most of the gold seekers came in 1849 and were therefore called “Forty-Niners”.
In a few years San Francisco grew from a small place into a big city.
As early as 1850 California became the 31st state of the USA.
For the native peoples of California the Gold Rush was a catastrophe.

abschnitte.text: In January 1848 the carpenter **James W. Marshall** was building a sawmill on the American River. In the water of the mill race he discovered shining grains: it was **gold**. People tried to keep the find secret, but the news spread quickly. Soon people in America, Europe and even China were talking about it. So began one of the biggest gold rushes in history.

The sawmill belonged to **Johann August Sutter**, an emigrant from the area around Basel. He had built up a large colony in California with fields and cattle and called it **“New Helvetia”**. But the gold find brought him no luck. His workers ran off to look for gold themselves, and gold seekers occupied his land. Sutter lost almost everything and became poor.

Most of the gold seekers arrived in the year 1849. That is why they were called **“Forty-Niners”**. They travelled in covered wagons right across North America or on ships around South America. Many looked for gold by **panning**: they swirled sand and water in a flat pan. The heavy gold stayed at the bottom. Only a few really got rich, and often traders earned more than the gold seekers.

abschnitte.titel: San Francisco and the new state
abschnitte.text: **San Francisco** was the most important port for those arriving. From a small place it became, in a few years, a city with tens of thousands of inhabitants. Shortly before the gold find, Mexico had ceded the area to the USA after a war. Because so many people came, California was admitted to the USA as the 31st state as early as **1850**.

For the **native peoples of California** the Gold Rush had terrible consequences. Gold seekers pushed into their lands and drove them out. Many people died through violence, hunger and imported **diseases**. In a few decades the indigenous population fell sharply. Today this dark side of the Gold Rush is also remembered.

gewusst: The football team of San Francisco is still called the “San Francisco 49ers” today.
California has the nickname “Golden State”.
The trader Levi Strauss sold goods to workers in San Francisco and later became famous for jeans.

teile.einleitung: The Helvetic Republic was the first modern unitary state on the territory of Switzerland. It arose in 1798, when French troops conquered the Old Swiss Confederacy, and lasted only until 1803. Even so, it brought ideas such as equal rights for all citizens, which are still important today.
wichtigste: The Helvetic Republic lasted from 1798 to 1803.
It arose after France marched into the Old Swiss Confederacy.
It was proclaimed in Aarau on 12 April 1798.
It was a unitary state on the French model, and the cantons were only administrative districts.
The subject territories were abolished and all citizens were equal before the law.
The first constitution was written by Peter Ochs of Basel.
With Napoleon's Act of Mediation the Helvetic Republic ended in 1803.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 18th century the ideas of the **French Revolution** also spread in Switzerland. Frédéric-César de La Harpe from Vaud pressed in Paris for the freeing of Vaud from Bern. At the start of 1798 France marched into the **Old Swiss Confederacy**. On 5 March 1798 the Bernese were defeated by the French in the Battle of Grauholz, and the French took the Bernese state treasure with them.

On 12 April 1798 the **Helvetic Republic** was proclaimed in Aarau. The constitution had been written by Peter Ochs of Basel on behalf of France. The republic was a **unitary state** on the French model, and the old cantons lost their independence. It was governed by a Directory of five members and a parliament.

The subject territories were abolished, and all men became citizens with equal rights. New were **freedom of religion**, freedom of the press and freedom of settlement across the whole country. Torture was banned. The flag of the Helvetic Republic had the three colours green, red and yellow.

Many people, especially in Central Switzerland, rejected the new order. In September 1798 **Nidwalden** resisted the French and the new constitution particularly fiercely, and hundreds of people were killed. Afterwards, in 1799, the educator Johann Heinrich **Pestalozzi** looked after the orphaned children in Stans. In 1799 Switzerland also became a battleground between France, Austria and Russia.

The Helvetic Republic was marked by disputes between supporters of the unitary state and supporters of the old cantons. There were several coups, and in 1802 an uprising took place, the **Stecklikrieg** (“War of the Sticks”). Then Napoleon Bonaparte intervened and issued the **Act of Mediation** in 1803. With it Switzerland became a confederation of states again, now of 19 cantons.

From former subject territories, new cantons arose such as Aargau, Thurgau, St Gallen, Ticino and Vaud. The idea of equal rights for all citizens lived on and later shaped the **federal state** of 1848. The promotion of the primary school by Minister Philipp Albert Stapfer was also groundbreaking. Many historians therefore see the Helvetic period as the start of modern Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state run centrally by one government, without independent member states.
An area that was ruled by other places and had no rights of its own.
The constitution that Napoleon gave to Switzerland in 1803.
The government of the Helvetic Republic, made up of five members.

gewusst: The capital of the Helvetic Republic changed several times, lying in turn in Aarau, Lucerne and Bern.
The Stecklikrieg got its name because the rebels were partly armed only with clubs, or “Stecken”.
Peter Ochs and La Harpe are seen as pioneers of the Helvetic period, but were soon pushed out of the government themselves.

teile.einleitung: Globalisation means that the countries of the world are more and more closely connected, through trade, travel, the internet and ideas. Your T-shirt may have been sewn in Bangladesh and your phone assembled in China. Globalisation brings many opportunities, but also problems.
wichtigste: Globalisation is the worldwide interconnection of the economy, politics, culture and communication.
The standardised shipping container of the 1950s made world trade much cheaper.
The World Trade Organization (WTO) has its seat in Geneva.
The WTO was founded with the Marrakesh Agreement in April 1994; its predecessor was the GATT of 1947.
China joined the WTO in December 2001 and became the “workshop of the world”.
The World Economic Forum (WEF) meets every year in Davos.
Critics complain that not everyone benefits equally from globalisation.

abschnitte.text: **Globalisation** means that goods, money, people and information flow across borders faster and faster. There was already worldwide trade in the Age of Discovery and colonialism. Since about 1990, however, this development has speeded up greatly. The reasons are cheap transport, the internet and the removal of trade barriers.

In the 1950s the American Malcolm McLean developed the standardised **shipping container**. Because all containers are the same size, cranes can quickly move them from ships onto lorries and trains. As a result, transport costs fell sharply. Today huge container ships carry more than 20,000 containers across the oceans.

After the Second World War the **GATT**, an agreement to reduce customs duties, was concluded in 1947. From it, with the Marrakesh Agreement signed in April 1994, the **World Trade Organization** (WTO) arose. It has its seat in Geneva and settles disputes in world trade. In December 2001 populous China also joined the WTO.

Many companies make their products where it is cheapest. Moving parts of a company abroad is called **offshoring**. Large companies that operate in many countries are called **multinational corporations**. A single smartphone contains parts from dozens of countries.

Switzerland is a small country without many raw materials and earns a large part of its money from exports. Worldwide famous companies such as Nestlé in Vevey or Roche and Novartis in Basel have their seats here. In Geneva, besides the WTO, there are many other international organisations. The World Economic Forum **WEF** traditionally meets in January in Davos.

Globalisation has helped millions of people out of poverty in many countries such as China. We can buy goods from all over the world cheaply and get to know the cultures of other countries. Critics, however, complain about poor working conditions in low-wage countries and environmental damage caused by long transport routes. Movements for **fair trade** campaign for fairer conditions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sale of goods abroad.
A fee that has to be paid when goods are brought across a border.
Moving work or parts of a company abroad.
A large company with sites in many countries.

gewusst: A large container ship is longer than three football pitches in a row.
The word globalisation comes from the Latin “globus”, which means sphere.
Switzerland earns about every second franc through exchange with other countries.

teile.einleitung: The Hubble Space Telescope is a large telescope that has been orbiting the Earth since 1990. It has taken some of the most famous pictures of space.
wichtigste: Hubble is a telescope in space.
It was launched in April 1990 on board the Space Shuttle “Discovery”.
It is named after the American astronomer Edwin Hubble.
Above the atmosphere, Hubble takes sharper pictures than telescopes on Earth.
The first pictures were blurred because the mirror had been ground very slightly wrongly.
The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier helped to repair Hubble.
Hubble is about 13 metres long, roughly as long as a bus.

abschnitte.text: Hubble is a **telescope** that orbits the Earth. In April **1990** the Space Shuttle **“Discovery”** carried it into space in its cargo bay and released it there. Hubble is about **13 metres** long, roughly as long as a big bus. Its main mirror has a diameter of about 2.4 metres. It orbits the Earth at a height of several hundred kilometres.

The Earth's **air** is constantly moving. It shimmers and makes pictures of stars blurred. You know this from the twinkling of the stars. Hubble flies **above the atmosphere**. That is why it sees space much more clearly. It can also observe light that the air does not let through at all.

After the launch there was a shock: the first pictures were **blurred**. The big mirror had been ground very slightly wrongly. In **1993** astronauts flew to Hubble and fitted a correction, a kind of pair of glasses. After that the pictures were razor sharp. In all, astronauts visited the telescope five times to repair and improve it. Among them was the Swiss **Claude Nicollier**, the first Swiss person in space.

The telescope is named after the astronomer **Edwin Hubble** from the USA. He showed that besides our Milky Way there are many other **galaxies**. The Hubble telescope photographed regions where stars form, distant galaxies and planets of our solar system. With its help, researchers were able to determine the age of the universe more precisely.

gewusst: In the picture “Hubble Deep Field” of 1995 you can see thousands of galaxies in a tiny patch of sky.
Since 2021 there has been a large successor to Hubble, the James Webb Space Telescope.

teile.einleitung: The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 was the most dangerous moment of the Cold War. For 13 days the USA and the Soviet Union stood on the brink of nuclear war, because the Soviet Union had secretly placed missiles on the island of Cuba. In the end, fortunately, both sides found a way out.
wichtigste: In October 1962 US reconnaissance aircraft photographed Soviet missile sites on Cuba.
Cuba was then ruled by Fidel Castro, who was closely allied with the Soviet Union.
On 22 October 1962 President John F. Kennedy announced a naval blockade of Cuba, which was officially called a “quarantine”.
On 28 October 1962 the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev announced the withdrawal of the missiles.
In return the USA secretly promised to withdraw its Jupiter missiles from Turkey.
As a lesson from the crisis, both powers set up the “hotline” between Washington and Moscow in 1963.
With its embassy in Havana, Switzerland represented the interests of the USA in Cuba as protecting power.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other in the **Cold War**. In 1959 Fidel Castro took power in Cuba through a revolution, only about 150 kilometres from Florida. In April 1961 the US-backed **Bay of Pigs invasion**, with which Cuban exiles wanted to overthrow Castro, failed. After that Castro sought protection from the Soviet Union even more. For their part, the USA had placed nuclear Jupiter missiles in Turkey and Italy, close to the Soviet Union.

In the summer of 1962 the Soviet Union secretly brought missiles, soldiers and nuclear warheads to Cuba. On 14 October 1962 an American reconnaissance aircraft of the **U-2** type photographed the missile sites. Experts recognised launch pads for **medium-range missiles** in the pictures. From Cuba these missiles could have reached many big cities in the USA within minutes.

Kennedy consulted his advisers in secret for days, and some wanted to bomb Cuba at once. He decided on a **naval blockade**, which he announced on television on 22 October. US warships were to stop Soviet ships carrying weapons. On 27 October, “Black Saturday”, a U-2 aircraft was shot down over Cuba and the pilot was killed. On the same day the Soviet officer Vasili Arkhipov, on a submarine, prevented a nuclear torpedo from being fired.

Kennedy and Khrushchev wrote each other several letters in those days. On 28 October 1962 Khrushchev announced on the radio that the missiles would be dismantled. In return the USA publicly promised not to attack Cuba. They also secretly agreed on the withdrawal of their **Jupiter missiles** from Turkey, which took place in 1963. The public only learned of this many years later.

Both sides had realised how quickly a misunderstanding can lead to nuclear war. That is why the **hotline** was set up in 1963, a direct teleprinter link between Washington and Moscow. In the same year the USA, the Soviet Union and Britain signed a treaty banning nuclear tests in the air, in space and under water. The crisis is still seen today as an example of how important talks and diplomacy are.

The USA had broken off its relations with Cuba at the beginning of 1961. Since then Switzerland had represented the interests of the USA in Cuba as **protecting power**. The Swiss ambassador in Havana served in the crisis as an important go-between for the governments. This protecting power mandate lasted until 2015, when the USA and Cuba opened embassies of their own again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long period of hostility between the USA and the Soviet Union after 1945, without a direct war between the two.
Warships block the sea route so that certain ships can no longer arrive.
A country that represents the interests of another country when that country no longer has an embassy.
An aircraft that takes photos from a great height to gather information about an opponent.
A direct connection between the governments in Washington and Moscow for emergencies.

gewusst: The hotline was at first not a telephone at all, but a teleprinter link over which texts were sent.
Because the crisis lasted about 13 days, it is often called “Thirteen Days” in English.
Switzerland represented the USA in Cuba for over 50 years, from 1961 to 2015.

teile.einleitung: The Manifesto of the Communist Party is a short political work by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. It appeared in 1848 and called on workers to fight against the ruling conditions. It is one of the most influential and most controversial texts in history.
wichtigste: Karl Marx wrote the Manifesto together with Friedrich Engels.
It appeared in 1848.
They wrote it for the Communist League.
The first sentence speaks of a “spectre of communism” haunting Europe.
The bourgeoisie is the class that owns factories and machines.
Facing it stands the proletariat, the class of workers.

abschnitte.text: **Karl Marx** and **Friedrich Engels** wrote the Manifesto on behalf of the **Communist League**. This was a small association of craftsmen and workers. The Manifesto appeared in early **1848** in German in **London**. Shortly afterwards revolutions broke out in many countries of Europe. The Manifesto, however, at first had hardly any influence on them, and only became famous later.

The Manifesto begins with the sentence: **“A spectre is haunting Europe, the spectre of communism.”** By this Marx and Engels meant that many powerful people were afraid of communism. In the Manifesto they wanted to explain what the communists really wanted. It ends with the well-known call: **“Workers of all countries, unite!”**

According to the Manifesto, history is a history of **class struggles**. In modern society two classes face each other. The **bourgeoisie** owns the factories and machines. The **proletariat** owns nothing except its labour and has to work for wages. Marx and Engels expected that the proletariat would overthrow the bourgeoisie and abolish private ownership of factories.

The Manifesto was translated into a great many languages. It influenced workers’ movements, socialist parties and later communist states. These states were dictatorships in which many people were persecuted. That is why the Manifesto is judged very differently. Some see in it an important criticism of exploitation, others a dangerous doctrine.

gewusst: The first edition of the Manifesto had only 23 pages.
UNESCO has included a manuscript of the Manifesto in the Memory of the World Register.

teile.einleitung: An email is an electronic message that is sent over the internet. In seconds you can send texts, pictures and files to people all over the world with it.
wichtigste: Email stands for “electronic mail”.
Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between two computers in 1971.
Every email address contains the sign @, in English “at”.
You can attach files to an email.
Unwanted advertising emails are called spam.
An email needs no postage stamp.

abschnitte.text: The “E” in **email** stands for **electronic**. The word comes from the English “electronic mail”. Unlike a letter, an email does not travel by post, but over the **internet**. It usually arrives in a few seconds, even if the receiver lives far away. That is why it needs no **postage stamp**. But you do need a device with internet, for example a computer or a mobile phone.

Every email address has two parts, separated by the sign **@**. In front is the name of the user, behind it the **provider**. In English @ is pronounced **“at”**. The address therefore means: name at provider. In German the sign is often called the **“Klammeraffe”**, the spider monkey. Every address exists only once, so that the message arrives in the right place.

The American **Ray Tomlinson** sent the first email between two computers in **1971**. The two machines stood right next to each other, but were joined by a network. Tomlinson chose the sign **@** to separate the name from the computer. What was in the first message he himself later no longer knew exactly. Today billions of emails are sent every day.

You can attach files such as photos, texts or tables to an email. Such an **attachment** is sent along, and the receiver can open it. Unfortunately there is also **spam**: emails that you did not ask for, mostly advertising. Many programs sort them out automatically. Some fraudulent emails want to steal passwords. That is why you should not open attachments or links from strangers.

gewusst: The name spam comes from a brand of tinned meat that is mentioned over and over in a funny sketch by the British group Monty Python.
The sign @ existed long before email, and merchants used it, for example, for prices.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Britain was a fight in the air between the German Luftwaffe and the British Royal Air Force in the summer and autumn of 1940. Germany wanted to make Britain ripe for invasion and then cross the English Channel with troops. It was the first big battle in history fought almost entirely with aircraft.
wichtigste: The Battle of Britain took place in the Second World War mainly from July to October 1940.
The German Luftwaffe wanted to win air superiority in order to make the planned invasion, “Operation Sea Lion”, possible.
On “Eagle Day”, 13 August 1940, the major German offensive began.
The British radar chain Chain Home warned the Royal Air Force early of approaching formations.
From September 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked mainly London and other cities, which took the pressure off British airfields.
15 September is celebrated in Britain as “Battle of Britain Day”.
Germany did not achieve its aim, and the invasion of Britain was postponed and never carried out.

abschnitte.text: On the German side stood the **Luftwaffe** under the supreme command of Hermann Göring. Facing it was Fighter Command of the **Royal Air Force**, led by Hugh Dowding. The most important British fighters were the Hawker Hurricane and the Supermarine Spitfire. The Germans flew mainly fighters of the Messerschmitt Bf 109 type and bombers such as the Heinkel He 111.

After the victory over France in June 1940, Britain stood alone against Germany in Western Europe. Hitler planned a landing on the English south coast, **Operation Sea Lion**. For that the Luftwaffe first had to knock out the British fighters and win **air superiority**. Otherwise the Royal Air Force and the British fleet could have attacked the ships crossing the English Channel.

Along the British coast stood tall aerial masts of the **Chain Home radar chain**. They could detect approaching aircraft while they were still over the sea. The reports came together in command centres, where the situation was followed on large map tables. In this way the Royal Air Force could send its fighters exactly where they were needed, instead of having to patrol constantly in the air.

From July 1940 the Luftwaffe first attacked ships in the English Channel and ports. With **Eagle Day** on 13 August 1940, major attacks on airfields and radar stations began, and the Royal Air Force got into great difficulty. From 7 September, however, the Luftwaffe attacked mainly London. On 15 September the Germans suffered heavy losses in daytime attacks on London, after which Hitler postponed the invasion.

After the change of strategy the Germans increasingly flew night attacks on cities. The British call this phase the **Blitz**, and it lasted until May 1941. On 14 November 1940 the city of Coventry was badly destroyed, including its medieval cathedral. Tens of thousands of civilians lost their lives in British cities, and many families slept in air-raid shelters or in the stations of the London Underground.

The Battle of Britain was the first big defeat for Hitler’s Germany in the Second World War. Britain stayed in the war and later became the starting point for the liberation of Western Europe. Prime Minister **Winston Churchill** praised the pilots with the famous sentence “Never was so much owed by so many to so few”. Since then the fighter pilots of the Royal Air Force have been called “The Few”.

begriffe.erklaerung: When one side controls the airspace so that the opponent can hardly fly there any more.
A technology that uses radio waves to detect aircraft or ships from a great distance.
An armed advance into a foreign country.
A fast, manoeuvrable combat aircraft that fights other aircraft in the air.
The British name for the German bombing raids on British cities in 1940 and 1941.

gewusst: Many pilots from other countries also fought in the Royal Air Force, for example from Poland, Czechoslovakia, Canada and New Zealand.
The Polish No. 303 Squadron was among the most successful units of the whole battle.
The ruin of the destroyed cathedral in Coventry still stands today as a memorial to peace and reconciliation.

teile.einleitung: For a long time coal was the most important fuel for industry. To get it, people dug deep mines and worked underground. The work was hard and dangerous, but without coal industrialisation would not have happened in the way it did.
wichtigste: Coal formed a very long time ago from ancient plants.
People who mine coal underground are called miners.
Canaries warned miners of poisonous gas.
In many mines ponies pulled the coal wagons.
Humphry Davy invented a safety lamp around 1815.
A large coalfield in Germany is the Ruhr area.
In the 19th century Switzerland got most of its coal from abroad.

abschnitte.text: Coal was formed from **plants** that grew many millions of years ago in huge swamp forests. Dead trees and ferns sank into the swamp and were covered by mud and rock. Under pressure and heat, over a very long time, they turned into **coal**. That is why you sometimes find imprints of leaves in coal. Like oil, coal is one of the **fossil fuels**.

The **miners** worked **underground**, that is, deep beneath the earth in tunnels and shafts. They knocked the coal out of the rock with picks and later with machines. The work was tiring, dusty and dark. In the 19th century children also had to work in mines. In many pits **ponies** pulled the heavy coal wagons through the narrow passages.

In mines **poisonous and flammable gases** could collect. That is why miners took **canaries** down with them. The birds reacted much faster to poisonous gas than humans, and so warned the workers. **Firedamp** was also dangerous, because it could be ignited by naked flames. Around 1815 **Humphry Davy** invented a **safety lamp** in which a fine wire gauze shielded the flame.

Coal powered **steam engines**, locomotives and blast furnaces. That is why it was the most important fuel of **industrialisation**. In Germany the **Ruhr area** became a huge coal and industrial region. **Switzerland** had hardly any coal of its own and in the 19th century got most of its coal from **abroad**. Only in a few places was some coal mined, for example in Käpfnach near Horgen on Lake Zurich.

Burning coal produces a lot of **carbon dioxide**, which contributes to climate change. In addition, mining became too expensive in many countries. That is why many mines were closed. In Germany the mining of hard coal ended in 2018. In other countries, however, a lot of coal is still mined today.

gewusst: The phrase “canary in the coal mine” is used today for an early warning sign.
Many pit ponies lived underground for years and even had their stables there.

teile.einleitung: The gramophone is an old device for playing music. It plays round records and could be found in many living rooms about a hundred years ago.
wichtigste: Emil Berliner invented the gramophone and applied for a patent for it in 1887.
On a gramophone you play round, flat records.
A fine needle runs through the grooves of the record and vibrates as it does so.
A big horn makes the sound louder.
Old gramophones were wound up with a hand crank.
As early as 1877 Thomas Edison had invented the phonograph, which stored sounds on cylinders.

abschnitte.text: As early as **1877** **Thomas Edison** invented the **phonograph**. With it, sounds could be recorded and played back for the first time. The sounds were cut into a **cylinder**, which looks like a roll. Edison first spoke a nursery rhyme into it. But cylinders were hard to make in large numbers.

**Emil Berliner** came from Germany and lived in the USA. He had a new idea: instead of cylinders he used flat, round discs, the **records**. In 1887 he applied for a patent for his **gramophone**. Records could easily be pressed many times from a mould. In this way music became a product that many people could buy.

On a record there is a fine, spiral **groove**. It is not completely smooth but has tiny waves. A **needle** glides through the groove and vibrates as it does so. This vibration becomes a quiet sound. The big **horn** makes it louder, so that it can be heard all over the room.

Old gramophones did not need electricity. You turned a **hand crank** and wound up a **spring**. The spring turned the turntable on which the record lay. The early records were made of **shellac** and turned about 78 times a minute. Later there were electric record players and records made of vinyl.

gewusst: In 1898 Emil Berliner founded a company with his brother in Hanover, which became the famous Deutsche Grammophon.
Even today many people are buying vinyl records again, although music can be streamed.

teile.einleitung: Charles V was one of the most powerful rulers in Europe in the 16th century. He was King of Spain and Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire. His realm was so large that people said the sun never set on it.
wichtigste: Charles V was born in Ghent in 1500.
He belonged to the ruling House of Habsburg.
His realm also included Spanish territories in America.
In 1527 his troops sacked the city of Rome.
In 1530 the Pope crowned him Emperor in Bologna.
In 1555 and 1556 he abdicated of his own free will.
After that he withdrew to a monastery in Spain.

abschnitte.text: Charles was born in **Ghent** in the year **1500**; the city is in Belgium today. He belonged to the ruling **House of Habsburg**. Through clever marriages of his ancestors he inherited a great many lands: the Netherlands, Spain with its territories in Italy, and the Habsburg lands in Austria. In 1516 he became King of Spain, and in 1519 the electors chose him as Roman-German king.

abschnitte.titel: A realm where the sun never set
abschnitte.text: The realm of Charles V also included the new Spanish territories in **America**. Because his lands were spread around the world, it was always daytime somewhere. That is why the saying is linked with him: **“In my realm the sun never sets.”** Ruling such a large realm was very difficult, however. Charles travelled a lot and fought many wars, above all against France and the Ottoman Empire.

In **1527** troops of Charles V conquered and plundered the city of **Rome**. Many soldiers had not been paid for a long time. This event is called the **“Sacco di Roma”**. Later the Emperor and the Pope made peace. In 1530 the Pope crowned Charles Emperor in **Bologna**. He was the last emperor to be crowned by a pope.

The **Reformation** began in the time of Charles V. In 1521 Martin Luther had to answer to the Emperor at the Imperial Diet in Worms. Charles wanted to preserve the unity of the Catholic Church, but he did not succeed. In 1555 the **Peace of Augsburg** was concluded. After it, the territorial rulers in the Empire were allowed to choose between the Catholic and the Lutheran faith.

In **1555 and 1556** Charles did something very unusual: he **abdicated of his own free will**. He handed Spain and the Netherlands to his son **Philip II**, and the imperial dignity went to his brother Ferdinand. Tired and ill, Charles withdrew to the **Monastery of Yuste** in Spain. There he died in 1558.

gewusst: Charles V spoke several languages, but he only learned Spanish as a young king.
After his retirement the House of Habsburg split into a Spanish and an Austrian line.

teile.einleitung: Artificial intelligence, AI for short, means that computers solve tasks for which people normally need their minds. They recognise pictures, translate languages, play chess or write texts. Since chatbots such as ChatGPT, AI has become part of everyday life for many people.
wichtigste: In 1950 the British mathematician Alan Turing proposed a test to check whether a machine can think in a human-like way.
At the Dartmouth Conference in 1956 “artificial intelligence” was established as a field of research of its own.
In 1997 the computer Deep Blue beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match.
In March 2016 the programme AlphaGo from DeepMind beat the Go professional Lee Sedol 4 to 1.
On 30 November 2022 OpenAI released the chatbot ChatGPT to the general public.
The EU AI Act has been in force since 1 August 2024 and classifies AI systems by their risk to people and fundamental rights.
In 2024 John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton received the Nobel Prize in Physics for foundations of machine learning with neural networks.

abschnitte.text: AI is a branch of computer science. An AI programme does not just follow fixed commands, but learns from many examples. Most of today’s systems use **machine learning**. A programme sees, for example, millions of photos of cats and dogs and in this way learns to tell the two apart. Even so, an AI does not think or feel in the way a human does.

In 1950 **Alan Turing** asked in a famous essay whether machines can think. His **Turing test** checks whether a person, in a conversation, notices that they are writing with a machine. In 1956 researchers met at Dartmouth College in the USA, where the term “artificial intelligence” became known. In the 1960s the programme ELIZA appeared, which imitated simple conversations. Because expectations were often too high, there were later periods with little money for research.

Games are a popular testing ground for AI, because the rules are clear. In 1997 the IBM computer **Deep Blue** beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov. The board game Go was regarded as much harder, because there are an unbelievable number of possible moves. Even so, **AlphaGo** from the company DeepMind beat Lee Sedol 4 to 1 in Seoul in March 2016. AlphaGo had learned beforehand from a great many games and had also played against itself.

Many modern AI systems are based on **neural networks**, which are loosely modelled on the structure of the brain. For their foundational work on this, John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024. Large language models are trained on huge amounts of text and can then write texts themselves. On 30 November 2022 **ChatGPT** made such chatbots known worldwide. But they can also make mistakes and claim wrong things very convincingly.

AI is now inside many devices and services. It suggests videos and music, recognises faces on the phone and translates texts. In medicine it helps doctors to find diseases on X-ray images. The programme AlphaFold can predict the shape of proteins, for which its developers received a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024.

AI can make work easier, but it also raises questions. Fake pictures and videos, so-called **deepfakes**, can deceive people. An AI can also judge unfairly if its training data is one-sided. The EU has therefore issued an **AI Act**, which has applied since 1 August 2024 and sorts AI by its risk. In Switzerland, among others, ETH Zurich, EPFL in Lausanne and the IDSIA institute in Ticino do research on AI.

begriffe.erklaerung: An exact step-by-step set of instructions by which a computer solves a task.
A computer learns from many examples instead of being given every rule individually.
A computer programme made of many connected computing nodes that works roughly like nerve cells in the brain.
A programme you can have a conversation with in writing or by voice.
The examples, that is texts, pictures or numbers, from which an AI learns.

gewusst: The idea that machines could think is much older than the computer and already appears in old legends about artificial humans.
AlphaGo played such an unusual move against Lee Sedol that experts at first took it for a mistake.
A chatbot does not really know what is true; it calculates which words are most likely to follow.

teile.einleitung: The colonisation of Africa was the conquest and partition of almost the whole African continent by European powers, above all between 1880 and 1914. This period is also called the “Scramble for Africa”. For the people of Africa it brought oppression, exploitation and in part genocide.
wichtigste: In 1884 Otto von Bismarck invited the powers to the Berlin Congo Conference.
No African state was represented at the conference.
Under the principle of effective occupation, territorial claims only counted if a territory was actually occupied.
From 1885 to 1908 the Congo Free State belonged personally to King Leopold II of Belgium.
Around 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were not under European colonial rule.
German South West Africa became the first German colony in Africa in 1884.
From 1904 to 1908 German colonial troops committed a genocide against the Herero and Nama.

abschnitte.text: Around 1880 Europeans controlled only about a tenth of Africa, mostly coastal areas. In just over 30 years they conquered almost the whole continent. They wanted **raw materials**, new markets and standing as a great power. Better weapons and medicines against malaria made the conquest of the interior possible.

From November 1884 to February 1885, representatives of European states and the USA met in Berlin, invited by Otto von **Bismarck**. African representatives were not there. They laid down the **principle of effective occupation**: only those who actually occupied a territory could claim it. After that the colonial powers drew borders, often with a ruler, without regard for the people on the spot.

The huge **Congo Free State** belonged personally to King Leopold II from 1885 to 1908. The population was forced to collect **rubber**, from which rubber goods are made. Anyone who brought too little was cruelly punished, and often hands were even cut off. After the British consul Roger Casement published a report in 1904, Leopold had to hand the Congo over to the Belgian state in 1908.

Britain wanted a north-south link from Cairo to Cape Town, France an east-west axis across Africa. At Fashoda in Sudan the two plans collided in 1898, and France finally gave way. Many Africans offered **resistance**. In 1896 Ethiopia defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa and, like Liberia, remained independent.

From 1884 Germany acquired colonies, including German South West Africa, Togo, Cameroon and German East Africa. In German South West Africa, today’s Namibia, the Herero and Nama rose up in 1904. General Lothar von Trotha issued an **extermination order** in October 1904. Tens of thousands of people died, and in 2021 the German federal government described the acts, from today’s point of view, as **genocide**.

After the First World War Germany lost its colonies to other powers. From the 1950s the African states became independent, Ghana in 1957 as one of the first colonies south of the Sahara. Many **colonial borders** still apply today and lead to conflicts. The Swiss Basel Mission was also active in Africa during the colonial period, for example in today’s Ghana and in Cameroon.

begriffe.erklaerung: A territory that is ruled by a foreign state.
The rule that only those who really occupy a territory may claim it.
The milky sap of certain plants, from which rubber goods are made.
A crime aimed at destroying a whole ethnic group.

gewusst: On many maps of Africa you can still see dead straight borders drawn by colonial powers.
The Battle of Adwa of 1896 is still celebrated in Ethiopia as a national holiday.
