teile.einleitung: Johann Sebastian Bach was one of the greatest composers in the history of music. He lived in the Baroque period and wrote music for organ, choir and orchestra that is still played all over the world today.
wichtigste: Bach was born on 21 March 1685 in Eisenach, in present-day Germany.
He came from a large family of musicians.
Bach was a magnificent organ player and wrote many organ pieces.
From 1723 he was Thomaskantor in Leipzig.
In 1734 he wrote the Christmas Oratorio.
With two wives, Bach had 20 children, many of whom died as babies.
He died in 1750 in Leipzig.

abschnitte.text: Johann Sebastian Bach was born on **21 March 1685** in **Eisenach**. In his family there were very many **musicians**: town pipers, organists and cantors. He lost both parents early and grew up with his older brother. His brother taught him to play keyboard instruments. Bach lived and worked all his life in German lands.

Bach became a magnificent **organ player**. He worked as an organist in several towns, for example in Arnstadt and Weimar. He wrote many pieces for the **organ**, the big instrument in the church. As a young man he even walked to Lübeck to hear the famous organist Dietrich Buxtehude. Later he often tested new organs to see whether they were well built.

From **1723** Bach was **Thomaskantor** in **Leipzig**. He led the boys' choir of the **Thomaskirche**, taught the pupils and wrote music for the services. Every Sunday a **cantata** was needed, a piece of music for choir, singers and orchestra. In 1734 he wrote the **Christmas Oratorio**, which tells the Christmas story in music. The **St Matthew Passion** was also written in Leipzig.

Bach had **20 children** with his two wives. Many of them died as babies. Several sons became well-known **composers**, such as Carl Philipp Emanuel and Johann Christian Bach. Bach died in 1750 in Leipzig. After his death his music was somewhat forgotten. In 1829 Felix Mendelssohn performed the St Matthew Passion again, and Bach became famous anew.

gewusst: On the golden record of the Voyager space probes, which have been flying through space since 1977, there is also music by Bach.
In 1717 the Duke of Weimar had Bach locked up for about four weeks because he wanted to take up a new post without permission.

teile.einleitung: On a loom you make cloth by crossing threads. In the past people wove by hand, often at home. The mechanical loom was driven by machines and changed the lives of many people in the 19th century, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: On a loom, cloth is made from threads.
In weaving two kinds of thread cross: warp and weft.
Before the factories, many people wove at home.
A factory in which cloth is woven is called a weaving mill.
Joseph-Marie Jacquard controlled his loom with punched cards.
In the 19th century many Swiss factories processed cotton.
In 1832 home weavers in Uster set fire to a factory.

abschnitte.text: In weaving, many threads are stretched side by side lengthwise. These threads are called the **warp**. Across them another thread is passed alternately over and under the warp threads. This cross thread is called the **weft**. It is pushed to and fro with a tool, the **shuttle**. In this way a firm cloth is made, row after row.

Before there were factories, many families wove **at home** in their living room. This is called **cottage industry**. Merchants brought the yarn and collected the finished cloth again. In the Zurich Oberland and in eastern Switzerland many farming families earned a little extra money in this way. The work was long and tiring, but you could stay at home.

In 1785 the Englishman Edmund Cartwright had a **mechanical loom** patented. It was no longer moved by hand, but driven by water power and later by steam engines. A machine could weave much faster than a person. In big factories, the **weaving mills**, hundreds of such looms soon stood. Many Swiss factories processed mainly **cotton**.

Many home weavers were afraid of losing their work because of the machines. On 22 November 1832 angry weavers in **Uster** in the canton of Zurich set fire to a factory with mechanical looms. This event is called the **Usterbrand**. The culprits were harshly punished. But the machines could not be stopped, and soon new weaving mills arose everywhere.

At the beginning of the 19th century the Frenchman **Joseph-Marie Jacquard** of Lyon invented a special loom. It was controlled with **punched cards**. The holes determined which warp threads were raised. In this way the machine could weave difficult patterns by itself. The idea of controlling a machine with punched cards was later also used for early calculating machines and computers.

gewusst: Swiss firms also later built weaving machines, for example in Rüti in the Zurich Oberland.
Jacquard’s punched cards are seen as early forerunners of computer programs.

teile.einleitung: Television transmits pictures and sounds over long distances. In the 20th century it became one of the most important media, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Unlike radio, a television also shows moving pictures.
The Scot John Logie Baird demonstrated an early television picture in 1926.
In 1939 ETH Zurich showed a television experiment at the National Exhibition.
In 1953 the SRG began an experimental programme in Zurich.
From 1958 Swiss television broadcast regularly.
The first pictures were black and white.
In 1968 colour television came to Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Radio** transmits only sounds. **Television** also shows **moving pictures**. For this a picture is broken into many lines, transmitted and put together again at the receiver. This happens so fast that our eye sees smooth movement. In the past the signals came through **aerials**, later also through cables, satellites and the internet.

Many inventors worked on the idea of television. The Scot **John Logie Baird** showed moving pictures on a television set in London in **1926**. The pictures were still very small and blurred. Even so it was a sensation. In the following years the sets and the pictures became better and better.

At the **National Exhibition of 1939** in Zurich, **ETH** showed a first television experiment, and the visitors marvelled. In **1953** the **SRG** broadcast a first **experimental programme** in Zurich. It ran for only about an hour in the evening. From **1958** Swiss television broadcast **regularly**. More and more families bought a set, and soon there were programmes in several national languages.

abschnitte.titel: From black and white to colour
abschnitte.text: The first televisions showed only **black, white and shades of grey**. In **1968** Swiss television began broadcasting in **colour**. At first there were only a few colour programmes, and colour sets were expensive. The old sets had a big **picture tube** and were very heavy. Today's flat screens are thin and show much sharper pictures.

gewusst: The German word Fernsehen means exactly what it does: you see something that is happening far away. The word “television” also means seeing from afar.
In the early years you had to pay a fee in Switzerland for a television, just as you still do today for radio and television.

teile.einleitung: Harriet Tubman was an African American woman who herself escaped from slavery. After that she returned to the South in secret again and again and led other people to freedom.
wichtigste: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland around 1822.
In 1849 she escaped to Philadelphia in Pennsylvania.
Through the secret network called the “Underground Railroad” she helped many people to escape.
On about 13 journeys she personally led about 70 people to freedom.
She was called “Moses” because she led people out of slavery.
She took many of those who escaped as far as Canada.
In the Civil War she worked as a scout for the Northern states.

abschnitte.text: Harriet Tubman was born around **1822** in the state of **Maryland**. Her birth name was Araminta Ross. In the Southern states of the USA, **slavery** was allowed at that time. Enslaved people belonged to others like property and had to work without pay. Families were often torn apart. In 1849 Harriet escaped alone to **Philadelphia** in the North, where slavery was banned.

The **Underground Railroad** was not a real railway. It was a secret network of helpers and safe houses. People escaping usually travelled at night from hiding place to hiding place. The helpers used railway words: someone who guided people was called a **conductor**, and the hiding places were called **stations**. Harriet Tubman became one of the most famous conductors.

Tubman returned secretly to Maryland about **13 times**. She brought about **70 people** to freedom, including family members and friends. To many more she gave exact instructions for escaping. Because, like **Moses** in the Bible, she led her people out of slavery, she was called “Moses”. From 1850, people who had escaped could also be caught in the North. So she led people as far as **Canada**.

From 1861 to 1865 the Northern states fought the Southern states in the **American Civil War**. Tubman served the North as a **scout**, a spy and a nurse. In 1863 she helped with an attack in which over 700 enslaved people were freed. After the war slavery was abolished across the whole USA. Tubman died in 1913 in the state of New York.

gewusst: Harriet Tubman later said that she never lost a single person on her escape journeys.
In 2016 the US government announced that it would put her picture on the 20-dollar bill.

teile.einleitung: A steamship is driven by a steam engine. In the 19th century steamships changed travel on lakes, rivers and seas, because they no longer depended on the wind.
wichtigste: A steamship moves with the power of a steam engine.
Many old steamships had big paddle wheels at the sides, and they are called paddle steamers.
A great advantage: steamships did not need wind.
The engineer operated the steam engine in the engine room.
In 1823 the first steamship in Switzerland, the “Guillaume Tell”, sailed on Lake Geneva.
On Swiss lakes old paddle steamers still sail today, for example the “Uri” and the “Blüemlisalp”.
The Titanic sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg.

abschnitte.text: In a **boiler** water is heated by a fire, in the past mostly with coal or wood. This produces **steam**, which is under great pressure. In the **steam engine** this steam moves pistons back and forth. The movement is passed on to a shaft that turns. On many old ships the shaft turned big **paddle wheels** at the side, whose paddles pushed the ship through the water. Later the **propeller** under the stern won out.

A sailing ship has to wait when there is no wind and can only with difficulty sail against it. A steamship, on the other hand, moves **even without wind** and even against it. That is why steamships could keep to **timetables** for the first time. This was a huge step forward for trade and for travellers. On rivers steamships could also travel well against the current.

Down in the **engine room** the **engineer** worked. He made sure that the steam engine ran properly and was well oiled. **Stokers** shovelled coal into the fire so that enough steam was made. Up on the bridge the captain gave the orders. The work in the hot, loud engine room was very hard.

The first steamship in Switzerland was called the **“Guillaume Tell”**. It sailed on **Lake Geneva** from 1823. Soon steamships followed on many other lakes. On **Lake Lucerne** several old paddle steamers still sail today, for example the “Uri”, which has been in service since 1901, and the “Unterwalden”. On **Lake Thun** the **“Blüemlisalp”** has sailed since 1906, named after a mountain range in the Bernese Oberland.

In time steamships grew bigger and bigger and crossed the oceans. Large **passenger ships** brought many people from Europe to America. The most famous is the **Titanic**. On her first voyage in 1912 she hit an **iceberg** and sank. Over 1,500 people died. Afterwards the rules for safety on ships were made stricter, for example enough lifeboats for everyone.

gewusst: The old paddle steamers on Swiss lakes are carefully looked after and are very popular with day trippers.
With a steam engine a ship could travel against the current of a river, which was often hardly possible with sails.

teile.einleitung: Henry Ford was an American businessman and the founder of the Ford Motor Company. With the assembly line he made cars so cheap that many people could afford one.
wichtigste: Henry Ford built his first vehicle, the Quadricycle, in 1896.
Before that he worked as an engineer at an electricity company of Thomas Edison.
In 1903 he founded the Ford Motor Company.
From 1908 to 1927, more than 15 million cars of the Model T were built.
The Model T had the nickname “Tin Lizzie”.
Ford got the idea of the assembly line from slaughterhouses in Chicago.
With the assembly line, building a chassis took only about an hour and a half.

abschnitte.text: Henry Ford was born in 1863 on a farm in the state of **Michigan**. Even as a boy he liked taking machines apart. Later he worked as chief engineer at an electricity company of **Thomas Edison** in **Detroit**. In his spare time, in a shed behind his house, he built his first vehicle, the **Quadricycle** of 1896. It had four bicycle wheels and a small petrol engine.

After two failed attempts, Ford founded the **Ford Motor Company** in **1903**. In 1908 the **Model T** came onto the market. It was simple, sturdy and fairly cheap. It was affectionately called the **“Tin Lizzie”**. By 1927 more than **15 million** of them had been built. For a long time it was one of the most widely built cars in the world.

Ford had seen the idea for the **assembly line** in the **slaughterhouses** of Chicago. There the carcasses moved on hooks from worker to worker. From 1913, in Ford's factory, the cars moved past the workers. Each person always did the same task. Before, building a chassis took over twelve hours; afterwards it took only about **93 minutes**.

In 1914 Ford introduced a daily wage of 5 dollars. That was a lot at the time, and so his own workers could afford a car too. But work on the assembly line was monotonous and tiring. In the 1920s Ford also spread **antisemitic writings**. He is still sharply criticised for this today. Henry Ford died in 1947.

gewusst: Work on assembly lines on Ford's model is also called **Fordism**.
For several years the Model T came in only one colour: black.

teile.einleitung: The Yugoslav Wars were a series of wars between 1991 and 2001 in which the state of Yugoslavia broke apart. The fighting was mainly between Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks and Kosovo Albanians. The wars cost well over 100,000 people their lives and were the worst in Europe since the Second World War.
wichtigste: After the death of head of state Josip Broz Tito in 1980, tensions grew in Yugoslavia.
On 25 June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence.
From 1992 to 1995 the war raged in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
In the Srebrenica massacre in July 1995, more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.
The Dayton Agreement ended the Bosnian War; it was signed on 14 December 1995 in Paris.
In 1999, in the Kosovo War, NATO attacked the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from the air.
The UN war crimes tribunal in The Hague convicted numerous war criminals.
Since 1999 the Swiss army has served in Kosovo with the Swisscoy.

abschnitte.text: Yugoslavia consisted of six republics: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia. Many peoples with different religions lived together here. The communist head of state **Tito** held the country together until his death in 1980. After that, the economy and politics fell into crisis, and **nationalism** grew stronger, especially under the Serbian politician Slobodan Milošević.

On 25 June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared their **independence**. In Slovenia the war lasted only about ten days. In Croatia there was fighting until 1995, and the town of Vukovar was almost completely destroyed in 1991. Many people were driven out of their villages, which was called **ethnic cleansing**.

The Bosnian War of 1992 to 1995 was the bloodiest part of the wars. The capital **Sarajevo** was besieged and shelled for almost four years. In July 1995 Bosnian Serb troops killed more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys in **Srebrenica**, although the town was a UN protected zone. The Dayton Agreement ended the war in December 1995.

In Kosovo, a province of Serbia with a mostly Albanian population, the conflict escalated in 1998. From 24 March to 10 June 1999 **NATO** flew air strikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. After that an international peacekeeping force called **KFOR** took over security. On 17 February 2008 Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia.

The UN tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, **ICTY** for short, had its seat in The Hague. Among others, it sentenced the Bosnian Serb politician Radovan Karadžić and the general Ratko Mladić to life imprisonment. Slobodan Milošević died in custody in 2006 before a verdict. Seven states have now emerged from Yugoslavia, if you count Kosovo.

During the wars many people fled from the former Yugoslavia to **Switzerland**. Today many families with roots in Bosnia, Croatia, Serbia or Kosovo live here. Since 1999 the Swiss contingent **Swisscoy** has served in KFOR in Kosovo. It is the largest foreign deployment of the Swiss army.

begriffe.erklaerung: A constituent state within a federal state, similar to a canton in Switzerland.
The violent expulsion or killing of an ethnic group from an area.
A serious crime in war, such as deliberate attacks on civilians.
An international peacekeeping force in Kosovo under NATO leadership.

gewusst: The siege of Sarajevo lasted almost four years and was the longest siege of a capital in modern history.
The famous Old Bridge of Mostar was destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt in 2004 true to the original.
The Dayton Agreement was negotiated at an air force base in Dayton in the USA, but signed in Paris.

teile.einleitung: The division of Germany means the split of Germany after the Second World War into two states, the Federal Republic of Germany in the west and the GDR in the east. It began with the division into occupation zones in 1945 and lasted until reunification on 3 October 1990. A heavily guarded border separated families and friends for over 40 years.
wichtigste: After 1945 Germany was divided into four occupation zones of the USA, Britain, France and the Soviet Union.
The Potsdam Conference from 17 July to 2 August 1945 set aims for Germany, the “four Ds”.
The western zones grew together, and in 1947 the Bizone came into being.
The introduction of the Deutsche Mark on 20 June 1948 deepened the split.
The Berlin Blockade lasted from 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949.
In May 1949 the Federal Republic came into being, in October 1949 the GDR.
The division only ended with reunification in 1990.

abschnitte.text: From 17 July to 2 August 1945 the heads of government of the USA, Britain and the Soviet Union met in **Potsdam** near Berlin. France was not invited, but still received its own occupation zone in the south-west, which also bordered on Switzerland. The victorious powers agreed on the so-called **four Ds**: demilitarisation, denazification, democratisation and decentralisation. The areas east of the **Oder-Neisse line** came under Polish administration, and millions of Germans had to flee from there or were expelled.

Soon the cooperation of the victorious powers broke down, and the **Cold War** began. From 1 January 1947 the USA and Britain joined their zones economically into the **Bizone**, and later the French zone was added. The western zones received help from the American Marshall Plan. In the Soviet zone, on the other hand, factories were nationalised and big landowners dispossessed, and the communist SED took power.

On 20 June 1948 the **Deutsche Mark** was introduced in the western zones. The Soviet Union answered with the Berlin Blockade from 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949. The US military governor Lucius D. Clay then ordered the **airlift**. Almost two thirds of the freight was coal. Berlin children called the aircraft “raisin bombers”, because pilots dropped sweets on little parachutes.

In the **Parliamentary Council** in Bonn politicians from the western zones drew up the Basic Law, and the president of the Council was Konrad Adenauer. The lawyer **Elisabeth Selbert** won through with the sentence “Men and women have equal rights”. On 23 May 1949 the Federal Republic of Germany was founded, and Adenauer became its first Chancellor. On 7 October 1949 the **GDR** followed in the east, a state dependent on the Soviet Union and without free elections.

The inner German border was almost 1,400 kilometres long and was secured by the GDR with fences, mines and watchtowers. On 17 June 1953 Soviet tanks put down a popular uprising in the GDR. In 1961 the GDR built the **Berlin Wall** to stop flight to the West. From the 1970s the **Ostpolitik** of Chancellor Willy Brandt improved relations somewhat, and in 1973 both states became members of the UN. Only the peaceful revolution of 1989 opened the border, and on 3 October 1990 Germany was united again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A territory that is administered by a foreign army after a war.
Removing National Socialists from important posts and dealing with their deeds.
The constitution of the Federal Republic of Germany.
The long conflict between West and East without direct war between the USA and the Soviet Union.

gewusst: The Basic Law was deliberately not called a constitution, because it was only meant to apply until reunification, but it still applies today.
The small town of Bonn became the capital of the Federal Republic in 1949, also because Konrad Adenauer lived nearby.
Mödlareuth, a village right on the border, was called “Little Berlin” because of its wall.

teile.einleitung: Lenin was a Russian revolutionary who came to power in 1917 with the October Revolution and founded the world’s first communist state. His real name was Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov. Before the revolution he lived for several years in exile, including in Bern and Zurich.
wichtigste: Lenin’s family name was Ulyanov, and he was born in Simbirsk on the Volga in 1870.
In 1887 his brother Alexander was executed for a planned assassination of the Tsar, which strongly shaped Lenin.
In his work “What Is to Be Done?” of 1902 he sketched a tightly organised party of professional revolutionaries.
In 1903 Russian social democracy split into Bolsheviks and Mensheviks, and Lenin led the Bolsheviks.
From February 1916 Lenin lived in Swiss exile in Zurich, at Spiegelgasse 14.
In April 1917 the Swiss socialist Fritz Platten organised his journey back by train through Germany.
In the April Theses Lenin demanded: no support for the Provisional Government and all power to the Soviets.
In his political testament around the turn of the year 1922/23 he warned against Joseph Stalin.

abschnitte.text: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov was born on 22 April 1870 in **Simbirsk**; his father was a school inspector. In 1887 his older brother Alexander was executed because he had taken part in a planned assassination of the Tsar. Shortly afterwards Lenin was expelled from Kazan University because of student protests and later became a lawyer. He became enthusiastic about the teachings of Karl Marx and in 1897 was banished to **Siberia** for three years.

He used the name “Lenin” as a pen name for his writings. In “What Is to Be Done?” he demanded in 1902 a small, strictly led party of **professional revolutionaries**. Over this question Russian social democracy fell out at a party congress in London in 1903. Lenin’s followers called themselves **Bolsheviks**, which means “those of the majority”, and the opponents were called Mensheviks.

Lenin lived abroad for a long time, including in Munich, London and Paris. From 1914 to 1916 he lived in Bern, and from February 1916 in Zurich at **Spiegelgasse 14** in the old town. He worked a lot in libraries and took part in meetings of opponents of the war in Zimmerwald and Kiental in the Bernese Oberland. When the Tsar was overthrown in March 1917, he wanted to go back to Russia at once. The Swiss socialist **Fritz Platten** organised the journey in April 1917 in a train right across Germany, which hoped this would weaken Russia.

Back in Petrograd, Lenin announced his **April Theses**: no support for the Provisional Government and all power to the Soviets, that is, the councils of workers and soldiers. In the **October Revolution** of 1917 the Bolsheviks took power. In 1918 Lenin made peace with Germany and lost large territories in doing so. In the civil war that followed, until about 1921, he ruled with violence, and opponents were persecuted and often killed by the secret police, the Cheka. In 1922 the Soviet Union was founded.

From 1922 Lenin suffered several strokes and soon could hardly work any more. In his **political testament** he warned that Joseph Stalin was too rude and should be removed. Lenin died on 21 January 1924 near Moscow, and his embalmed body lies to this day in the **mausoleum** on Red Square. Despite the warning Stalin prevailed and built an even harsher dictatorship. In the Soviet Union Lenin was revered like a hero; today he is judged very differently.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rapid, often violent overthrow of the existing government and order.
Lenin’s wing of Russian social democracy, from which the Communist Party grew.
The Russian word for “council”, at that time assemblies of workers and soldiers.
Living abroad because one is persecuted at home.
The idea of a society without private ownership of factories and land, in which everyone is meant to be equal.

gewusst: In Zurich Lenin lived only a few houses away from the Cabaret Voltaire, where the art movement Dada arose in 1916.
The city of Simbirsk, where he was born, has been called Ulyanovsk since 1924.
Lenin’s body has been elaborately preserved in the mausoleum in Moscow since 1924.

teile.einleitung: The COVID-19 pandemic was a worldwide spread of the disease COVID-19 that gripped the whole world from the end of 2019. It was caused by the new coronavirus SARS-CoV-2. To slow the infections, many countries, including Switzerland, temporarily closed schools, shops and borders.
wichtigste: COVID-19 is caused by the virus SARS-CoV-2.
The first cases became known at the end of 2019 in the Chinese city of Wuhan.
On 11 March 2020 the WHO classed COVID-19 as a pandemic.
The first case in Switzerland was confirmed on 25 February 2020 in Ticino.
On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation.
At the end of 2020 the first vaccines were approved, in Switzerland on 19 December 2020.
On 5 May 2023 the WHO declared the end of the global health emergency.

abschnitte.text: COVID-19 is a contagious disease that mainly affects the airways. It is caused by the coronavirus **SARS-CoV-2**, which spreads mainly through tiny droplets and aerosols in the air. Many people have only mild symptoms such as fever, a cough or the loss of the sense of taste. In older people and people with existing illnesses, however, the disease can be severe or deadly. Some people still suffer from tiredness and other complaints for a long time after the infection, which is called **long Covid**.

At the end of 2019 the first cases became known in the Chinese city of **Wuhan**, home to millions of people. Through travel the virus spread across the whole world within a few weeks. On 11 March 2020 the World Health Organization, the WHO, declared the disease a **pandemic**, that is, a worldwide epidemic. According to the WHO, about seven million deaths had been reported by 2024, but experts estimate that the real number is clearly higher.

On 25 February 2020 the first case in Switzerland was confirmed in **Ticino**. On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council declared the **extraordinary situation** under the Epidemics Act. Schools switched to distance learning, restaurants, shops and leisure businesses had to close, and the army helped in hospitals. Later rules applied such as the mask requirement on public transport and the Covid certificate. On 13 June 2021 the voters accepted the Covid-19 Act with about 60 per cent in favour. From 1 April 2022 the normal situation applied again.

Researchers developed effective **vaccines** in less than a year. On 19 December 2020 the Swiss medicines authority Swissmedic approved the vaccine from **Pfizer/BioNTech** as the first, for a limited period. This one and the vaccine from Moderna use the new mRNA technique, which gives the body a set of instructions for a harmless part of the virus. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2023 for their basic research on it.

For children and teenagers the pandemic meant distance learning, cancelled trips and fewer meetings with friends. Many adults worked from **home**, and video conferences suddenly became everyday. The state supported firms with loans and short-time work so that as few people as possible lost their jobs. On 5 May 2023 the WHO declared the end of the global health emergency. Since then states have been thinking about how they can prepare better for future pandemics.

begriffe.erklaerung: A contagious disease that spreads across many countries and continents.
A tiny germ that can only multiply inside living cells.
A vaccine that gives the body a set of instructions so that it makes defences against a virus.
When public life is strongly restricted.
Very fine droplets in the air that form when we breathe and speak.

gewusst: The word “corona” means crown in Latin, because under the microscope the virus looks as if it is surrounded by a wreath.
The name COVID-19 stands for “coronavirus disease 2019”.
In spring 2020 toilet paper ran short in many countries, because people bought supplies out of fear.

teile.einleitung: Capitalism and communism are two opposite ideas about how the economy and society should be organised. In capitalism, factories and companies belong to private owners, who compete with one another in markets. In communism, all means of production are supposed to belong to the community, and in the 20th century this opposition shaped the Cold War.
wichtigste: Capitalism is based on private ownership of the means of production and on competition in markets.
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published the “Communist Manifesto” in 1848.
The Soviet Union had a centrally planned economy.
In the Soviet Union the Communist Party (CPSU) held the political monopoly of power.
The Marshall Plan of 1947 was meant to rebuild Europe and weaken communism.
In response, the Soviet Union and its allies founded the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance in 1949.
From 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev relied on “glasnost”, that is, openness and transparency.

abschnitte.text: In **capitalism**, factories, machines and land, the so-called **means of production**, belong to private persons or companies. They make goods and sell them in markets in order to make a profit. Prices arise from supply and demand. In 1776 the Scottish thinker Adam Smith described how markets are steered as if by an “invisible hand”.

In **communism**, all means of production are supposed to belong to the community, and there are to be no more classes of rich and poor. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published the “Communist Manifesto” in 1848. They criticised the way factory workers were exploited during industrialisation. Marx believed that the workers would overthrow capitalism through a **revolution**.

After the revolution of 1917 the Soviet Union arose with a central **planned economy**. In Five-Year Plans the state decided what was produced and how much. The Communist Party held the monopoly of power, and there were no free elections or free press. Goods were often missing, and people had to queue for a long time.

After 1945 the capitalist West under the leadership of the USA faced the communist East under the Soviet Union. The states of eastern Europe became Soviet **satellite states**. The USA supported western Europe with the Marshall Plan, and the East founded the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance in 1949. This contest between the systems is called the **Cold War**.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Eastern Bloc
abschnitte.text: From 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev tried to reform the Soviet Union with “glasnost” and “perestroika”, meaning restructuring. In 1989 the Berlin Wall fell, and the states of eastern Europe became free. At the end of 1991 the Soviet Union dissolved. China kept the rule of the Communist Party, but from 1978 opened its economy to markets.

Switzerland has a **market economy** with private property and competition. At the same time there are social safeguards such as the AVS and state rules, for example to protect employees. Many Western countries combine market and welfare state in this way, which in Germany is called the social market economy. The revolutionary Lenin, by the way, lived for some years in exile in Switzerland before 1917.

begriffe.erklaerung: Things with which goods are made, for example factories, machines and land.
An economy in which the state decides what is produced and what it costs.
An economy in which supply and demand determine prices and production.
Tension between East and West from 1947 to 1991 without a direct war between the great powers.

gewusst: The word “capitalism” only became common in the 19th century, mainly through its critics.
Karl Marx lived in London for most of his life and is also buried there.

teile.einleitung: Electricity is a form of energy that comes from tiny electrically charged particles. Today it simply comes out of the socket, but only in the 19th century did researchers and inventors learn to produce and use electric current. These discoveries have changed people's lives as strongly as hardly any other invention.
wichtigste: Around 1800 Alessandro Volta built the first usable battery with the voltaic pile.
In 1831 Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction, the basis of every generator.
In 1866 and 1867 Werner von Siemens described the dynamo-electric principle and so made large generators possible.
Thomas Edison and Joseph Swan developed usable light bulbs around 1879.
In 1879 the first electric light in Switzerland burned in a hotel in St Moritz.
Electric motors gradually replaced the steam engine in factories.
For over a hundred years Switzerland has produced most of its electricity from hydropower.

abschnitte.text: All things are made of atoms, and inside them there are tiny, negatively charged particles, the **electrons**. When electrons move through a wire, **electric current** flows. You can imagine it like water in a pipe: the voltage is like the pressure that drives the water. Electricity also exists in nature, for example as lightning or as a little spark when you touch a door handle after walking across a carpet.

Even the ancient Greeks knew that rubbed amber attracts small particles. The Greek word for amber is “elektron”, which is where the name electricity comes from. Around 1800 the Italian **Alessandro Volta** piled up discs of copper and zinc with cardboard soaked in salt water between them. This **voltaic pile** gave a steady current for the first time. The unit of electrical voltage, the **volt**, is named after Volta.

In 1831 the Englishman **Michael Faraday** discovered that current is produced in a coil of wire when a magnet moves inside it. This **electromagnetic induction** is still the basis of almost all power stations today. In 1866 and 1867 Werner von Siemens described the **dynamo-electric principle**, with which generators strengthen themselves. Now current could be produced in large amounts and cheaply, driven by waterwheels, turbines or steam engines.

The Englishman **Joseph Swan** showed a light bulb in public in 1879, independently of the American **Thomas Edison**. Edison received a patent for his light bulb in 1880 and put it into mass production. For particularly long-lasting filaments he soon used carbonised bamboo fibres. Around 1910 **tungsten** won out as the material for filaments, because it can stand very high temperatures. Edison also built power stations and electricity networks so that whole districts could be lit.

In the first factories a single large steam engine drove all the machines by long shafts and belts. With the **electric motor** every machine could have a small drive of its own. This made work safer and factories more flexible. Soon electric trams ran too, and new devices such as the telephone, the radio and the refrigerator came into homes. This is why people often speak of the **Second Industrial Revolution**.

In 1879 the first electric light in Switzerland burned in a hotel in **St Moritz**. Switzerland has no coal, but many mountains, rivers and lakes. That is why hydropower was also called **white coal**, because it replaced the missing coal as a source of energy. For over a hundred years most Swiss electricity has come from hydroelectric power stations, for example from large reservoirs such as the Lac des Dix in the Valais. The Swiss railways too were electrified early on.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, negatively charged particle in every atom. When electrons move, current flows.
The “pressure” that drives the current. It is measured in volts.
A machine that turns movement into electric current.
Current is produced in a wire when a magnet moves near it.
Electricity that is produced with the force of flowing or falling water.

gewusst: The name electricity comes from the Greek word for amber, “elektron”.
For a time Edison used carbonised bamboo for his filaments.
Hydropower was so important for Switzerland that it was called “white coal”.

teile.einleitung: The Jesuits are a Catholic men's order, that is, a community of religious brothers and priests. They were founded in the 16th century and are still known today for their schools and their work all over the world.
wichtigste: The official name is the Society of Jesus, in Latin Societas Jesu, abbreviated SJ.
The order was founded by Ignatius of Loyola, and the Pope confirmed it in 1540.
Francis Xavier worked as a missionary in India and Japan in the 16th century.
In Europe the Jesuits were especially known for their schools.
In 1773 the Pope dissolved the order, and in 1814 it was permitted again.
In Switzerland the Jesuits were banned from 1848 to 1973.
In 2013 Francis became the first pope from the Jesuit order.

abschnitte.text: The founder of the order was **Ignatius of Loyola**, a nobleman from Spain. After a serious wound as a soldier, he turned wholly to the faith. Together with friends he founded a community in Paris. In **1540** the Pope confirmed the new order, the **Society of Jesus**. That is why Jesuits still write the abbreviation **SJ** after their names.

Jesuits travelled as **missionaries** to many countries. **Francis Xavier**, a companion of Ignatius, went to **India**, to the Moluccas and to **Japan**. The Italian **Matteo Ricci** learned Chinese and around 1600 lived at the imperial court in **Beijing**. He brought knowledge of mathematics and astronomy to China. Many Jesuits were scholars and researchers at the same time.

In Europe the Jesuits became especially famous for their **schools**. They founded many grammar schools and **colleges**, in Switzerland too, for example in **Lucerne**, **Fribourg** and **Solothurn**. There young people learned Latin, mathematics, theatre and religion. Many of these schools still exist in another form today.

The order also had opponents. Under pressure from several kings, **Pope Clement XIV** dissolved it in **1773**. In 1814 it was permitted again. In Switzerland the Jesuits were controversial when the **Sonderbund War** came in 1847. The first **Federal Constitution** of 1848 banned them from any activity. Only in **1973** did the people and the cantons strike this ban out in a vote.

gewusst: In 2013 the Argentine Jorge Mario Bergoglio became, as Francis, the first pope from the Jesuit order.
In the past Jesuits also worked as astronomers. Several craters on the Moon are named after them.

teile.einleitung: The Haitian Revolution began in 1791 with a great uprising of enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue. It ended in 1804 with the founding of the independent state of Haiti.
wichtigste: As a French colony, Haiti was called Saint-Domingue and lay in the west of the island of Hispaniola.
Because of sugar and coffee, Saint-Domingue was the richest colony of France.
In August 1791 the great slave uprising began in the north.
In 1802 Napoleon sent General Charles Leclerc with a large army, which failed.
On 1 January 1804 Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed independence.
Haiti was the first state to arise from a successful slave uprising.
In 1825 Haiti had to promise France a large compensation payment.

abschnitte.text: In the west of the Caribbean island of **Hispaniola** lay the French colony of **Saint-Domingue**. **Sugar** and **coffee** were grown on large plantations. The work had to be done by hundreds of thousands of **enslaved people** who had been taken from Africa by force. They had no rights and were treated harshly. Saint-Domingue was the richest colony of France.

In August 1791 enslaved people met at **Bois-Caïman** for a religious ceremony at night and decided on an uprising. A few days later thousands rose up in the north of the colony. An important leader became **Toussaint Louverture**, a formerly enslaved man. In 1794 France abolished slavery in its colonies. Toussaint became the most powerful man on the island.

**Napoleon** wanted to regain full control of the colony. In 1802 he sent his brother-in-law, General **Charles Leclerc**, with several tens of thousands of soldiers. Toussaint Louverture was captured and taken to France, where he died in 1803. But the resistance went on. Fighting, and above all **yellow fever**, destroyed the French army, and Leclerc himself died in 1802.

On **1 January 1804** General **Jean-Jacques Dessalines** proclaimed independence. He gave the country the indigenous name **Haiti**. It was the first state to emerge from a successful slave uprising, and after the USA the second independent state in the Americas. After Dessalines' death the country split. In the north **Henri Christophe** had himself crowned king in 1811 and built the mighty **Citadelle Laferrière**.

France did not recognise Haiti for a long time. In **1825** it threatened with warships and demanded **compensation of 150 million francs** for the former plantation owners. Haiti had to agree. The sum was later reduced, but it still weighed on the poor country for decades.

gewusst: The Citadelle Laferrière is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The revolution in Haiti gave many enslaved people all over the Americas hope of freedom.

teile.einleitung: A refrigerator keeps food cool so that it stays fresh for longer. Before it existed, people cooled food with ice and in cool cellars. Today there is a refrigerator in almost every kitchen.
wichtigste: In the past food was cooled with ice and in cellars.
Around 1876 the engineer Carl von Linde built an important refrigeration machine.
His machines were first used mainly in breweries.
Albert Einstein invented a refrigerator together with Leo Szilard.
In Switzerland many families got a refrigerator in the 1950s and 1960s.
A modern refrigerator needs electricity to cool.

abschnitte.text: In the past food was kept in cool **cellars**. In winter people sawed **ice** out of frozen lakes and ponds. The ice was stored well covered in **ice cellars**, so it lasted into the summer. Later there were wooden ice boxes in which a block of ice was put at the top. Food was also preserved by salting, smoking or drying.

The German engineer **Carl von Linde** built an important **refrigeration machine** around **1876**. It could produce cold artificially, entirely without natural ice. It was used first of all in **breweries**. For brewing beer you need low temperatures all year round. Later such machines were also used to cool slaughterhouses and warehouses.

A modern refrigerator needs **electricity**. Inside it a special substance flows through tubes, the **refrigerant**. Inside the fridge it absorbs heat and evaporates as it does so. A compressor squeezes it together, and at the back it gives the heat off again. That is why the grille at the back of the refrigerator is warm. In this way the heat is pumped from the inside to the outside.

In **Switzerland** many families got a refrigerator in the **1950s and 1960s**. That changed shopping: you no longer had to fetch fresh milk every day. **Milk** is put in the refrigerator **so that it stays fresh for longer**. In the cold, germs grow much more slowly. Along with the refrigerator, frozen products also came into the shops.

gewusst: The physicist Albert Einstein invented a refrigerator without moving parts together with Leo Szilard and had it patented in 1930.
Older refrigerators contained substances that damaged the ozone layer, which is why they are banned today.

teile.einleitung: The incandescent light bulb, often just called a bulb, was one of the most important inventions of the 19th century. It brought bright, safe light into homes, factories and streets.
wichtigste: In a light bulb, electricity flows through a very thin filament, which gets hot and glows.
Thomas Edison presented a long-lasting light bulb in 1879.
Edison came from the USA and filed over 1,000 patents.
Before the light bulb, candles, oil lamps and gas lamps gave light.
A light bulb turns most of the electricity into heat instead of light.
Today LED lamps are replacing the light bulb, because they use much less electricity.

abschnitte.text: In the past, people made light in the evening with **candles** and **oil lamps**. Later there were also **gas lamps** in towns and cities. All these lights had an open flame. They smelled, gave off soot and could easily start a fire. That is why many inventors looked for a light that works with electricity.

Inside a light bulb is a very thin thread, the **filament**. When electricity flows through it, it gets so hot that it glows and shines. So that the filament does not burn up, it is surrounded by a **glass bulb**. Inside there is either no air or a special gas. The first filaments were made of carbon, and later the metal **tungsten** was used.

Many researchers worked on the light bulb, for example **Joseph Swan** in England. But it was **Thomas Edison** from the USA who became famous. He was born in 1847 in the state of Ohio. With his team he presented a light bulb in **1879** that shone for many hours. Edison also built power stations and power lines so that the lamps could get electricity at all. In his life he filed **over 1,000 patents**.

abschnitte.titel: From the light bulb to the LED
abschnitte.text: A light bulb has one big drawback: it turns most of the electricity into **heat** and only a little into light. That is why it gets very hot. Modern **LED lamps** give the same amount of light and use much less electricity. In Switzerland and in the European Union, the traditional light bulbs were therefore gradually taken out of the shops from 2009.

gewusst: For his filaments, Edison's team tried many materials, including charred fibres of bamboo.
A filament gets hotter than 2,000 degrees. That is why you cannot touch a light bulb that is on.

teile.einleitung: A steam engine is a machine that produces movement with the power of hot steam. In the 18th century it was developed in Britain and decisively improved by James Watt. It drove factories, locomotives and ships and was the engine of the Industrial Revolution.
wichtigste: Thomas Newcomen built the first usable steam engine in 1712.
The first steam engines mainly pumped water out of mines.
In 1769 James Watt had his improved steam engine with a separate condenser patented.
The fuel was mainly coal.
With steam engines, factories no longer had to stand on rivers.
The unit watt and horsepower go back to James Watt.
Steam engines soon also drove railways and ships.

abschnitte.text: In a boiler water is heated by a fire until it turns into **steam**. The steam needs much more room than the water and therefore pushes with great force. In a cylinder it pushes a **piston** back and forth. Through a rod and a wheel this movement is turned into a rotation that can drive machines. In a similar way, steam also lifts the lid of a pan of boiling water.

As early as 1698 the Englishman **Thomas Savery** built a steam pump, which was not very reliable, though. In 1712 **Thomas Newcomen** set up the first usable steam engine. It was used mainly to pump water out of coal mines, which would otherwise have flooded. Newcomen's engine used a great deal of coal, however, because the cylinder had to be cooled and heated up again with every stroke.

The Scotsman **James Watt** had an important improvement patented in 1769: a separate **condenser**, in which the steam is cooled while the cylinder stays hot. As a result the engine needed much less coal. Together with the businessman Matthew Boulton, Watt built many engines in Birmingham. Later he also invented mechanisms with which the engine could turn wheels. To compare the power with draught animals, he introduced the unit **horsepower**.

In the second half of the 18th century the **Industrial Revolution** began in Britain, in which machines replaced more and more handwork. Before that, factories had to stand on rivers, because they were driven by waterwheels. With the steam engine they could be built anywhere, for example near coal mines or in towns. Spinning mills and weaving mills in particular now produced huge amounts of cloth. At the same time many people, children too, had to work in the factories under harsh conditions.

In 1807 Robert Fulton's successful steamship “Clermont” sailed on the Hudson River in America. In 1825 the first public railway with steam locomotives opened in England, between Stockton and Darlington. In 1829 George Stephenson's locomotive “Rocket” won a famous race. On Swiss lakes historic paddle steamers still sail today, for example on Lake Lucerne and Lake Geneva. In 1847 the **Spanish Bun Railway** between Zurich and Baden became the first railway to run entirely in Switzerland.

Today hardly any steam engines with pistons are still used. The principle lives on, however, in **steam turbines**, which produce electricity in many power stations, for example in nuclear power stations. In honour of James Watt the unit of power is called the **watt**, which you can find on light bulbs or vacuum cleaners, for example. The steam engine changed people's lives as strongly as hardly any invention before it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A moving part that is pushed back and forth in a cylinder.
A container in which steam is cooled and turns back into water.
The time when machines and factories greatly changed work and life.
An old unit of power, abbreviated hp.

gewusst: Even in ancient Greece Hero of Alexandria described a ball that turned by steam, but it was only used as a toy.
One horsepower is roughly equal to 735 watts.
On Lake Lucerne five historic paddle steamers still run on the regular timetable.

teile.einleitung: Louis XIV was King of France and is still called the Sun King today. He reigned for about 72 years, longer than any other king of a large European country. With his magnificent Palace of Versailles he became a model for many princes in Europe.
wichtigste: Louis XIV bears the nickname the Sun King.
He became king in 1643 at the age of 4 and reigned for about 72 years until his death in 1715.
For the young king his mother and Cardinal Mazarin ruled.
The uprising of the Fronde frightened him as a child and made him distrustful of the nobility.
His finance minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert strongly promoted the economy of France.
The sentence “I am the state.” is attributed to him, which he probably never said.
In 1685 he revoked the Edict of Nantes with the Edict of Fontainebleau, after which many Huguenots fled, also to Switzerland.
After his death in 1715 his great-grandson Louis XV followed him on the throne.

abschnitte.text: Louis was born on 5 September 1638 in Saint-Germain-en-Laye near Paris. When his father Louis XIII died in 1643, he became king at only 4 years old. For him his mother Anne of Austria and **Cardinal Mazarin** ruled. From 1648 to 1653 nobles and the Parlement of Paris rose up in the uprising of the **Fronde**. The young king even had to flee from Paris and remained distrustful of the nobility for ever.

After Mazarin’s death in 1661 Louis decided to rule himself, without a first minister. He chose the **sun** as his emblem, for just as everything revolves around the sun, everything was to revolve around him. Even as a teenager he danced in the ballet himself and in 1653 appeared as the rising sun. His form of rule is called **absolutism**, because the king had almost unlimited power. The sentence “I am the state.” fits that, but probably does not come from him.

Louis had his father’s hunting lodge at **Versailles** extended into a huge palace. From 1682 the whole court lived there, often several thousand people. Famous are the Hall of Mirrors and the great gardens with fountains and canals. The nobles had to live at court and take part in strict ceremonies, so the king could control them well. Many princes in Europe later built palaces on the model of Versailles.

Finance minister **Jean-Baptiste Colbert** promoted manufactories, roads, canals and trade with the colonies. France was to export as much as possible and import little; this policy is called **mercantilism**. At the same time Louis fought many wars to enlarge France, most recently the War of the Spanish Succession from 1701 to 1714. The wars and the expensive court life left the country with high debts.

abschnitte.titel: Faith and the flight of the Huguenots
abschnitte.text: Louis wanted everyone in France to be Catholic. In 1685 he revoked, with the Edict of Fontainebleau, the **Edict of Nantes** of 1598, which had granted freedom of faith to the Reformed **Huguenots**. After that hundreds of thousands of Huguenots fled abroad, for example to the Netherlands, to Brandenburg-Prussia and to Reformed places in Switzerland. Many brought knowledge of watchmaking, textiles and trade with them, especially to Geneva.

France was an important partner for the Confederation. Many **mercenaries** from the Confederation served in the army of Louis XIV, for example in the Swiss Guards regiment. In 1663 envoys of the Confederate cantons in Paris solemnly renewed an alliance with the king. After Louis’s death on 1 September 1715 he was followed by his five-year-old great-grandson Louis XV.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of rule in which a king decides almost alone and without control.
The name given to the Reformed Protestants in France.
An economic policy in which a state wants to sell a lot and buy little in order to become rich.
Soldiers who fight for money in a foreign army.
A decree or law of a king.

gewusst: Louis XIV outlived his son and his grandson, which is why his great-grandson became his successor.
The Sun King often wore shoes with red heels, which only nobles at court were allowed to wear.
His reign of about 72 years is still a record among the kings of large European countries.

teile.einleitung: The caravel was a small wooden sailing ship. In the 15th and 16th centuries sailors ventured far out onto unknown seas in it. It was one of the most important ships of the voyages of discovery.
wichtigste: The caravel is a sailing ship made of wood.
The Portuguese built the first caravels for their voyages of discovery.
Many caravels had triangular sails, the lateen sails.
It was fast and nimble.
It was driven by the wind alone.
Because it had a shallow draught, it could sail close to the coast.

abschnitte.text: The **caravel** was a fairly small sailing ship. It was often only 20 to 30 metres long and had a small crew. It was built entirely of **wood**, because ships of iron or steel did not exist yet. In caravels, sailors sailed into the unknown and discovered new coasts and sea routes.

In the 15th century the **Portuguese** were the first to use caravels for big voyages of exploration. Prince **Henry the Navigator** supported these journeys. Step by step the Portuguese explored the **west coast of Africa**. In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias sailed around the southern tip of Africa with caravels. Soon the Spanish also built such ships.

Many caravels had **triangular sails**, which are called **lateen sails**. With them the ship could also sail at an angle against the wind. When doing so you sail in a zigzag, which is called **tacking**. Later some caravels also got square sails, which were better with a following wind. The caravel was always driven only by the **wind**.

A big advantage of the caravel was that it was **fast and nimble**. It also had a shallow **draught**: the hull did not reach far below the surface of the water. That is why it could sail close to coasts and even into river mouths without running aground. That was ideal for exploring unknown coasts closely. For carrying a lot of cargo, however, it was rather too small.

gewusst: Two of the three ships of Christopher Columbus on his first voyage in 1492, the “Niña” and the “Pinta”, were caravels.
The lateen sail had been known in the Mediterranean long before; the caravel made it useful for voyages on the Atlantic.

teile.einleitung: The European Union, the EU for short, is an association of 27 European states. It came into being after the Second World War so that the countries of Europe would never again make war on each other and would trade together. Switzerland is not a member, but works closely with the EU through many treaties.
wichtigste: Since the withdrawal of the United Kingdom the EU has 27 member states.
Its starting point was the European Coal and Steel Community, founded in 1951 by six states.
In 1957 the Treaties of Rome founded the European Economic Community and Euratom.
The Maastricht Treaty created the European Union and came into force on 1 November 1993.
Since 1 January 2002 the euro has existed as cash.
The United Kingdom left the EU on 31 January 2020.
In 1992 Switzerland narrowly rejected the EEA and instead concluded bilateral treaties with the EU.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War many politicians wanted to prevent Europe from ever going to war again. On 9 May 1950 the French foreign minister **Robert Schuman** proposed that the coal and steel industry be managed together. For without coal and steel no country could build weapons. In 1951 Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands founded the **European Coal and Steel Community**. The 9th of May is celebrated today as Europe Day.

In 1957 the six states signed the **Treaties of Rome** and founded the European Economic Community (EEC) and Euratom. With the **Maastricht Treaty** the European Union came into being on 1 November 1993. Gradually many countries joined. In the great **eastern enlargement** on 1 May 2004, 10 states joined at once, among them Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary. The latest country so far, Croatia, became a member in 2013.

The EU has several important bodies. The **European Parliament** has been elected directly by the citizens since 1979 and meets in Strasbourg and Brussels. The **European Commission** in Brussels proposes laws and makes sure that they are kept. In the Council of the EU the ministers of the member states help to decide. The Court of Justice of the EU in Luxembourg makes sure that EU law is applied in the same way everywhere.

In the **single market** goods, services, money and people can cross borders freely. The **euro** was introduced in 1999 as book money and on 1 January 2002 as cash. Not all EU states have the euro, and Denmark and Sweden, for example, keep their own krone. Thanks to the **Schengen Agreement** there are no passport checks any more at many borders. The EU has 24 official languages, and its motto is “United in diversity”.

In 2016 a narrow majority in the United Kingdom voted in a **referendum** to leave the EU. This withdrawal is called **Brexit**, from “Britain” and “exit”. After long negotiations the United Kingdom left the EU on 31 January 2020. It was the first country to leave the EU again. Since then the EU has had 27 member states.

On 6 December 1992 the Swiss voters narrowly rejected joining the **European Economic Area** (EEA). After that Switzerland negotiated individual treaties with the EU, the **bilateral treaties**. Bilaterals I came into force on 1 June 2002 and regulate, for example, the free movement of persons and land transport. Since 2008 Switzerland has also been part of the Schengen Agreement. The EU is Switzerland's most important trading partner, and the future relations are discussed again and again in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A common market without customs duties in which goods and people may cross borders freely.
The common currency of many EU states, in coins and notes since 2002.
Treaties between two partners, here between Switzerland and the EU.
The withdrawal of the United Kingdom from the EU in 2020.

gewusst: The twelve stars on the European flag do not stand for twelve countries, but are a sign of perfection and unity.
In 2012 the European Union received the Nobel Peace Prize.
Switzerland is surrounded entirely by EU states and little Liechtenstein.

teile.einleitung: The Congo Conference took place in Berlin in 1884 and 1885. There European states, the USA and the Ottoman Empire laid down rules for trade and for the colonies in Africa. Africans were not asked.
wichtigste: The Congo Conference met in 1884 and 1885 in the Reich Chancellery in Berlin.
Not a single African representative took part.
Besides European states, the USA and the Ottoman Empire were present.
Free navigation was agreed for the Congo and Niger rivers.
The final document is called the General Act of Berlin.
Leopold II of Belgium received the Congo territory as his personal property.
From it came the Congo Free State, today mostly the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

abschnitte.text: The Congo Conference began in November **1884** and ended in February **1885**. It was convened by the German Chancellor **Otto von Bismarck**. The envoys met in the **Reich Chancellery** in Berlin. Besides many European states, the **United States** and the **Ottoman Empire** took part as well. **No** African representatives were invited.

Even before the conference, King **Leopold II of Belgium** wanted a territory of his own in Africa. From **1879** the explorer **Henry Morton Stanley** explored the **Congo Basin** on his behalf. Stanley concluded treaties with many chiefs which they often could not understand. In this way Leopold secured large territories. At the conference he got the other states to recognise his claim.

The final document of the conference is called the **General Act of Berlin**. In it, free navigation was agreed for the **Congo and Niger** rivers. In the Congo Basin all states were to be allowed to trade freely. It was also laid down how a state could claim new territories on the coast for itself. It had to notify the others and actually set up an administration there.

After the conference the **Congo Free State** came into being in 1885 as the private property of Leopold II. There the people were later brutally exploited. The conference did not directly divide up Africa, but it speeded up the **Scramble for Africa**. In the following decades European powers took almost the whole continent into possession as colonies. Today most of the territory of the Congo Free State is the **Democratic Republic of the Congo**.

gewusst: The Reich Chancellery, where the conference took place, stood on the Wilhelmstrasse in Berlin.
Many borders in Africa were later drawn with a ruler, without regard for the peoples who lived there.

teile.einleitung: Mao Zedong was a Chinese revolutionary and politician. In 1949 he founded the People’s Republic of China and ruled the country until his death in 1976. His rule brought great changes, but also severe suffering for millions of people.
wichtigste: Mao Zedong was born in 1893 in Shaoshan in Hunan province.
On the Long March in 1934 and 1935 he became the leader of the communists.
In the civil war his communists defeated the Kuomintang.
On 1 October 1949 he proclaimed the People’s Republic of China in Tiananmen Square.
The Great Leap Forward from 1958 led to a huge famine.
The Cultural Revolution from 1966 brought persecution and destruction.
Switzerland recognised the People’s Republic of China as early as 1950.

abschnitte.text: Mao was born in 1893 in the village of Shaoshan in **Hunan** province. His parents were farmers. As a young man he read a lot and became a teacher. He became enthusiastic about **communism**, a doctrine according to which all property is to be held in common. In 1921 he was among the participants at the founding meeting of the Communist Party of China.

In China the communists fought against the Nationalist **Kuomintang** under Chiang Kai-shek. In 1934 the communists had to flee from its troops. On the **Long March** they covered around 12,000 kilometres, through mountains, rivers and swamps. Many did not survive this retreat. During the march Mao rose to become the leading figure of the Party.

After the Second World War the **civil war** went on, and the communists won. On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People’s Republic of China in Beijing from the Gate of Heavenly Peace, **Tiananmen**. The Kuomintang government fled to the island of **Taiwan**. The Republic of China still exists there today. Switzerland recognised the People’s Republic on 17 January 1950 as one of the first Western states.

From 1958 Mao wanted to turn China into an industrial country very quickly. In this campaign, called the **Great Leap Forward**, peasants were grouped together in huge **people’s communes**. Everywhere people were to make steel in small furnaces instead of tilling the fields. Unrealistic targets, crop failures and false reports of success led to one of the worst **famines** in history. Many millions of people died.

From 1966 Mao proclaimed the **Cultural Revolution**. Young **Red Guards** took action against supposed enemies, above all teachers, artists and Party members. Many were persecuted, and temples and old works of art were destroyed. Mao was revered like a hero, which is called a **personality cult**. A little red book with his sayings was found everywhere. The Cultural Revolution only ended with Mao’s death in 1976.

gewusst: A large portrait of Mao still hangs on the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing today.
Mao’s picture can be seen on the banknotes of the Chinese currency, the renminbi.
In 1972 the American President Richard Nixon visited Mao in Beijing, which was a political sensation.

teile.einleitung: Industrialisation changed Switzerland in the 19th century from a poor farming country into one of the richest industrial countries in the world. Instead of by hand, goods were now produced with machines in factories. Because there was hardly any coal, Switzerland used above all the power of its rivers.
wichtigste: At the start of industrialisation in Switzerland, the textile industry was the most important.
Around 1802 the Hard spinning mill, the first successful mechanical spinning mill in Switzerland, was built in Wülflingen near Winterthur.
Instead of coal, Swiss factories mainly used water power.
In 1832 home weavers set fire to a mechanical weaving mill in the Uster fire.
Alfred Escher promoted railway building, founded the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt in 1856 and supported ETH.
ETH Zurich began teaching in 1855.
Well-known sectors were watches in the Jura, embroidery in St Gallen and chemicals in Basel.

abschnitte.text: Even before the factories, many families in the Zürcher Oberland, eastern Switzerland and the Glarus region spun and wove as **home workers**. Around 1802 the **Hard spinning mill** was built in Wülflingen near Winterthur, seen as the first successful mechanical spinning mill in Switzerland. In 1805 Escher Wyss was founded in Zurich as a cotton spinning mill. At first the **textile industry** was the most important branch of industry.

Switzerland has hardly any coal, which in England drove the steam engines. So businessmen built their factories on rivers and used **water power** with large water wheels and later turbines. In this way many factories arose along the Töss, Aa, Linth and Limmat. Later water power was also used to generate electricity.

Many **home weavers** feared that the machines would take their work away. On 22 November 1832 they set fire to a mechanical weaving mill in Uster in the Zürcher Oberland, which is called the **Uster fire**. The factory burned down, and the culprits were severely punished. But they could not stop mechanisation.

From workshops for textile machines grew a strong **engineering industry**; Escher Wyss later built steamships and turbines. In the Jura arc the **watch industry** developed, and eastern Switzerland around St Gallen was world famous for its embroidery. In Basel a large chemical industry arose, first with dyes. Foods such as chocolate and infant cereal from Henri Nestlé in Vevey were also sold all over the world.

The Zurich politician and businessman **Alfred Escher** founded railways and a major bank and supported ETH. He founded the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt in 1856 to finance railway building. From 1847 the first railway line entirely within Switzerland linked Zurich with Baden. In 1855 **ETH** in Zurich began teaching and trained engineers.

In the factories men, women and children too often worked more than twelve hours a day. Only the federal **Factory Act** of 1877 introduced the eleven-hour day and banned factory work for children under 14. Even so, poverty remained great. Because of poverty and lack of work, many people emigrated from Switzerland to America in the 19th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: Work that families did at home for a merchant, for example spinning and weaving.
The replacement of hand work by machines.
A law of 1877 that regulated working hours and child labour in factories.
The energy of flowing water, with which machines are driven.

gewusst: The first railway line in Switzerland was called the “Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn” (“Spanish bun railway”), because it could be used to bring fresh pastries from Baden to Zurich.
Around 1900 Switzerland was one of the most heavily industrialised countries in Europe.
Many of today's global companies, such as Nestlé or the Basel chemical and pharmaceutical firms, have their roots in industrialisation.

teile.einleitung: Photography means producing a lasting picture with light. The first photos were made in the 19th century and needed very long exposure times, while today a mobile phone takes a photo in a moment.
wichtigste: Nicéphore Niépce made the oldest surviving photograph around 1826.
It shows the view from a window of his country house.
The exposure took many hours.
In 1839 the daguerreotype of Louis Daguerre was presented in Paris.
William Henry Fox Talbot invented the negative-positive process.
The first photos were black and white or brownish.
“Photography” means roughly “drawing with light”.

abschnitte.text: The word **photography** comes from Greek and is made up of the words for **light** and for **writing or drawing**. In a photograph light makes the picture. People had long known the **camera obscura**, a dark box with a small hole. In it a picture of the surroundings forms. The problem was how to keep this picture permanently.

The French inventor **Nicéphore Niépce** lived in a village in Burgundy. Around **1826** he exposed a coated **pewter plate** in his camera. He pointed the camera out of an upstairs **window** of his country house. In the picture you can see roofs and buildings. The plate had to lie in the light for **many hours**, perhaps even days. This picture is the **oldest surviving photograph** in the world.

**Louis Daguerre** first worked together with Niépce. Later he developed a process for sharp pictures on **silver plates**. It was named after him the **daguerreotype**. In **1839** it was presented publicly in Paris. That is why 1839 is often seen as the **birth year of photography**. Every daguerreotype, however, was a one-off and could not be copied.

The Englishman **William Henry Fox Talbot** took a different path. He first made a **negative** on paper, in which light places appear dark. From it any number of **positive prints** could be made. This **negative-positive process** became very important for photography with film. It was used right into the digital age.

Early cameras took a long time until the picture was ready. People who were photographed therefore had to **sit still for a long time**. Anyone who moved was **blurred** in the photo. Sometimes stands supported the head. The first photographs had **no bright colours**, they were black and white or brownish. Colour photos only came much later.

gewusst: In many early photos of towns the streets are empty, although people were out and about there: they moved too fast to show up in the picture.
In a daguerreotype of Paris from 1838 you can see a man having his shoes polished. He is regarded as one of the first people ever photographed.

teile.einleitung: Imperialism is the name for the drive of powerful states to extend their rule over other countries and peoples. Especially between about 1870 and 1914, the European great powers divided up almost the whole world among themselves. The consequences can still be felt today in many countries in Africa and Asia.
wichtigste: The word imperialism comes from the Latin word “imperium”, meaning rule or empire.
The time from about 1870 to 1914 is called High Imperialism.
Important motives were access to raw materials and to markets for goods.
Rule was justified with social Darwinism and the idea of a civilising mission.
Even states that were formally independent were dominated, which is called informal imperialism.
In 1898 the USA acquired the Philippines after the war against Spain.
The rivalry of the great powers helped cause the outbreak of the First World War.

abschnitte.text: The term **imperialism** comes from the Latin word “imperium”. It means that a state extends its power over foreign territories, for example through colonies. In **informal imperialism**, formally independent states are dominated economically and politically, such as China in the 19th century. The time from about 1870 to 1914 is called **High Imperialism**.

A central role was played by access to **raw materials** such as cotton, rubber, gold or copper. The industrial countries were also looking for new markets for their goods. In addition there were the drive for power, national pride and military interests. In 1897 the German state secretary Bernhard von Bülow demanded a “place in the sun” for Germany.

Many Europeans thought themselves superior and believed in a **civilising mission**, that is, that they had to bring “civilisation” to other peoples. **Social Darwinism** applied Darwin's theory of the “struggle for existence” to peoples. The writer Rudyard Kipling wrote the poem “The White Man's Burden” in 1899, which was used as a justification. Today we know that these ideas were racist and wrong.

At the **Berlin Conference** on the Congo in 1884 and 1885, the European powers set rules for the division of Africa. By 1914 almost only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent in Africa. The British Empire was the largest and covered about a quarter of the Earth's land area. Under Kaiser Wilhelm II, Germany pursued a **world policy** with colonies and a large fleet, and in 1898 the USA acquired the Philippines.

The local population was often oppressed, forced to work and exploited. In the Congo, which belonged to the Belgian King Leopold II, millions of people died through forced labour and violence. In German South West Africa, the crushing of the uprisings of the Herero and Nama from 1904 led to a genocide. The borders drawn by Europeans in some places still cause conflicts in Africa today.

Even then there was criticism of imperialism. The British economist John A. Hobson published the influential book “Imperialism: A Study” in 1902. In 1916 Lenin described imperialism as the highest stage of **capitalism**. After the Second World War most colonies became independent, a process called decolonisation.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area ruled and administered by a foreign state.
The false idea that in the struggle between peoples only the stronger may survive.
The path of the colonies to independence, mainly after 1945.
Domination of a country that officially remains independent.

gewusst: In 1896 Ethiopia defeated an Italian army at the Battle of Adwa and therefore stayed independent.
It was said that the sun never set on the British Empire, because it had territories on all continents.
Switzerland had no colonies, but Swiss merchants, missionaries and researchers were active in many colonies.

teile.einleitung: The “Golden Twenties” is the name given to the years from about 1924 to 1929. After the First World War and the great loss in the value of money, many countries, especially Germany, enjoyed a few years of upswing, new freedom and a flourishing culture.
wichtigste: The Golden Twenties lasted in Germany from about 1924 to 1929.
From 1924 the Dawes Plan brought loans from the USA and helped the economy.
Jazz and the Charleston dance came from the USA to Europe.
Many women wore the short bob as a sign of more freedom.
In 1919 Walter Gropius founded the art school Bauhaus in Weimar.
In 1927 the film “Metropolis” by Fritz Lang came to the cinemas.
The stock market crash of 1929 ended the Golden Twenties.

abschnitte.text: After the First World War Germany was doing badly, and in 1923 money lost almost all its value. With a new currency and the **Dawes Plan** of 1924 things got better. This plan arranged the **reparations**, that is, the payments to the victorious countries, in a new way and brought loans from the USA. The economy recovered, and many people found new hope.

A new kind of music came from the USA: **jazz**. It had arisen in African American communities, for example in New Orleans. In dance halls people danced the fast **Charleston**. Big cities such as **Berlin** had many theatres, cinemas and cabarets. **Radio** and the record also spread.

Many young women had their hair cut short. This hairstyle was called the **bob**. With it they wore shorter dresses. Women more often worked in offices and shops and went out on their own. This was seen as modern and stood for more **independence**. Not everyone liked it, and there were lively discussions about it.

In 1919 **Walter Gropius** founded the **Bauhaus** in Weimar. This school combined art, crafts and technology and designed simple, practical forms. In 1927 the silent film **“Metropolis”** by Fritz Lang came to the cinemas. It shows a big city of the future and today belongs to UNESCO's Memory of the World.

The upswing stood on shaky ground, because it depended heavily on loans from the USA. Many people also stayed poor. In October 1929 prices crashed on the New York stock exchange. This turned into the **Great Depression**. It ended the Golden Twenties and brought a great deal of unemployment.
