gewusst: In 1928 the second Winter Olympics took place in **St Moritz** in the Engadine.
In the USA this time is called the “Roaring Twenties”.

teile.einleitung: The Cultural Revolution was a political campaign in China from 1966 to 1976. With it Mao Zedong wanted to secure his power and have everything old fought. The consequences were chaos, persecution and great suffering for millions of people.
wichtigste: Mao Zedong proclaimed the Cultural Revolution in 1966.
Young activists, the Red Guards, attacked teachers and officials.
They constantly carried the Little Red Book with quotations from Mao.
They were to destroy the “Four Olds”: old ideas, culture, customs and habits.
President Liu Shaoqi was overthrown and died in custody in 1969.
Millions of young people from the cities were sent to the countryside.
In October 1976 the Gang of Four was arrested.

abschnitte.text: **Mao Zedong** was the leader of the Communist Party of China. After failures in economic policy he had lost influence. In **1966** he proclaimed the **Cultural Revolution**. He claimed that enemies in the Party and in society wanted to bring back capitalism. With the campaign he wanted to eliminate his opponents and secure his power.

Above all schoolchildren and students joined the **Red Guards**. They constantly carried the **Little Red Book** with quotations from Mao Zedong. They attacked teachers, professors and officials and humiliated them in public. Schools and universities were closed for a long time. Many people were persecuted, imprisoned or lost their lives.

The Red Guards were to destroy the **“Four Olds”**: **old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits**. In the process temples, works of art, old books and historic buildings were damaged or destroyed. Religion was also suppressed. A great deal of China’s valuable cultural heritage was lost in this time.

High politicians also became victims. President **Liu Shaoqi** was overthrown as a “person in power taking the capitalist road” and died **in custody in 1969**. From 1968 the government sent millions of young people from the cities **to the countryside**. They were to learn from the peasants, and often they stayed there for many years. The group around Mao’s wife **Jiang Qing** had great influence.

Mao Zedong died in September **1976**. In **October 1976** the group around Jiang Qing, called the **Gang of Four**, was arrested. With that the Cultural Revolution ended. In 1981 the Communist Party described it as a serious mistake. How many people lost their lives is not known exactly, and estimates differ widely.

gewusst: The Little Red Book is among the most printed books in the world.
The later Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping was himself removed from power in the Cultural Revolution and sent to the countryside.

teile.einleitung: Joseph Stalin was the dictator of the Soviet Union from the 1920s until his death in 1953. Under his rule the country was industrialised quickly, but at the same time millions of people were persecuted, imprisoned or killed.
wichtigste: Stalin was born in 1878 in Gori in Georgia, which then belonged to the Russian Empire.
His real name was Ioseb Jughashvili; “Stalin” means “man of steel”.
In 1922 he became General Secretary of the Communist Party.
From 1928 he had industry built up with Five-Year Plans.
Millions of people were deported to the labour camps of the Gulag.
From 1936 to 1938 came the wave of persecution of the Great Terror.
Stalin died in March 1953 near Moscow.

abschnitte.text: Stalin was born in **1878** in **Gori** in **Georgia**. His real name was **Ioseb Jughashvili**. As a young man he joined the revolutionaries and took the fighting name **“Stalin”**, derived from the Russian word for steel. After the Russian Revolution of 1917 he rose in the **Communist Party**. In 1922 he became its **General Secretary**.

As General Secretary, Stalin filled important posts with his supporters. After Lenin's death in 1924 he gradually removed all his rivals. By the end of the 1920s he ruled alone as a **dictator**. A **personality cult** grew up around him: pictures and songs praised him as a wise leader. Criticism was dangerous and harshly punished.

From **1928** Stalin had factories, power stations and mines built in a short time with **Five-Year Plans**. The state decided exactly what had to be produced. At the same time, farms were forcibly merged into large enterprises, the **kolkhozes**. Anyone who resisted was persecuted. In 1932 and 1933 there was a severe **famine**, especially in Ukraine, in which millions of people died.

In the **Gulag**, a huge system of labour camps, millions of prisoners had to do **forced labour** in harsh conditions. A great many died of hunger, cold and exhaustion. From 1936 to 1938, in the **Great Terror**, Stalin had hundreds of thousands arrested and shot as alleged enemies, including many party members and officers. There were public **show trials** with forced confessions.

In 1941 Germany attacked the Soviet Union. After heavy losses, the Soviet Union was among the victors of the **Second World War** in 1945. After that, many countries of eastern Europe came under its influence. Stalin died in **March 1953**. Three years later his successor **Nikita Khrushchev** criticised his crimes in a speech.

gewusst: The Russian city of Volgograd was called Stalingrad from 1925 to 1961.
After Khrushchev's criticism, many monuments to Stalin were removed in the Soviet Union.

teile.einleitung: On 18 January 1871 the German Empire was founded. For the first time most of the German states were united in a common state, under the leadership of Prussia.
wichtigste: The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 in the Palace of Versailles.
The King of Prussia became German Emperor as William I.
Otto von Bismarck became the first Imperial Chancellor.
Three wars came before the founding: 1864, 1866 and 1870/71.
The Empire came into being under the “smaller German solution”, that is, without Austria.
France had to give up Alsace-Lorraine.
The parliament was called the Reichstag.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the 19th century Germany consisted of many separate states, such as Prussia, Bavaria or Saxony. Many people wished for a common state. It was disputed whether **Austria** should belong to it. The **greater German solution** wanted to include Austria. In the **smaller German solution** Germany was to be united without Austria and under the leadership of **Prussia**. This is what finally happened.

In 1864 Prussia and Austria fought together against **Denmark** over the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein. In 1866 Prussia and Austria fought the **German War** against each other. Prussia won the battle of **Königgrätz**, and Austria left German politics. In 1867 the **North German Confederation** came into being. In the **Franco-Prussian War** of 1870/71 the German states then fought together against France.

abschnitte.titel: Proclamation of the Emperor at Versailles
abschnitte.text: While the war was still going on, on **18 January 1871** the Prussian king was proclaimed German Emperor in the **Hall of Mirrors** of the Palace of Versailles near Paris. He was called **William I** and ruled until his death in 1888. The founding in France was a humiliation for the French. In the **Treaty of Frankfurt** France had to give up **Alsace-Lorraine** in 1871. This burdened the relationship of the two countries for decades.

The Empire was a **federal state** with an emperor at the top. The most important person in the government was the **Imperial Chancellor**, at first **Otto von Bismarck**. The parliament was called the **Reichstag**. It was elected by men aged 25 and over in general and equal elections and passed laws and the budget. In the **Bundesrat** the individual states were represented.

For Switzerland a powerful new neighbour came into being to the north. At the end of the war in 1871 there was also a special event: the French **Bourbaki army** fled into Switzerland with about 87,000 soldiers. It was disarmed and looked after. The **Bourbaki Panorama** in Lucerne still recalls it today.

gewusst: The Empire lasted from 1871 to 1918. After the First World War Germany became a republic.
The peace treaty after the First World War was signed in 1919 in the same Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

teile.einleitung: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a philosopher, writer and composer from Geneva who lived from 1712 to 1778. His ideas about freedom, equality and education shaped the French Revolution and thinking about democracy to this day. At the same time he was an uncomfortable thinker whose books were banned and burned.
wichtigste: Rousseau was born in 1712 in Geneva, which was then a republic of its own and not part of the Swiss Confederacy.
His most important political work is “The Social Contract” of 1762.
According to Rousseau, all power in the state should come from the people.
In his book “Emile” of 1762 he describes how children should be brought up.
Rousseau saw private property as one origin of inequality among people.
His books were banned and burned in Paris and Geneva in 1762.
After the French Revolution he was buried in the Panthéon in Paris.

abschnitte.text: Rousseau was born on 28 June 1712 in Geneva. His mother died a few days after his birth, and his father was a watchmaker. Even as a child Rousseau read a great deal, often with his father until late at night. At the age of 16, in 1728, he left his **home town** and wandered for years, including to Savoy.

In Paris in 1750 Rousseau won a prize from the Academy of Dijon with an essay in which he claimed that science and the arts had not made people better. In 1755 followed his essay on the **origin of inequality**. In it he saw private property as one origin of inequality. He also wrote music, for example the little opera “The Village Soothsayer”, which was performed at the royal court in 1752.

In 1762 “**The Social Contract**” appeared. Its first chapter begins with the famous sentence: “Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.” In it Rousseau demands that power should come from the people. Laws should correspond to the **general will**, that is, to what is good for everyone. This idea of the sovereignty of the people is a foundation of modern democracies.

In the book “**Emile**” Rousseau tells how a boy should grow up as naturally and freely as possible. Children should learn from their own experiences and not just learn by heart. The slogan “Back to nature!” is often linked with him, although it does not appear in those words in his works. His love novel “Julie, or the New Heloise” of 1761 was a huge success in the 18th century.

After the banning of his books in 1762, Rousseau had to flee. He lived for some years in Môtiers in the Val-de-Travers, which then belonged to the Principality of Neuchâtel. In 1765 he found refuge for a few weeks on the **St Peter's Island** in Lake Biel, which he later described as a very happy time. After that he travelled to England and finally returned to France.

Rousseau died on 2 July 1778 in Ermenonville near Paris. The revolutionaries revered him and had him moved to the **Panthéon** in 1794. His autobiography, the “Confessions”, appeared only after his death. In Geneva the small Rousseau Island with his statue recalls the city's famous son.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imagined agreement by which people join together to form a state.
The principle that the highest power in the state lies with the people.
For Rousseau, the will that is aimed at the good of all, not just one's own.
A time in the 18th century when people relied on reason instead of blind obedience.

gewusst: Rousseau wrote a great book about education, but put his own five children in a foundling home.
At times Rousseau earned money by copying out sheet music.
On St Peter's Island you can still visit the room today in which Rousseau lived.

teile.einleitung: “Seizure of power” (Machtergreifung) describes how Adolf Hitler and the National Socialists took power in Germany in 1933. Within a few months they abolished democracy. Germany became a dictatorship.
wichtigste: On 30 January 1933 Adolf Hitler was appointed Reich Chancellor.
After the Reichstag fire in February 1933 opponents were persecuted.
With the Enabling Act, from March 1933 the government could pass laws without parliament.
The SPD was the only party present to vote against it.
The secret police, the Gestapo, persecuted opponents of the regime.
With Gleichschaltung (coordination) the National Socialists brought associations, states and trade unions under their control.
On 10 May 1933 books were burned in public in many cities.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 1930s Germany was in a severe **economic crisis**, and many people were unemployed. The party of the National Socialists, the **NSDAP**, grew strong. On **30 January 1933** Reich President Paul von Hindenburg appointed **Adolf Hitler** as **Reich Chancellor**. Conservative politicians believed they could control Hitler. That was a grave mistake.

In **February 1933** the parliament building in Berlin, the **Reichstag**, burned down. The National Socialists used the fire to persecute their opponents. With an emergency decree, important **fundamental rights** such as freedom of speech were suspended. Thousands of communists, social democrats and other opponents were arrested. In 1933 the secret police, the **Gestapo**, was also created.

In **March 1933** the Reichstag voted on the **Enabling Act**. It allowed Hitler’s government to pass laws **without parliament**. The communist deputies had already been arrested or had fled. The **SPD** was the only party present to vote against it. Its chairman Otto Wels gave a courageous speech against the law.

After that the National Socialists brought everything under their control step by step. This is called **Gleichschaltung** (coordination). The states lost their independence, trade unions were dissolved, and all other parties were banned. Associations, newspapers and the radio also had to follow the party. On **10 May 1933** students and National Socialists publicly burned **books** by writers they rejected.

When Reich President Hindenburg died in August 1934, Hitler took over his office too. He now called himself **“Führer and Reich Chancellor”**. With that he had all the power in the state. Many people who were persecuted fled abroad, some also to **Switzerland**. The dictatorship later led to the Second World War and to the murder of millions of people.

gewusst: The National Socialists themselves used the word “Machtergreifung”; today people also often speak of “Machtübernahme” or “Machtübergabe”.
The writer Thomas Mann lived for some years after 1933 in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist. On a voyage round the world on the ship Beagle he observed animals and plants very closely. From this he developed his famous theory of how living things change over a long time.
wichtigste: Charles Darwin was born in England in 1809.
From 1831 to 1836 he travelled round the world on HMS Beagle.
On the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific he made important observations.
The Galápagos Islands belong to Ecuador.
In 1859 he published the book “On the Origin of Species”.
His theory is called evolution, and an important part of it is natural selection.

abschnitte.text: Charles Darwin was born in **England** in 1809. Even as a child he collected beetles and stones. From 1831 to 1836 he sailed round the world as a naturalist on the ship **HMS Beagle**. He visited South America, islands in the Pacific, Australia and Africa. Everywhere he collected plants, animals, stones and fossils.

In 1835 Darwin came to the **Galápagos Islands**. They lie in the **Pacific**, about 1,000 kilometres off the coast of South America, and belong to **Ecuador**. **Giant tortoises** live there. The islands are even named after them, because “galápago” is an old Spanish word for tortoise. There are also **marine iguanas** there, lizards that dive in the sea and eat algae.

On the islands Darwin noticed different **finches**. Depending on their food, they had differently shaped **beaks**. Some cracked hard seeds, others ate insects. Darwin asked himself how these differences came about. Today these birds are called **Darwin's finches**.

Darwin explained that animals and plants change over a very long time. This is called **evolution**. Living things with helpful features survive more often. They pass these features on to their **offspring**. He called this process **natural selection**. In this way new species can gradually come into being.

In 1859 Darwin published the book **On the Origin of Species**. It caused great arguments, because many people at the time believed that species could not change. Today evolution is an important foundation of **biology**. Darwin died in 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey in London.

gewusst: The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace came up with the idea of natural selection almost at the same time as Darwin.
Giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands can live to be over 100 years old.

teile.einleitung: A nuclear weapon, also called an atom bomb, is a weapon that gets its enormous explosive power from the energy of atomic nuclei. A single such bomb can destroy a whole city. Nuclear weapons have been used in war only twice, in 1945 against the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
wichtigste: Nuclear weapons use the splitting or fusion of atomic nuclei.
The Hiroshima bomb used uranium, the Nagasaki bomb plutonium.
On 29 August 1949 the Soviet Union detonated its first atom bomb.
In 1952 the USA tested the first hydrogen bomb, “Ivy Mike”.
The Soviet “Tsar Bomba” of 1961 had an explosive power of around 50 megatons of TNT.
The Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 is meant to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.
During the Cold War Switzerland considered having nuclear weapons of its own, but finally gave up the programme in 1988.

abschnitte.text: In **nuclear fission**, heavy atomic nuclei such as uranium or plutonium are split, and a huge amount of energy is released. That uranium can be split was discovered by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin at the end of 1938. A **hydrogen bomb** also fuses light nuclei and is much more powerful still. Explosive power is measured in tonnes of the explosive TNT; one megaton equals a million tonnes of TNT.

In the **Manhattan Project** the USA built the first atom bombs during the Second World War, tested on 16 July 1945 in New Mexico. On 6 August 1945 they dropped a uranium bomb on Hiroshima, and on 9 August a plutonium bomb on Nagasaki. By the end of 1945 well over 150,000 people had died in the two cities together. Many survivors suffered from the **radiation** for decades.

In 1949 the Soviet Union also had the atom bomb, and the USA's monopoly came to an end. In 1952 the USA tested the first hydrogen bomb, and in 1961 the Soviet Union detonated the “Tsar Bomba” of around 50 megatons. Britain, France and, on 16 October 1964, China followed. During the Cold War the superpowers built tens of thousands of warheads, which is called the **arms race**.

The limited **Test Ban Treaty** of 1963 banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water. The Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1 July 1968 is meant to prevent further states from getting nuclear weapons. Since 2021 there has also been a treaty banning nuclear weapons, but the nuclear powers have not joined it. Today nine states have nuclear weapons, together about 12,000 warheads (as of 2025).

After 1945 Switzerland considered whether it should build nuclear weapons of its own in order to defend itself. There were studies and plans, but a bomb was never built. In 1969 Switzerland signed the **Non-Proliferation Treaty**. In 1988 the programme was finally given up.

Many people believe that nuclear weapons prevent great wars, because any attacker would itself be destroyed; this is called **deterrence**. At the same time a nuclear war could threaten the whole of humanity. The Japanese organisation Nihon Hidankyo, founded by survivors of the atom bombs, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2024. It works for a world without nuclear weapons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus, which releases a great deal of energy.
A unit of explosive power, as strong as a million tonnes of the explosive TNT.
Invisible, dangerous radiation that is produced when atomic nuclei decay.
The idea that nobody attacks because they must fear a devastating counterstrike.

gewusst: The Tsar Bomba was more than 3,000 times as powerful as the Hiroshima bomb.
In Hiroshima the ruin of the Industrial Promotion Hall, the so-called Atomic Bomb Dome, still stands as a memorial.

teile.einleitung: Radio broadcasting is another way of saying radio. A transmitter sends sounds through the air with invisible radio waves, and a radio set receives them. That is how we hear music, news and stories.
wichtigste: Radio is also called broadcasting.
From 1895 Guglielmo Marconi carried out experiments with radio without cables.
In 1909 Marconi received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with Ferdinand Braun.
A radio needs an aerial to pick up the radio waves.
When the Titanic sank in 1912, its radio operator sent distress calls.
The national transmitter Beromünster broadcast for German-speaking Switzerland from 1931.

abschnitte.text: A **radio transmitter** turns sounds into invisible **radio waves**. These spread out all around in every direction. That is why it is called **broadcasting**. A radio set has an **aerial** that picks up the waves. The set turns them back into sounds that come out of the loudspeaker.

The Italian **Guglielmo Marconi** carried out experiments from **1895** to send messages through the air without wires. At first he sent only Morse signals over short distances, later even across the Atlantic. For his work he received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** in **1909**, together with the German **Ferdinand Braun**. At first it was mainly ships that used radio.

When the **Titanic** sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg, its radio operator sent **distress calls**. The ship “Carpathia” received them and came to help. In this way many people could be rescued. After that, radio became compulsory on large ships. In the 1920s regular radio programmes for everyone began in many countries.

In 1931 the **national transmitter Beromünster** in the canton of Lucerne began operating. For decades it was the most important station for **German-speaking Switzerland**. In the same year the **Sottens** transmitter for western Switzerland was added, and later **Monte Ceneri** for Ticino. In the Second World War many people abroad also listened to Beromünster to get independent news. Today people often listen to the radio digitally, over DAB+ or the internet.

gewusst: As early as 1922 one of the first radio stations in Europe was broadcasting in Lausanne.
In the past, the name Beromünster was printed on the tuning dial of many radio sets.

teile.einleitung: A trade union is an association of employees who work together for better pay and working conditions. Alone, a worker has little power against the boss, but together workers are stronger. Trade unions arose in the 19th century during industrialisation.
wichtigste: Trade unions work for fair pay, shorter working hours and safety at work.
The Swiss Federation of Trade Unions was founded in Olten in 1880.
The biggest trade union in Switzerland is Unia, which arose from a merger in 2004.
With the Peace Agreement of 19 July 1937, employers and employees in the engineering and metal industry gave up strikes and lockouts.
A collective labour agreement sets pay and working conditions for a whole sector.
Besides the socialist-influenced SGB, Christian trade unions also arose.
The strike is the trade unions' most important means of struggle.

abschnitte.text: A **trade union** is an association of employees, that is, of people who work for a business in return for pay. The members pay a fee and in return receive advice and support, for example in a dispute with their employer. Trade unions negotiate with employers about pay, holidays and working hours. On the other side are the employers' associations.

Trade unions arose in the 19th century, when long working hours and low pay were usual in factories. In Britain they appeared early, and there they are called trade unions. In Switzerland the **Swiss Federation of Trade Unions** (SGB) was founded in Olten in 1880. Many workers, however, wanted a representation that was not socialist and had a religious character, so **Christian trade unions** also arose.

When negotiations fail, trade unions can call a **strike**, in which workers stop work. Employers can respond with a **lockout** and temporarily shut the workers out of the business. In November 1918 the General Strike took place in Switzerland, in which around 250,000 people stopped work. Among other things, they demanded the 48-hour week and votes for women.

On 19 July 1937 the **Peace Agreement** was signed in the engineering and metal industry. For the employees' side the trade unionist Konrad Ilg signed. Both sides committed to an absolute **peace obligation**, that is, to giving up strikes and lockouts for the length of the agreement. Disputes were instead to be settled at the negotiating table, which still shapes Switzerland today.

A **collective labour agreement** (GAV) is a contract between employers and trade unions about pay and working conditions. It applies to many businesses in a sector, for example in construction or in hotels and restaurants. It sets out things such as minimum wages, the number of holiday days or working hours. The Federal Council can declare a GAV generally binding for a whole sector.

The biggest trade union in Switzerland is **Unia**, which arose in 2004 from the merger of several associations such as GBI and SMUV. There are also, for example, the transport staff union SEV and the umbrella organisation Travail.Suisse. The Federal Constitution of 1999 expressly guarantees the right to join together in trade unions and, under certain conditions, to strike. On 1 May, Labour Day, rallies take place in many towns and cities.

begriffe.erklaerung: Workers stop work together in order to push through demands.
The employer temporarily shuts workers out of the business.
A contract between trade unions and employers about pay and working conditions in a sector.
The agreement to settle disputes without strikes and lockouts.

gewusst: In international comparison there are very few strikes in Switzerland, which many explain by the Peace Agreement of 1937.
The German word “Streik” comes from the English “to strike”, which means, among other things, to hit or to lay down.
During the General Strike of 1918 the Federal Council used the army, and in Grenchen three young workers were shot dead.

teile.einleitung: Climate change is the warming of the Earth, which is caused above all by humans since industrialisation. Burning coal, oil and gas releases greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide into the air, and they hold back more heat. The consequences are melting glaciers, more heatwaves and rising sea levels, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide strengthen the Earth's natural greenhouse effect.
In 1988 the UN organisations WMO and UNEP founded the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
In 2007 the IPCC shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Al Gore.
In 1997 a protocol with binding targets for industrialised states was agreed in Kyoto.
The Paris Agreement of 2015 aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees, if possible at 1.5 degrees.
Under the Climate and Innovation Act, Switzerland aims to emit net zero greenhouse gases by 2050.
In 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Switzerland had violated the rights of the KlimaSeniorinnen.

abschnitte.text: Gases such as **carbon dioxide** (CO2) and methane act in the air like the glass of a greenhouse, which is called the **greenhouse effect**. Without it the Earth would be icy cold. Since industrialisation, however, the CO2 content of the air has risen sharply, from about 280 to over 420 parts per million. Worldwide it is now about 1.3 degrees warmer than before 1900 (as of 2025).

As early as 1896 the Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius calculated that more CO2 would warm the Earth. Today the **IPCC** gathers the knowledge of thousands of researchers. It was founded in 1988 by the WMO and UNEP. Its reports show clearly that humans are the main cause of today's warming.

In Switzerland it has become almost 3 degrees warmer since measurements began, so more than the worldwide average. The **glaciers** are melting fast; in 2022 and 2023 together they lost about a tenth of their ice. There are more hot days and less snow at low altitudes. Debris flows and rockfalls can also become more frequent when the permafrost thaws.

The **Kyoto Protocol** of 1997 obliged industrialised states for the first time to emit fewer greenhouse gases. The Paris Agreement of 2015 came into force on 4 November 2016 and applies to almost all states in the world. The USA left in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and left again in 2026. Every year the states meet at a **climate conference**.

On 18 June 2023 the Swiss electorate accepted the Climate and Innovation Act. It sets the goal of **net zero** greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. On 9 April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights decided in the case of the **KlimaSeniorinnen** that Switzerland had done too little for climate protection and had thereby violated a human right. It was the first such climate ruling by this court.

Above all it is important to burn less coal, oil and gas and to use more **renewable energy** such as sun, wind and water. Well insulated houses, heat pumps and electric cars help with this. Every person can, for example, cycle and take the train, eat less meat and use things for longer. Since 2018 many young people have also taken to the streets at the climate strike.

begriffe.erklaerung: Warming of the Earth because gases in the air hold back heat.
A gas produced when coal, oil, gas and wood are burned, CO2 for short.
No more CO2 is emitted than is removed from the air again.
Ground in the mountains that stays frozen all year round.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which gathers the knowledge about climate change.

gewusst: The Rhone Glacier is partly covered with white sheets in summer so that it melts more slowly.
The year 2024 was the warmest worldwide since measurements began.

teile.einleitung: The decolonisation of Africa means the path of the African countries from colonial rule to independence. Mainly between 1957 and the 1970s almost all colonies in Africa became states of their own. Some won freedom peacefully through negotiations, others only after bloody wars.
wichtigste: At the Berlin Conference of 1884/85 European powers set rules for the division of Africa.
In 1945 the Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester demanded the end of colonialism.
In 1957 the Gold Coast became Ghana, the first independent colony in sub-Saharan Africa.
In 1960 seventeen African colonies became independent, which is why it is called the “Year of Africa”.
The Congo became independent from Belgium on 30 June 1960.
Algeria won its independence from 1954 to 1962 in a war against France.
Switzerland helped to mediate at the Évian Accords, which ended the Algerian War in 1962.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 19th century European states divided up almost the whole of Africa among themselves. At the **Berlin Conference** of 1884/85 they set rules for this division, without Africans being allowed to have a say. Britain and France owned the largest territories, but Belgium, Portugal, Germany, Italy and Spain also had **colonies**. Only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed largely independent. The borders were often drawn with a ruler and split peoples or forced hostile groups together.

In the Second World War many Africans fought for the colonial powers and afterwards demanded more rights. The Fifth **Pan-African Congress** demanded the end of colonialism in 1945 in Manchester. Educated Africans founded parties and movements for independence. At the same time the colonial powers were weakened after the war, and the USA and the Soviet Union rejected colonies. The newly founded United Nations also stood up for the right of peoples to decide their own future.

abschnitte.titel: Ghana and the Year of Africa
abschnitte.text: In 1957 the British Gold Coast became independent under the name **Ghana**, the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to do so. Its leader **Kwame Nkrumah** later warned of “neocolonialism”: even after independence Africa remained economically dependent on the rich countries. In 1958 Guinea, as the only French colony, voted against staying in the French Community and became independent at once. In 1960 seventeen African countries gained independence, among them Nigeria, Senegal and Madagascar, which is why it is called the **Year of Africa**. In February 1960 the British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan declared in his “Wind of Change” speech that Britain recognised African nationalism.

The **Congo** became independent from Belgium on 30 June 1960. The Belgians had hardly trained any local people, and soon unrest and breakaway attempts broke out, for example in the raw-material-rich province of Katanga. The first prime minister, **Patrice Lumumba**, was removed from office and murdered in Katanga in January 1961. The Congo crisis showed how hard a new beginning could be, also because the great powers meddled in it during the Cold War.

abschnitte.titel: The Algerian War and the role of Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In **Algeria** about a million European settlers lived, and France regarded the country as part of France. From 1954 to 1962 the liberation front **FLN** fought a bloody war for independence. Switzerland acted as a go-between and organised secret preliminary talks between France and the FLN. In March 1962 the **Évian Accords** were signed in Évian on Lake Geneva. On 5 July 1962 Algeria declared its independence.

The Portuguese colonies such as Angola and Mozambique only became free in 1975, after long wars and the fall of the dictatorship in Portugal. Zimbabwe followed in 1980 and Namibia in 1990. In South Africa **apartheid**, the rule of the white minority, only ended in 1994 with the election of Nelson Mandela as president. In 1963 the African states founded the Organisation of African Unity, which became the **African Union** in 2002. Today Africa has 54 recognised independent states.

begriffe.erklaerung: A territory that is ruled and exploited by a foreign state.
The process in which colonies become independent states.
The economic dependence of former colonies on rich countries after independence.
The idea that all Africans belong together and should work together.

gewusst: Ghana took its name from an old West African kingdom that existed over a thousand years ago.
Many national borders in Africa are dead straight, because they were drawn on maps in Europe.
Évian lies directly opposite Lausanne, and the Algerian delegation stayed in Switzerland during the negotiations.

teile.einleitung: The Wright brothers were two American inventors. On 17 December 1903 they achieved the first controlled powered flight in an aeroplane that was heavier than air.
wichtigste: The brothers were called Orville and Wilbur Wright.
They lived and worked in Dayton, Ohio, and had a bicycle shop.
Their first powered aeroplane was called the Flyer.
The first powered flight took place on 17 December 1903 near Kitty Hawk.
Orville was at the controls on the first successful flight.
The flight lasted about 12 seconds and covered about 37 metres.
They learned a great deal from the German flight pioneer Otto Lilienthal.

abschnitte.text: **Wilbur** and **Orville Wright** grew up in the USA. In **Dayton** in the state of Ohio they had a **bicycle shop**. They sold and repaired bicycles and also built their own. They paid for their flying experiments with the money. In their workshop they first built **gliders** and later an aeroplane with an engine. From building bicycles they knew a lot about light and stable structures.

Even before the Wrights, the German **Otto Lilienthal** flew from 1891 in **gliders** he had built himself, without an engine. The Wright brothers learned a lot from his experiments. They realised that an aeroplane has to be easy to **steer** in the air. So they developed a technique that let them twist the wings slightly. They also built a small **wind tunnel** to test wing shapes.

Their first powered aeroplane was called the **Flyer**. It had two wings, one above the other, and a small engine that drove two propellers. On **17 December 1903** they flew near **Kitty Hawk** in North Carolina. To be exact, they took off from the hills of **Kill Devil Hills**. **Orville** lay on the aeroplane at the controls, while Wilbur ran alongside. The flight lasted about **12 seconds** and covered about **37 metres**, shorter than a football pitch.

The brothers were looking for a place with **steady wind** so that their aeroplane could take off more easily. The **sand dunes** on the Atlantic coast also offered soft places to land. That is why they travelled there from Dayton. On the same day they flew three more times, and each flight was longer. The longest lasted almost a minute. This began the age of **powered flight**.

gewusst: The Wrights' first flight was shorter than the wingspan of some of today's passenger planes.
A piece of fabric from the wing of the first Flyer flew to the Moon with Apollo 11 in 1969.

teile.einleitung: Deng Xiaoping was a Chinese politician. From 1978 he was the most powerful man in China and began great economic reforms that changed the country greatly.
wichtigste: Deng Xiaoping lived from 1904 to 1997.
From 1978 he began the policy of reform and opening up.
In 1980 Shenzhen became one of the first special economic zones.
His programme was called the “Four Modernisations”.
For Hong Kong he developed the principle “One country, two systems”.
In 1989 the leadership around Deng had the democracy movement put down by force.
With his Southern Tour in 1992 he pushed the reforms further forward.

abschnitte.text: Deng Xiaoping was born in 1904 in the province of Sichuan. While still young he became a member of the **Communist Party**. Under Mao Zedong he held important posts. During the **Cultural Revolution** he lost his posts several times and was sent to the countryside. After Mao's death in 1976 he returned. In December 1978 he won through in the party leadership with his **course of reform**.

Deng wanted China to become economically strong. He carried out the **Four Modernisations**: agriculture, industry, defence, and science and technology. Farmers were allowed to sell part of their harvest themselves. Step by step China opened up to the **market** and to foreign countries. His saying is well known: “It does not matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice.” It means that success matters more than ideology.

From 1980 China set up **special economic zones**. There simpler rules applied for firms from abroad. One of the first was **Shenzhen**, which borders directly on Hong Kong. Foreign money and knowledge were meant to come into the country in this way. The small town became a huge metropolis with millions of inhabitants.

Hong Kong was for a long time a British colony. For its return Deng developed the principle **“One country, two systems”**. In 1984 China and Britain agreed on it. After the return in 1997 Hong Kong was to keep its own **economic and legal system** for 50 years. Deng died in February 1997, a few months before the handover.

Economically Deng opened China up, but politically the party stayed alone in power. In spring 1989 mainly students demonstrated in **Tiananmen Square** in Beijing for reforms and freedom of speech. On **4 June 1989** the leadership around Deng had the army step in, and many people were killed. Afterwards the reforms stalled. With his **Southern Tour** in 1992 Deng called for the opening of the market to be speeded up.

gewusst: Deng Xiaoping was never head of state or party leader, yet for years he was regarded as the most powerful politician in China.
As a young man Deng lived in France for several years. There he studied and also worked in factories.

teile.einleitung: The Gotthard Tunnel is the old railway tunnel of the Gotthard Railway between Göschenen in the canton of Uri and Airolo in Ticino. At about 15 kilometres it was the longest tunnel in the world when it opened in 1882. Its construction is among the greatest achievements, but also among the saddest chapters, of Swiss history.
wichtigste: The Gotthard Tunnel is about 15 kilometres long and links Göschenen with Airolo.
It was built from 1872 to 1882, and the breakthrough came on 29 February 1880.
The construction manager was the Geneva contractor Louis Favre, who died in the tunnel in 1879.
Italy and Germany helped finance it, alongside Switzerland.
During the strike in Göschenen in 1875, a police unit fired into the crowd, and four workers died.
Since 2016 there has been the Gotthard Base Tunnel, about 57 kilometres long.
For cars there is also the Gotthard Road Tunnel of 1980.

abschnitte.titel: A tunnel through the Gotthard massif
abschnitte.text: The Gotthard Tunnel lies under the **Gotthard massif** in the Central Alps. It is also called the **summit tunnel**, because it lies high up on the mountain line. Its north portal is in Göschenen at about 1,100 metres, and its south portal in Airolo. The tunnel is the centrepiece of the Gotthard Railway, which opened in full in 1882.

The Geneva contractor **Louis Favre** won the contract to build the tunnel and promised to finish it in only eight years. From 1872 workers dug at the same time from the north and the south. In 1879 Favre died of heart failure during an inspection in the tunnel. On 29 February 1880 the two galleries met, and the deviation was only a few centimetres.

For the construction, new **drilling machines** driven by compressed air were used. The compressed air was produced with water power from the rivers Reuss and Ticino. Blasting was done with **dynamite**, which Alfred Nobel had invented a few years earlier. The rubble was taken out in small wagons, some of them pulled by horses.

In the tunnel it was often over 30 degrees hot, and the air was full of dust and blasting fumes. Most of the workers came from Italy, and about 200 of them died in accidents. Many more fell ill, for example with a worm disease. In July 1875 the workers in Göschenen went on strike; a police unit fired into the crowd and four workers died.

Besides the railway tunnel there are now more tunnels through the Gotthard. The **Gotthard Road Tunnel** for cars opened in 1980 and is just under 17 kilometres long. Since 2016 the roughly 57 kilometre long **Gotthard Base Tunnel** has been in operation, passing under the massif much lower down. A second tube is currently being built for the road tunnel.

The Gotthard Tunnel made Switzerland an important transit country between northern and southern Europe. Journeys from Zurich to Milan suddenly took only hours instead of days. The **Gotthard** became a symbol of cohesion and Swiss engineering. Beside Airolo station, a monument by Vincenzo Vela recalls the victims of the work.

teile.einleitung: The women's movement is the work of women and men for equal rights for women in politics, education, work and family life. It began over 200 years ago and has changed the world greatly. In Switzerland, the fight for the right to vote took especially long.
wichtigste: Mary Wollstonecraft published “A Vindication of the Rights of Woman” in 1792.
At the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848, the Declaration of Sentiments was adopted.
In 1893 New Zealand became the first country to introduce a general right for women to vote; in Europe, Finland followed in 1906.
Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903.
Simone de Beauvoir and Betty Friedan shaped the second wave of the women's movement with their books.
In Switzerland, men rejected votes for women in 1959, with about 67 per cent voting No.
Swiss women only gained the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971.

abschnitte.text: During the French Revolution, brave women demanded the same rights as men. The Frenchwoman Olympe de Gouges wrote a declaration of the rights of woman in 1791. The Englishwoman **Mary Wollstonecraft** published “A Vindication of the Rights of Woman” in 1792. Above all, she demanded that girls should be educated just as well as boys.

In 1848, around 300 people met in Seneca Falls in the US state of New York for the first big women's rights convention. It was organised by **Elizabeth Cady Stanton** and Lucretia Mott, among others. There the **Declaration of Sentiments** was adopted, which demanded equal rights for women. Many of the women taking part also fought against slavery.

In 1893 New Zealand became the first country to introduce a general right for women to vote; in Europe, Finland was the first country in 1906. In Britain, Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903, and its members were called **suffragettes**. They demonstrated loudly, went to prison and went on hunger strike. In 1918 women aged 30 and over were allowed to vote in Britain, and in the USA the 19th Amendment to the Constitution has guaranteed women's right to vote since 1920.

After the Second World War, it was no longer just about the vote but about equality in everyday life. The Frenchwoman **Simone de Beauvoir** wrote “The Second Sex” in 1949. The book “The Feminine Mystique” by Betty Friedan, from 1963, is seen as the starting point of the **second wave** in the USA. Now the issues were equal pay, jobs, education and the role of women in the family.

In Switzerland, women's associations appeared around 1900, and in 1909 a national association for women's suffrage was founded. In 1958 the lawyer **Iris von Roten** started fierce debates with her book “Frauen im Laufgitter” (“Women in the Playpen”). In 1959 Swiss men rejected votes for women, with about 67 per cent voting No. Only on 7 February 1971 did they say Yes, and in 1990 the Federal Supreme Court forced the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden to introduce votes for women at cantonal level too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right of women to take part in votes and elections.

gewusst: Switzerland was one of the last countries in Europe to introduce votes for women at national level.
The suffragette Emily Davison died in 1913 after running onto the track at the Epsom horse race.
Even before 1971, women in some Swiss cantons, such as Vaud and Neuchâtel, were allowed to vote at cantonal level.
